Are Dental Implants Safe After an Organ Transplant?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

For many people who have undergone an organ transplant, the idea of restoring a confident, functional smile with dental implants is an understandably appealing prospect. However, it is also a question that quite naturally gives rise to concern. If you have had a kidney, liver, heart, or other organ transplant, you may be wondering whether dental implants after organ transplant are a viable and safe option for you.

This is one of the most common questions patients with complex medical histories bring to dental consultations — and it is a very sensible one to ask. Organ transplant recipients face unique clinical considerations, particularly around immunosuppressive medications, infection risk, and bone healing capacity. Each of these factors can have a meaningful bearing on how the body responds to a surgical dental procedure.

This article aims to provide clear, balanced, and educational information to help you understand the key clinical considerations involved. It is not a substitute for personalised dental advice, but it can help you ask the right questions when you speak with your dental team.

Can You Have Dental Implants After an Organ Transplant?

Dental implants after organ transplant may be possible for some patients, but careful clinical assessment is essential. Immunosuppressive medications can affect healing, infection risk, and bone integration. Suitability depends on transplant stability, medication regime, and overall health. A detailed dental assessment by an appropriately qualified clinician, ideally in liaison with your transplant team, is always required before treatment proceeds.

Understanding the Relationship Between Organ Transplants and Dental Health

Organ transplantation is a life-changing procedure, and for many recipients, it marks the beginning of a new chapter. However, it also introduces long-term medical management that can significantly affect overall health — including oral health.

Transplant recipients are typically prescribed immunosuppressive medications to prevent organ rejection. These drugs work by reducing the activity of the immune system, which is necessary to stop the body attacking the new organ. However, a suppressed immune system also means a reduced ability to fight infection, which is directly relevant when considering any form of surgical dental treatment.

Additionally, some immunosuppressive medications — particularly ciclosporin — are associated with gingival overgrowth, a condition where the gum tissue becomes enlarged and can create pockets where bacteria accumulate. This makes maintaining excellent oral hygiene both more challenging and more important for transplant recipients.

Certain medications may also affect bone density over time, which is a key factor when assessing whether the jawbone can adequately support a dental implant. Understanding these interconnected factors is why a thorough and personalised clinical assessment is always the necessary starting point.

What Are Dental Implants and How Do They Work?

Dental implants are small titanium posts that are surgically placed into the jawbone to act as artificial tooth roots. Once the implant has integrated with the surrounding bone — a natural biological process called osseointegration — a custom-made crown, bridge, or denture can be attached to restore the appearance and function of missing teeth.

The success of dental implants depends on a number of biological factors, including:

  • Sufficient bone volume and density to support the implant post
  • Healthy gum tissue free from active infection or disease
  • The body's capacity to heal following a minor surgical procedure
  • Absence of systemic conditions that could interfere with osseointegration

For patients in good general health, dental implants have a well-established track record as a reliable tooth replacement option. However, for those with complex medical histories — such as organ transplant recipients — each of these factors requires additional clinical scrutiny before treatment can be considered appropriate.

You can learn more about how the dental implant procedure works and what to expect at each stage of treatment.

Clinical Considerations for Transplant Recipients Considering Implants

For organ transplant recipients, the decision to proceed with dental implants involves a careful, multi-disciplinary approach. The following are among the most clinically significant considerations:

Immunosuppression and Infection Risk

Because immunosuppressive medications reduce the body's natural defences, the risk of post-surgical infection may be elevated. Infections following implant placement, if not identified and treated promptly, can have serious consequences for overall health. This is why pre-operative screening, meticulous surgical technique, and appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis are considered on an individual basis.

Osseointegration and Healing

The process of osseointegration — where the titanium implant fuses with the jawbone — requires normal bone metabolism and healing responses. Some immunosuppressive medications and corticosteroids can interfere with bone healing and affect the long-term stability of implants. If you are currently taking these medicines, this guide on dental implants while on immunosuppressant medication provides useful additional context.

Medication Interactions

Some anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications taken by transplant recipients may affect bleeding during and after surgery. The dental team must be aware of the full medication list before any surgical procedure is carried out.

Transplant Stability

Research and clinical guidance generally suggest that dental implant procedures should be considered only once the transplant organ is stable and the medication regime is well established. In the period immediately following transplantation — typically within the first one to two years — the immune system is often most significantly suppressed, and elective surgical procedures are generally avoided.

The Importance of Multi-Disciplinary Communication

One of the most important principles in managing dental care for organ transplant recipients is communication between the dental team and the patient's transplant or specialist medical team. This collaborative approach ensures that:

  • The current level of immunosuppression is understood
  • Any necessary adjustments to medication (such as antibiotic prophylaxis) are agreed upon prior to treatment
  • The transplant team is fully informed of any planned dental surgical procedures
  • Overall health status is assessed to determine whether the timing of treatment is appropriate

Patients should always inform their dentist of their full medical history, including details of the transplanted organ, the date of transplantation, and all current medications. This information is essential for safe and appropriate clinical planning.

If you are considering tooth replacement options and have a complex medical history, speaking with an experienced dental team in full-mouth reconstruction planning can be a helpful first step.

Oral Health Considerations Specific to Transplant Recipients

Maintaining excellent oral health is particularly important for organ transplant recipients — not just as a precondition for potential future implant treatment, but as a matter of general systemic wellbeing.

There is a recognised body of evidence suggesting that poor oral health, particularly untreated periodontal (gum) disease, may have implications for systemic health. For individuals with suppressed immune systems, an untreated source of oral infection is a concern that warrants prompt attention.

Transplant recipients should be aware of the following oral health considerations:

  • Gingival overgrowth: As mentioned earlier, certain medications such as ciclosporin can cause the gums to enlarge. Regular professional cleaning and careful oral hygiene can help manage this condition.
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia): Some medications can reduce saliva flow, which increases the risk of tooth decay and gum disease.
  • Oral ulceration: Immunosuppression can make the mouth more susceptible to ulcers or opportunistic infections such as oral thrush (candidiasis).
  • Increased caries risk: A combination of dry mouth, dietary changes, and reduced immune function can elevate the risk of dental decay.

Regular dental check-ups — ideally every three to six months for higher-risk patients — are particularly valuable in this context.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

There are several situations in which organ transplant recipients should seek professional dental advice without delay. These include:

  • Signs of gum infection such as persistent redness, swelling, tenderness, or bleeding of the gums
  • Toothache or dental pain that does not resolve within a day or two
  • Loose teeth or changes in the way your teeth fit together
  • Swelling in the face, jaw, or neck that may indicate a spreading infection
  • Mouth sores or ulcers that do not heal within two weeks
  • Difficulty eating or chewing due to dental discomfort or tooth loss

It is worth noting that transplant recipients may not always experience typical signs of infection in the same way as immunocompetent individuals, due to their suppressed immune response. This is another reason why regular professional monitoring is so important — issues can sometimes progress with fewer obvious symptoms.

If you have not had a dental check-up recently or have concerns about your oral health, arranging a consultation with a dental professional is a sensible course of action.

Prevention and Oral Health Maintenance for Transplant Recipients

Proactive oral health care is one of the most effective strategies for transplant recipients who wish to maintain good dental health and remain potential candidates for restorative treatment in the future. The following practical steps are widely recommended:

  • Brush twice daily using a fluoride toothpaste, taking care to clean along the gumline
  • Clean between teeth daily using interdental brushes or floss to remove plaque from areas a toothbrush cannot reach
  • Use a fluoride mouthwash if recommended by your dental team, to help reduce decay risk
  • Stay well hydrated and consider sugar-free chewing gum to stimulate saliva production if dry mouth is a concern
  • Limit sugary foods and drinks, particularly between meals, to reduce the risk of dental decay
  • Attend regular dental check-ups — the frequency will be guided by your dentist based on your individual risk profile
  • Inform your dentist of any changes to your medication or medical status at every appointment

Being proactive about oral health before and after a transplant not only protects your teeth and gums but also reduces the likelihood of oral infection that could have wider implications for your health.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants after organ transplant may be possible for some patients, but clinical suitability must be assessed on an individual basis.
  • Immunosuppressive medications can affect healing, increase infection risk, and impact bone integration — all of which are clinically relevant to implant placement.
  • Multi-disciplinary communication between your dental team and transplant team is essential before any surgical dental procedure is undertaken.
  • Transplant stability is an important factor; implant treatment is generally not considered in the early post-transplant period when immunosuppression is at its most significant.
  • Regular dental maintenance is especially important for transplant recipients to manage medication-related oral health changes and reduce infection risk.
  • Early professional assessment of any dental symptoms or concerns is advisable, given that infection signs may be less pronounced in immunosuppressed individuals.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long after an organ transplant can I consider dental implants?

There is no universal timeframe, as individual clinical circumstances vary considerably. However, clinical guidance generally suggests that elective surgical dental procedures are typically deferred until the transplanted organ is stable and the immunosuppressive regimen is well established — often at least one to two years post-transplant. Your dental team will need to liaise with your transplant specialist to determine whether the timing is appropriate for you personally.

Do I need to take antibiotics before dental implant surgery if I have had an organ transplant?

Whether antibiotic prophylaxis is required depends on your individual medication regime, the level of immunosuppression, and guidance from your transplant team. This is not a blanket recommendation — it is a decision made on a case-by-case basis in consultation with your medical and dental teams. Always ensure your dentist is fully aware of your medical history before any treatment.

Can immunosuppressant drugs cause dental implants to fail?

Some immunosuppressive medications and corticosteroids may affect bone metabolism and the body's capacity to heal, which can have an impact on the osseointegration process. However, this does not mean implants will inevitably fail in transplant recipients — rather, it means that careful pre-treatment assessment and monitoring are particularly important. Outcomes in appropriately selected patients with well-managed transplants may be positive in some cases, though long-term clinical evidence in this specific population remains limited and results will vary between individuals.

Are there alternatives to dental implants for tooth replacement if I have had a transplant?

Yes. Depending on individual clinical circumstances, options such as dental bridges or removable partial or full dentures may be appropriate alternatives to dental implants. These options do not require surgical intervention and may be suitable for patients for whom implant surgery carries elevated risk. Your dental team can discuss which tooth replacement options are most appropriate following a full clinical assessment.

How does gum disease affect my suitability for dental implants after a transplant?

Active gum disease (periodontal disease) is generally considered a contraindication to dental implant placement for any patient. For transplant recipients, the presence of gum disease is of particular concern, both because it can compromise implant outcomes and because it represents an active source of infection that may have broader health implications. Successful treatment of any existing gum disease would typically need to be completed and stable before implant treatment could be considered. You can find further information about implant maintenance and gum health and how it relates to implant suitability.

Should I see an experienced dentist if I have had an organ transplant and need dental treatment?

Seeing an experienced dental team familiar with medically complex patients is advisable. A dentist with experience in implant treatment for medically complex patients will be better placed to liaise with your transplant team, interpret your medications, and plan treatment safely. Open communication between all members of your healthcare team is important. Treatment suitability and outcomes will depend on your individual clinical circumstances and must be assessed during a formal clinical consultation.

Conclusion

Understanding whether dental implants after organ transplant are a suitable option is a nuanced question that requires careful individual assessment rather than a generalised answer. The good news is that, for some transplant recipients whose health is stable and whose transplant team is in agreement, dental implant treatment may indeed be a realistic possibility. However, the clinical landscape is complex, and the unique factors involved — including immunosuppression, medication interactions, bone health, and infection risk — mean that a thorough and personalised approach is always essential.

What is clear is that maintaining excellent oral health is a priority for all organ transplant recipients, regardless of whether dental implants are under consideration. Regular professional dental monitoring, attentive daily oral hygiene, and prompt attention to any new symptoms all contribute meaningfully to both oral and systemic wellbeing.

If you have had an organ transplant and are exploring your options for tooth replacement, the most important first step is an open conversation with a qualified dental professional who can review your full medical history and work collaboratively with your transplant team. If you also manage cardiovascular risk factors, this guide on dental implants with high blood pressure may help you prepare focused consultation questions.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

Are Dental Implants Safe During an MRI Scan?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Many patients with dental implants feel anxious when their doctor recommends an MRI scan. This concern is understandable, as people often worry about how metal implants might interact with the powerful magnetic fields used during magnetic resonance imaging. The uncertainty can cause patients to delay necessary medical investigations or feel stressed about upcoming scans.

Understanding the relationship between dental implants and MRI safety is important for anyone who has received implant treatment or is considering this tooth replacement option. Modern dental implants are typically made from titanium, which has specific properties that affect their behaviour during medical imaging procedures.

This article will explain the safety considerations surrounding dental implants and MRI scans, helping you understand what to expect if you need medical imaging. We'll explore the materials used in implant construction, how they interact with MRI machines, and what steps you might need to take before your scan. Professional dental assessment can provide personalised guidance based on your specific implant type and medical imaging requirements.

Are Dental Implants Safe During MRI Scans?

Yes, modern dental implants made from titanium are generally considered safe during MRI scans. Titanium is non-ferromagnetic, meaning it won't be attracted to the MRI's magnetic field or cause dangerous movement within your mouth.

Understanding Dental Implant Materials

Most contemporary dental implants are manufactured from commercially pure titanium or titanium alloy. These materials were specifically chosen for dental applications due to their excellent biocompatibility and their non-magnetic properties. Titanium integrates well with bone tissue through a process called osseointegration, making it an ideal material for permanent tooth replacement.

The non-ferromagnetic nature of titanium means that dental implants are not expected to be pulled or moved by the powerful magnetic fields generated during MRI scanning. This characteristic distinguishes titanium implants from ferromagnetic materials like iron or steel, which could potentially be dangerous during MRI procedures.

However, whilst titanium implants are safe during MRI scans, they can still cause image distortion or artefacts on the scan results. These artefacts appear as dark areas or distorted regions around the implant site, which may obscure nearby anatomical structures in the images.

How MRI Technology Interacts with Implants

Magnetic resonance imaging uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of internal body structures. When ferromagnetic materials are present, they can be attracted to the MRI machine's magnet, potentially causing movement or heating. Titanium dental implants, being non-ferromagnetic, don't experience this attraction.

The interaction between titanium implants and MRI fields primarily results in image quality issues rather than safety concerns. The metal can cause signal loss and create dark spots or streaking on the resulting images. This effect is most noticeable when the area being scanned is close to the implant location.

Different MRI sequences and imaging parameters can influence the extent of artefacts caused by dental implants. Radiologists and MRI technologists may need to adjust scanning protocols or use specialised sequences to minimise image distortion and obtain the clearest possible diagnostic images.

Preparing for an MRI with Dental Implants

Before your MRI appointment, inform the medical team about your dental implants. This information helps them prepare appropriate scanning protocols and set realistic expectations about potential image quality in certain areas. You should provide details about when your implants were placed and, if possible, information about the specific implant system used.

The MRI facility may request documentation from your dentist confirming the implant materials and their MRI compatibility. Most modern implant systems are well-documented as MRI-safe, but older implants or those from certain manufacturers might require specific verification.

During the scanning procedure, you won't need to remove dental implants, as they're permanently integrated into your jawbone. The scanning process should feel no different from a standard MRI, with no additional sensations or discomfort related to your dental implants.

Potential Image Quality Considerations

Whilst dental implants don't pose safety risks during MRI scanning, they can affect the quality and interpretability of images in surrounding areas. The extent of image distortion depends on several factors, including the implant size, location, and the specific body area being examined.

For head and neck MRI scans, dental implants may create more noticeable artefacts due to their proximity to the imaging area. However, modern MRI technology includes various techniques to minimise these effects, and experienced radiologists are skilled at interpreting images that contain implant-related artefacts.

If the diagnostic area of interest is far from your dental implants, such as during a knee or abdominal MRI, the implants are unlikely to significantly impact image quality. The magnetic field effects of small titanium dental implants typically remain localised to the immediate surrounding area.

Alternative Imaging Options

In situations where dental implants might significantly compromise MRI image quality for critical diagnostic areas, alternative imaging methods may be considered. These might include CT scans, ultrasound, or X-rays, depending on the clinical requirements and the body system being examined.

Your medical team will determine the most appropriate imaging method based on your specific clinical needs, the location of your dental implants, and the diagnostic information required. In many cases, MRI remains the preferred imaging method despite the presence of dental implants, as the diagnostic benefits outweigh the image quality concerns.

Dental implant consultations can help you understand your specific implant specifications and provide documentation that may be useful for future medical imaging requirements.

When to Seek Professional Advice

If you have concerns about upcoming MRI scans and your dental implants, discuss these with both your medical doctor and your dental team. Your dentist can provide specific information about your implant materials and their MRI compatibility, whilst your medical team can explain how the implants might affect your particular scan.

Patients with older dental work or implants placed many years ago should pay particular attention to material verification, as some older restorative materials might contain ferromagnetic components. Modern implant placement follows strict material safety standards, but historical variations in dental materials mean that professional verification is always prudent.

Any unusual symptoms following dental implant placement, such as persistent pain, swelling, or changes in implant stability, warrant professional dental assessment regardless of MRI considerations.

Maintaining Oral Health with Implants

Proper oral hygiene remains essential for patients with dental implants, particularly as good overall health may reduce the need for certain medical investigations. Regular dental check-ups help ensure implant stability and surrounding tissue health, whilst also maintaining accurate records of your dental work.

Professional dental cleaning around implants requires specific techniques and instruments to avoid damage to the implant surface or surrounding tissues. Your dental hygienist can demonstrate appropriate home care methods and recommend suitable products for implant maintenance.

Good oral health practices, including effective plaque control and regular professional monitoring, contribute to long-term implant success and may help avoid complications that could require medical imaging for diagnosis.

Key Points to Remember

  • Modern titanium dental implants are generally safe during MRI scans due to their non-ferromagnetic properties
  • Image quality may be affected by artefacts, but this doesn't compromise safety
  • Always inform medical teams about your dental implants before MRI appointments
  • Documentation from your dentist about implant materials can be helpful
  • Alternative imaging methods are available if MRI quality is significantly compromised
  • Regular dental care helps maintain implant health and accurate medical records

Frequently Asked Questions

Can dental implants be damaged by MRI machines?

MRI machines are not expected to damage modern titanium dental implants. The magnetic fields used in MRI scanning do not typically affect titanium implants or cause structural changes to the implant or surrounding bone. However, individual implant specifications vary and your dental team can confirm the specific properties of your implants.

Will I feel anything unusual during an MRI if I have dental implants?

Most patients do not experience unusual sensations related to their dental implants during an MRI scan. The scanning procedure typically feels the same as it would for someone without implants. No significant heating, movement, or discomfort is generally associated with the interaction between titanium implants and MRI magnetic fields, though individual experiences may vary.

How much do dental implants affect MRI image quality?

The impact on image quality varies depending on the scan location and implant position. For areas close to the implants, there may be some image distortion or dark spots. However, for scans of distant body parts, dental implants typically have minimal effect on diagnostic image quality.

Do I need special preparation for an MRI if I have multiple dental implants?

The preparation process remains the same regardless of how many dental implants you have. Simply inform the medical team about all your dental work, including the approximate number and location of implants. Multiple implants don't create additional safety concerns, though they might cause more extensive image artefacts in the oral and facial region.

Should I delay getting dental implants if I need regular MRI scans?

Having regular MRI scans isn't a reason to avoid dental implant treatment. Modern implants are designed to be compatible with medical imaging requirements. Discuss your medical imaging needs with your dentist during treatment planning to ensure you have appropriate documentation for future scans.

Can dental implant crowns or bridges cause problems during MRI scans?

The crowns or bridges attached to dental implants are typically made from ceramic or other non-ferromagnetic materials that are also MRI-safe. However, some older dental work might contain metal alloys that could cause image artefacts. Your dentist can provide specific information about all materials used in your dental restorations.

Conclusion

Understanding the relationship between dental implants and MRI safety helps alleviate common patient concerns about medical imaging procedures. Modern titanium dental implants are generally considered safe during MRI scans, with the primary consideration being potential image quality effects rather than safety risks.

Effective communication between your dental and medical teams ensures appropriate preparation and realistic expectations for any required imaging procedures. Maintaining detailed records of your dental work, including implant specifications and materials, supports both your ongoing dental care and any future medical imaging requirements.

Good oral health practices and regular dental monitoring contribute to long-term implant success whilst supporting your overall health and wellbeing. Professional guidance can address specific concerns about your individual circumstances and help coordinate care between your dental and medical healthcare providers.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

Disclaimer: This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

Patient Education 29 Jul 2026 13 min read

Are Dental Implants Safe for People With Ankylosing Spondylitis?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you live with ankylosing spondylitis (AS) and are considering dental implants to replace missing teeth, it is entirely natural to wonder whether the procedure is appropriate for your situation. Many people with autoimmune or inflammatory conditions search online for guidance before speaking with a dental professional — wanting to understand potential risks before committing to any treatment.

Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic inflammatory condition that primarily affects the spine and joints, but it can have implications for oral health too. From the medications used to manage AS to changes in bone density and immune function, there are several factors a dental team will consider when assessing implant suitability.

This article aims to provide clear, balanced educational information about dental implants and ankylosing spondylitis. It covers what AS is, how it may interact with implant treatment, the questions you should raise with your clinician, and when a professional dental assessment would be appropriate. It is not a substitute for personalised clinical advice.

Dental implants may be a suitable tooth replacement option for people with ankylosing spondylitis, but individual suitability depends on a thorough clinical assessment. Factors including bone quality, disease activity, medication use — particularly biologic drugs or bisphosphonates — and immune health all influence whether dental implants are appropriate. A qualified dental professional will evaluate each case individually.

What Is Ankylosing Spondylitis?

Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of inflammatory arthritis that predominantly affects the spine, sacroiliac joints, and, in some cases, other joints throughout the body. The word "ankylosing" refers to the fusion of bones, which can occur in advanced stages of the condition. "Spondylitis" indicates inflammation of the spinal vertebrae.

AS is classified as an autoimmune-related condition, meaning the immune system plays a central role in driving inflammation. It most commonly presents in young adults and is more frequently diagnosed in men, though it affects people of all genders.

Common features of ankylosing spondylitis include:

  • Chronic lower back and pelvic pain, typically worse in the morning or after periods of inactivity
  • Stiffness in the spine and surrounding joints
  • Fatigue, which can be significant during active disease flares
  • Inflammation in other areas including the eyes (uveitis), bowel, and occasionally the jaw or temporomandibular joint (TMJ)

Because AS is a systemic inflammatory condition, its effects are not confined to the spine alone. This is why dental professionals need a comprehensive understanding of a patient's medical history before recommending any surgical treatment, including dental implants.

How Might Ankylosing Spondylitis Affect Oral Health?

People living with ankylosing spondylitis may experience a range of oral health considerations linked both to the condition itself and to the medications used to manage it.

Temporomandibular Joint Involvement

In some individuals, AS can cause inflammation in the temporomandibular joint (the jaw joint). This may lead to pain, limited mouth opening, or jaw stiffness — all of which can have implications for dental treatment, including the ability to undergo implant procedures comfortably.

Dry Mouth (Xerostomia)

Certain medications used to manage AS, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), may contribute to a reduction in saliva production. Saliva plays a critical protective role in oral health by neutralising acids, washing away bacteria, and aiding in the remineralisation of tooth enamel. Reduced saliva flow can increase the risk of tooth decay and gum disease.

Gum Disease and Inflammation

Research suggests a link between systemic inflammatory conditions and a higher susceptibility to periodontal (gum) disease. Since gum disease is also driven by inflammatory processes, individuals with AS may find they are more prone to gum-related problems. Notably, untreated gum disease is associated with poorer dental implant outcomes.

Bone Health Considerations

Chronic inflammation and certain medications — including corticosteroids — used in the management of AS can affect bone density over time. Since dental implants rely on healthy jawbone for successful osseointegration (the process by which the implant fuses with the bone), bone quality is an important clinical factor.

Understanding How Dental Implants Work

To assess whether dental implants are suitable for someone with ankylosing spondylitis, it helps to understand the clinical process involved.

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone to act as an artificial tooth root. Over a period of weeks to months, the implant undergoes a process called osseointegration, during which the surrounding bone gradually bonds with the titanium surface. Once integration is complete, a custom-made crown, bridge, or denture can be attached.

For osseointegration to succeed, certain biological conditions must be met:

  • Adequate bone volume and density to support and anchor the implant
  • Healthy gum tissue free from active infection or significant gum disease
  • A functioning immune response capable of healing after surgery without excessive risk of infection
  • Good blood supply to the implant site to support tissue healing

Each of these factors can be influenced by ankylosing spondylitis or by the medications commonly used to treat it. This is why a thorough pre-implant assessment is essential for every patient, and especially for those with complex medical histories.

You can learn more about the full implant placement process by visiting our single tooth implant treatment overview.

If you are weighing replacement designs for several missing teeth, this guide on implant bridge versus individual implants provides useful comparative context.

Medications for Ankylosing Spondylitis and Implant Considerations

One of the most clinically significant areas to discuss with your dental team when considering implants is your current medication regimen for AS.

Biologic Therapies (TNF-alpha Inhibitors and IL-17 Inhibitors)

Biologic medications such as adalimumab, etanercept, and secukinumab are increasingly used to manage moderate-to-severe ankylosing spondylitis. These drugs work by suppressing specific components of the immune system that drive inflammation. While highly effective for controlling AS, this immune modulation can potentially:

  • Increase susceptibility to post-operative infection
  • Slow wound healing following implant surgery
  • Affect the body's ability to integrate the implant successfully

It is important to note that many patients on biologic therapy do successfully undergo dental implant treatment. The key is that the dental team works in close liaison with your rheumatologist to assess and manage any additional risk before treatment begins.

Bisphosphonates

Although not universally prescribed for AS, bisphosphonates are sometimes used to address bone density concerns associated with chronic inflammation or long-term corticosteroid use. These medications are a known risk factor for a rare but serious condition called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), which involves poor healing or exposure of jawbone following dental surgery. Your dental team will carefully review any history of bisphosphonate use before recommending implant treatment.

NSAIDs and Corticosteroids

Long-term use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and steroids can affect bone health and wound healing. Your dental team will factor in the duration and dosage of these medications as part of their clinical assessment.

Clinical Assessment: What Your Dental Team Will Evaluate

Suitability for dental implants is never assumed — it is determined through a comprehensive clinical assessment. For patients with ankylosing spondylitis, this evaluation is likely to be particularly thorough.

Your dental clinician will typically assess:

  • Medical history including the duration and severity of your AS diagnosis
  • Current and recent medications including any biologics, bisphosphonates, NSAIDs, or corticosteroids
  • Bone quality and quantity using dental X-rays or CBCT (cone beam computed tomography) imaging to evaluate the jawbone in three dimensions
  • Gum health to identify any signs of active periodontal disease that would need treatment before implant placement
  • Mouth opening and TMJ function, particularly if jaw involvement is present
  • Overall systemic health and liaison with your GP or rheumatologist where appropriate

This multidisciplinary approach — where dental and medical teams work collaboratively — is considered an established approach for patients with complex health backgrounds. Our initial dental implant consultation provides the opportunity to discuss your specific medical history in full before any decisions are made.

Oral Health Maintenance for People Living With Ankylosing Spondylitis

Regardless of whether you proceed with dental implants, maintaining good oral health is particularly important when living with a systemic inflammatory condition. Below are some evidence-based recommendations:

Maintain a Consistent Oral Hygiene Routine

Brushing twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between teeth with interdental brushes or floss helps to reduce plaque accumulation, which is the primary cause of gum disease and tooth decay.

Stay Well-Hydrated to Combat Dry Mouth

If your medications contribute to dry mouth, drinking water regularly throughout the day can help. Sugar-free chewing gum containing xylitol may also stimulate saliva production.

Attend Regular Dental Check-Ups

Routine dental visits allow early detection of gum changes, decay, or bone loss before problems become significant. Patients with inflammatory conditions may benefit from more frequent hygienist appointments to support gum health.

Discuss Your Medications at Every Dental Visit

Always inform your dental team of any changes to your medications, including new prescriptions, dosage adjustments, or changes to your biologic therapy. This ensures your care plan remains clinically safe and appropriate.

Manage Disease Flares Proactively

Where possible, elective dental treatment — including implant placement — is often better planned during periods of stable disease activity rather than during a flare. Discuss timing with both your rheumatologist and dental team.

When to Seek Professional Dental Advice

If you are living with ankylosing spondylitis and have any of the following concerns, it would be appropriate to arrange a dental assessment:

  • Missing teeth that are affecting your ability to eat, speak, or feel confident
  • Swollen, bleeding, or tender gums that persist beyond a few days
  • Jaw pain or stiffness that is worsening or affecting your daily life
  • Tooth sensitivity to hot, cold, or sweet foods that has developed recently
  • Dry mouth that is persistent and not improving with hydration
  • Mouth soreness or ulcers that are not resolving within two weeks

These situations do not necessarily indicate a serious problem, but they do warrant professional evaluation. Early assessment often leads to simpler and more effective management of any developing issues.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants may be suitable for people with ankylosing spondylitis, but suitability is determined individually through clinical assessment — not assumed.
  • Medications matter: Biologics, bisphosphonates, corticosteroids, and NSAIDs all have potential implications for implant treatment and must be disclosed to your dental team.
  • Gum health is foundational: Active gum disease should be treated before implant placement is considered.
  • Jawbone quality is a critical factor; imaging will be used to evaluate this before any procedure.
  • A collaborative approach between your dental team and rheumatologist is considered an established and recommended approach for complex cases.
  • Good oral hygiene and regular dental visits are especially important for people with systemic inflammatory conditions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have dental implants if I am taking biologic medication for ankylosing spondylitis?

Many patients on biologic therapy for ankylosing spondylitis have successfully undergone dental implant treatment. However, biologic medications work by modifying immune function, which can affect healing and infection risk following surgery. Your dental team should be made fully aware of your medication and will likely liaise with your rheumatologist. In some cases, careful timing around medication cycles may be recommended. Each case is assessed on an individual basis, and no blanket statement about suitability can be made without a clinical examination.

Does ankylosing spondylitis affect the jawbone?

In most people with ankylosing spondylitis, jaw joint involvement is uncommon but does occur in a proportion of cases. When the temporomandibular joint is affected, it can cause pain, stiffness, or reduced mouth opening. Systemic inflammation and certain AS medications may also influence bone density more broadly, including in the jaw. A CBCT scan or dental X-rays can be used to evaluate jawbone quality accurately before any implant assessment is completed.

Will my dental implant be more likely to fail if I have ankylosing spondylitis?

The presence of ankylosing spondylitis alone does not automatically increase the risk of implant failure. However, factors associated with the condition — such as active inflammation, immunosuppressive medications, reduced bone density, or poorly controlled gum disease — can influence outcomes. With thorough pre-treatment planning, appropriate medical collaboration, and excellent oral hygiene, many patients with complex health backgrounds achieve good long-term implant outcomes. Your dental team will advise on your specific risk profile.

Should I tell my rheumatologist before having dental implant treatment?

Yes. It is good practice to inform your rheumatologist that you are planning dental implant surgery. They may wish to advise on medication management around the time of the procedure and can provide your dental team with relevant medical information. A collaborative approach between healthcare professionals helps to ensure your treatment is planned as safely as possible. Never discontinue any prescribed medication without discussing it with the clinician who prescribed it.

How do I maintain good oral health with ankylosing spondylitis?

Maintaining good oral health with AS involves consistent brushing and interdental cleaning, staying hydrated to counteract any dry mouth caused by medications, and attending regular dental check-ups. Discuss your full medication list with your dentist at every appointment. If your jaw is affected, your dental team can offer tailored advice to make oral hygiene more comfortable. Ensuring gum disease is well controlled is particularly important if you are considering implants in the future.

Can gum disease make it harder to get dental implants with ankylosing spondylitis?

Yes. Active gum disease is considered a contraindication for dental implant placement in most clinical scenarios, regardless of whether a patient has AS or not. Gum disease involves bacterial infection around the gum and bone — the same tissues that support a dental implant. If gum disease is present, it will typically need to be treated and stabilised before implant treatment can proceed. Find out more about peri-implant tissue inflammation and prevention and how addressing gum health can support implant candidacy.

Conclusion

Living with ankylosing spondylitis does not automatically rule out dental implants as a tooth replacement option. However, AS introduces a range of clinically relevant considerations — from the systemic effects of the condition itself to the medications used to manage it — that must be carefully evaluated before any treatment is recommended.

Bone quality, gum health, medication history, and overall disease activity are all factors that your dental team will assess thoroughly. For many patients with well-managed ankylosing spondylitis, dental implants remain a viable and effective option for restoring missing teeth and improving quality of life.

If you are considering dental implants and live with AS, the most important first step is to arrange a comprehensive consultation with an experienced dental implant clinician who can review your full medical history and develop a personalised, safe treatment plan.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

In the UK, patients may wish to confirm that their treating clinician is listed on the General Dental Council (GDC) register and that the provider is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), where applicable. No treatment outcome can be guaranteed, and suitability and expected results vary by individual clinical assessment.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

Are Dental Implants Safe for People With Epilepsy?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you live with epilepsy and are considering tooth replacement options, it is entirely natural to wonder whether dental implants are a safe and suitable choice for you. Many people with epilepsy search online for answers to this very question — and understandably so. Managing a long-term neurological condition adds a layer of complexity to nearly every healthcare decision, including dental treatment. If you also have cardiovascular concerns, this article on dental implants and high blood pressure may be useful to review alongside this guide.

Dental implants are a well-established solution for missing teeth, with clinical evidence supporting their effectiveness and longevity as a tooth replacement option. However, for patients living with epilepsy, specific considerations around seizure risk, medication effects, and surgical suitability must be carefully evaluated before any treatment begins.

This article aims to provide a clear, balanced, and clinically responsible overview of dental implants for people with epilepsy. It explores how epilepsy may influence implant candidacy, what your dental team should know, and why a thorough professional assessment is always the essential first step.

Can People With Epilepsy Have Dental Implants?

Dental implants can be safe for people with epilepsy, but suitability depends on individual clinical assessment. Factors such as seizure frequency, current medications, bone health, and gum condition all influence treatment decisions. A qualified dental professional must evaluate each patient's medical history and epilepsy management before recommending dental implants as a tooth replacement solution.

Understanding Epilepsy and Its Relevance to Dental Health

Epilepsy is a neurological condition characterised by recurrent seizures caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. It affects around 600,000 people in the United Kingdom and can vary considerably in severity — from infrequent, well-controlled episodes to frequent and unpredictable seizures.

For dental health professionals, epilepsy is a relevant medical factor for several reasons:

  • Seizure risk during treatment: Dental appointments can occasionally trigger anxiety, and in some individuals, stress or sensory stimuli may be associated with seizure onset. A calm, carefully managed clinical environment is therefore important.
  • Medication side effects: Many anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) can cause oral health changes, including gum overgrowth (gingival hyperplasia), dry mouth, and increased susceptibility to tooth decay.
  • Oral trauma from seizures: Falls or jaw movements during seizures can result in chipped, fractured, or lost teeth — which is precisely why many people with epilepsy seek tooth replacement options such as dental implants in the first place.

Understanding how epilepsy and oral health intersect is the first step in making an informed decision about implant treatment.

How Anti-Epileptic Medications Can Affect Oral Health

One of the most clinically significant factors for patients with epilepsy considering dental implants is the effect of long-term anti-epileptic medication on oral tissues.

Gingival hyperplasia (gum overgrowth) is a well-documented side effect of phenytoin, a commonly prescribed AED. When gum tissue becomes thickened or inflamed, it can complicate implant placement and long-term implant health, as healthy gum tissue is essential for supporting the implant and preventing infection.

Dry mouth (xerostomia) is another frequent side effect of several AEDs. Saliva plays a vital protective role in oral health, neutralising acids and preventing bacterial build-up. Reduced saliva flow increases the risk of tooth decay, gum disease, and peri-implant complications — conditions that can directly affect how well a dental implant integrates and remains stable over time.

Bone density considerations are also relevant. Some AEDs have been associated with reduced bone mineral density over long-term use, which may affect the jaw bone's ability to support an implant adequately.

Your dental team should always be informed of all medications you are taking, including the dosage and duration of use. This information directly shapes the clinical assessment and any treatment planning decisions.

What the Clinical Assessment for Dental Implants Involves

Before any dental implant procedure, every patient — regardless of medical history — undergoes a comprehensive clinical assessment. For patients with epilepsy, this assessment takes on additional importance.

A thorough implant assessment typically includes:

  • Medical history review: Your dental team will want to understand your type of epilepsy, how well it is currently controlled, and a complete list of your medications.
  • Seizure history: The frequency and nature of your seizures will help your clinician assess any additional precautions that may be appropriate during and after treatment.
  • Bone and gum evaluation: Dental X-rays and, in some cases, 3D cone beam CT (CBCT) scans are used to evaluate jaw bone volume, density, and structure — all of which influence implant suitability.
  • Gum health assessment: Active gum disease must be treated and resolved before implant placement can be considered.
  • Liaison with your neurologist or GP: In some cases, your dental team may wish to communicate with your wider medical team to ensure treatment is coordinated safely.

This individualised approach is central to responsible implant care and reflects GDC and CQC principles of patient-centred clinical practice.

The Clinical Science Behind Dental Implants

Understanding how dental implants work can help patients make more informed decisions about whether the treatment may be appropriate for them.

A dental implant is a small titanium post, surgically placed into the jawbone to act as an artificial tooth root. Titanium is used because it is biocompatible — meaning the body does not reject it — and it undergoes a process called osseointegration, whereby the surrounding bone gradually fuses with and bonds to the implant surface over a healing period of several weeks to months.

Once osseointegration is complete, a custom-made crown, bridge, or denture is attached to the implant, restoring both the appearance and function of the missing tooth or teeth.

For osseointegration to succeed, certain conditions must be met:

  • Sufficient and healthy jawbone: Adequate bone volume is needed to anchor the implant securely.
  • Healthy surrounding gum tissue: Gum disease significantly raises the risk of implant failure.
  • Good systemic health: Conditions or medications that impair healing or bone health can affect outcomes.

For patients with epilepsy, addressing any medication-related gum or bone changes before treatment — and maintaining excellent oral hygiene throughout — is particularly important for long-term implant success.

Seizure Risk During Dental Procedures: What Can Be Done

One concern many patients with epilepsy raise is whether a dental appointment itself could trigger a seizure. While there is no definitive evidence that routine dental treatment reliably triggers seizures in all patients, it is a reasonable consideration that your dental team should address proactively.

Several practical measures can help create a safer and more comfortable environment:

  • Morning appointments: Seizures are often more likely when a patient is fatigued. Morning appointments when energy levels are higher may be preferable for some patients.
  • Stress reduction: Anxiety management, such as relaxation techniques or, where appropriate, conscious sedation options, can help minimise procedural stress.
  • Shorter appointments: Breaking treatment into shorter, manageable sessions may be more suitable for patients with poorly controlled epilepsy.
  • Emergency preparedness: A well-trained dental team will have protocols in place for managing a seizure should one occur during treatment.
  • Clear communication: Informing your dental team of your seizure triggers, warning signs (aura), and what to do if a seizure occurs is essential.

If you are exploring options beyond conventional implants due to treatment complexity, learning about full arch implant bridge options may also be worth discussing with your clinician during your consultation.

Oral Health Maintenance for People Living With Epilepsy

Maintaining strong oral health is important for everyone, but for people with epilepsy, the combination of medication side effects, potential oral trauma from seizures, and the heightened importance of implant longevity makes it especially significant.

Practical oral hygiene guidance:

  • Brush twice daily using a fluoride toothpaste, ideally with a soft-bristled toothbrush or electric toothbrush, which can be particularly helpful if manual dexterity is affected.
  • Floss or use interdental brushes daily to remove plaque from between teeth and around any implants.
  • Stay hydrated to help combat dry mouth caused by AEDs. Sipping water regularly and using saliva substitutes if recommended can protect against decay.
  • Attend regular dental check-ups: Routine monitoring of gum health, bone levels around implants, and any medication-related oral changes is important. More frequent check-up intervals may be recommended for patients with complex medical histories.
  • Wear a protective mouthguard: If you experience falls or jaw clenching during seizures, a custom-fitted mouthguard may help protect your teeth and any existing restorations.
  • Avoid alcohol-based mouthwashes if dry mouth is an issue, as these can exacerbate the condition.

For daily cleaning techniques and long-term tissue health, this practical guide to dental implant maintenance can help reinforce your home-care routine.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

There are specific situations in which seeking prompt professional dental advice is recommended — particularly if you are living with epilepsy and have concerns about your oral health or tooth replacement options.

Consider contacting your dental team if you notice:

  • Tooth loss or damage following a seizure — teeth fractured or displaced during a seizure episode benefit from prompt evaluation.
  • Swollen, bleeding, or tender gums — these may indicate gum disease, which must be addressed before implant treatment can be considered.
  • Persistent dry mouth — if you are finding it difficult to eat, speak, or swallow comfortably, your dental team can offer supportive advice and refer where appropriate.
  • Gum overgrowth or thickening — particularly if you are taking phenytoin, as this can affect your suitability for implant treatment and may require management beforehand.
  • Jaw pain or difficulty opening your mouth — this may relate to seizure-related muscle strain or temporomandibular joint involvement and warrants clinical assessment.

Early assessment ensures that any developing issues are identified and managed before they become more complex. You are always encouraged to speak to a qualified dental professional rather than self-assess based on online information alone.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants can be a suitable option for people with epilepsy, but suitability must be determined through individual clinical assessment — there is no universal answer.
  • Anti-epileptic medications can affect oral health, including gum tissue, bone density, and saliva production, all of which are relevant to implant treatment.
  • Seizure frequency and control are important factors that your dental team will consider when planning treatment timing and approach.
  • Gum health must be established before implant placement can be considered, regardless of a patient's medical history.
  • Clear communication between you, your dental team, and your neurologist or GP supports safe and well-coordinated care.
  • Regular dental check-ups and excellent daily oral hygiene are fundamental to protecting both natural teeth and dental implants long term.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have dental implants if my epilepsy is not fully controlled?

Poorly controlled epilepsy does not automatically rule out dental implants, but it does require careful consideration. Your dental team will assess the frequency and nature of your seizures, evaluate your medical stability, and may wish to liaise with your neurologist before recommending treatment. In some cases, treatment may be postponed until seizure control improves. Each situation is assessed individually, and your clinician will discuss the most appropriate approach based on your specific circumstances.

Does phenytoin affect whether I can have a dental implant?

Phenytoin, a commonly prescribed anti-epileptic drug, is associated with gingival hyperplasia — a condition where gum tissue becomes enlarged or overgrown. This can complicate implant placement and maintenance. However, this does not necessarily prevent implant treatment; gum tissue changes may need to be managed prior to surgery. Your dental team will assess the condition of your gums thoroughly and discuss any necessary preparatory treatment before proceeding.

Will having a seizure damage a dental implant?

A well-integrated dental implant is robust, but a significant seizure involving jaw clenching or a fall could potentially affect surrounding teeth, gums, or even the implant restoration (the crown). A custom-fitted mouthguard may offer useful protection. If you experience a seizure and are concerned about the impact on your dental implants or teeth, it is worth arranging a check-up with your dental team for a reassessment.

How often should I see my dentist if I have epilepsy and dental implants?

The appropriate recall interval varies from patient to patient and will be determined by your dental team based on your overall oral health, medication use, and implant health. Many patients with complex medical histories benefit from more frequent monitoring — typically every three to four months rather than the standard six-month interval. Your clinician will advise you on the schedule that best supports your long-term oral health and implant stability.

Are there alternatives to dental implants for people with epilepsy?

Yes. If implant treatment is not immediately suitable — for example, due to active gum disease, insufficient bone, or poorly managed epilepsy — alternative options such as dentures or dental bridges may be considered as interim or long-term solutions. Your dental team can explain the advantages and limitations of each option in the context of your individual clinical needs and help you make an informed decision about the most appropriate tooth replacement approach.

Does sedation dentistry make implant treatment safer for people with epilepsy?

Conscious sedation can be a valuable option for anxious patients or those for whom stress management is a clinical priority. However, the use of sedation alongside anti-epileptic medications requires careful consideration, as certain sedative agents may interact with AEDs. Any discussion of sedation should involve full disclosure of your medication regimen, and your clinician may wish to consult with your GP or neurologist. If you are interested in finding out more, you could discuss sedation options at your consultation booking to understand what may be safely available to you.

Conclusion

Living with epilepsy should not automatically exclude you from considering dental implants as a tooth replacement solution. With careful planning, thorough clinical assessment, and open communication between you and your dental team, many people with epilepsy are able to undergo implant treatment safely and successfully.

The key lies in understanding how epilepsy and its treatment can influence oral health, bone quality, gum condition, and procedural safety — and ensuring that all of these factors are evaluated individually before any treatment decisions are made.

If you are considering dental implants and live with epilepsy, the most important first step is to arrange a professional consultation with a qualified implant dentist who will take the time to understand your full medical history. Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

Good oral health and well-informed decision-making go hand in hand — and professional guidance is always the right foundation for both.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.
