Are Dental Implants Safe for People With Psoriatic Arthritis?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you are living with psoriatic arthritis and considering tooth replacement options, it is entirely natural to have questions about whether dental implants are a safe and suitable choice for you. Many people search online for guidance on this topic, particularly because psoriatic arthritis is a systemic inflammatory condition that can affect multiple areas of the body — including oral health and bone tissue.

Dental implants with psoriatic arthritis is a subject that requires careful, individual consideration. The answer is not straightforward, because suitability depends on several factors, including your current disease activity, the medications you take, your overall bone health, and how well your immune system is functioning.

This article aims to provide clear, balanced, and educational information to help you understand the key considerations involved. It explains the relationship between psoriatic arthritis and dental implant treatment, outlines potential risks, and highlights why a thorough clinical assessment with a qualified dental professional is an essential first step.

Can People With Psoriatic Arthritis Have Dental Implants?

Dental implants with psoriatic arthritis can be considered in many cases, but suitability depends on a thorough clinical assessment. Factors such as disease activity, bone density, and immunosuppressive medications all influence outcomes. Many patients with psoriatic arthritis are suitable candidates, though careful planning and medical collaboration are essential before treatment begins.

What Is Psoriatic Arthritis and How Might It Affect Dental Health?

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a chronic autoimmune and inflammatory condition that typically affects people who have psoriasis. It causes joint inflammation, pain, and stiffness, and can also affect tissues beyond the joints — including the skin, eyes, and connective tissues throughout the body.

From a dental perspective, psoriatic arthritis may have several implications:

  • Gum (periodontal) disease: Systemic inflammation associated with PsA may increase susceptibility to gum disease. Research suggests a potential link between psoriatic conditions and higher rates of periodontal inflammation.
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia): Some medications used to manage PsA — including certain disease-modifying drugs — can reduce saliva production. A dry mouth increases the risk of tooth decay and gum problems.
  • Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) involvement: In some patients, PsA can affect the jaw joints, causing pain, stiffness, or limited mouth opening.
  • Bone health concerns: Systemic inflammation and some long-term medications may affect bone mineral density, which is important when considering implant placement.

Understanding these factors helps explain why a dental assessment is particularly important for patients with psoriatic arthritis who are exploring implant treatment.

How Do Dental Implants Work?

Dental implants are small titanium posts that are surgically placed into the jawbone to act as artificial tooth roots. Once integrated into the bone — a process known as osseointegration — they provide a stable foundation for a crown, bridge, or denture.

The success of a dental implant depends significantly on:

  • Sufficient bone volume and density to support the implant post
  • Healthy gum tissue free from active infection or significant disease
  • Good general health and healing capacity following the surgical procedure
  • Absence of conditions or medications that significantly impair bone healing or immune response

Osseointegration typically takes several months. During this period, the body must successfully integrate the titanium post with the surrounding bone tissue. Any condition or medication that disrupts normal bone metabolism or immune function may influence how well this process proceeds.

For people with psoriatic arthritis, these factors require individual evaluation by both a dental professional and, where appropriate, the patient's rheumatologist or specialist physician.

The Role of Medications in Implant Safety

One of the most important considerations for people with psoriatic arthritis exploring dental implants is the impact of medication on treatment outcomes.

Common medications used to manage psoriatic arthritis include:

Disease-Modifying Antirheumatic Drugs (DMARDs)

Medications such as methotrexate are widely used in PsA management. Some evidence suggests that methotrexate may influence bone metabolism and immune response, which could theoretically affect implant healing. However, many patients on low-dose DMARDs have undergone implant treatment successfully.

Biologic Therapies

Biologic agents — including TNF-alpha inhibitors such as adalimumab or etanercept — are prescribed for moderate to severe PsA. These medications suppress specific parts of the immune system to reduce inflammation. While they are highly effective for managing disease, their immunosuppressive effects may slightly increase the risk of post-surgical infection and could affect healing.

Corticosteroids

Long-term corticosteroid use can affect bone density and wound healing, both of which are relevant to implant treatment.

It is essential that your dental clinician liaises with your rheumatologist or GP before proceeding with implant treatment. A medication review can help ensure that treatment is timed and managed appropriately to optimise safety and outcomes.

Clinical Explanation: Osseointegration and Immune Function

To understand why systemic health matters for dental implants, it helps to understand what osseointegration involves at a biological level.

When a titanium implant is placed in the jawbone, the body responds by recruiting bone-forming cells called osteoblasts to the implant surface. These cells gradually deposit new bone around the implant, creating a stable biological bond. This process requires a well-regulated immune response to manage the initial surgical healing, clear any bacteria, and support tissue repair.

In people with autoimmune conditions such as psoriatic arthritis, the immune system is already dysregulated — it produces excessive inflammation even in the absence of infection. Additionally, immunosuppressive medications reduce the body's ability to mount a standard immune response.

This does not mean implant treatment is impossible. However, it does mean that the biological environment around the implant may respond differently, and that individual assessment of immune status, bone health, and disease activity at the time of treatment planning is particularly important.

Gum health is also a critical factor. Active gum disease significantly reduces implant success rates in any patient. For people with PsA, maintaining excellent gum health before and after implant placement is especially important.

Bone Density and Psoriatic Arthritis: What You Need to Know

Bone density is a key factor in dental implant treatment, as sufficient bone volume is needed to support and retain the implant post. People with psoriatic arthritis may face challenges in this area for a number of reasons.

Chronic systemic inflammation associated with PsA can accelerate bone resorption — the process by which bone tissue is gradually broken down. Long-term use of corticosteroids, which are sometimes prescribed to manage flares, is also associated with reduced bone mineral density over time.

A DEXA scan (bone density scan) may sometimes be relevant in understanding your overall bone health, though jaw bone quality is typically assessed through dental-specific imaging such as cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans during the implant planning process.

If bone density in the jaw is found to be insufficient for standard implant placement, options such as bone grafting procedures may be discussed as part of a staged treatment plan. Your dentist will explain whether this is relevant to your individual case following examination and imaging.

When a Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

If you are living with psoriatic arthritis and considering dental implants — or if you have noticed changes in your oral health — there are a number of situations where seeking a professional dental evaluation would be a sensible and proactive step.

Consider booking a dental assessment if you notice:

  • Loose teeth or teeth that have shifted position — this may indicate bone or gum changes that should be evaluated
  • Swollen, red, or bleeding gums — signs of gum inflammation that may require treatment before implants can be considered
  • Difficulty chewing or jaw pain — which may relate to TMJ involvement or dental problems
  • Dry mouth persisting over time — which can accelerate tooth decay and gum disease
  • Dental pain or sensitivity — which warrants professional assessment

It is also sensible to inform your dentist about your psoriatic arthritis diagnosis and current medications at every appointment, even if you are not currently considering implants. This allows your dental team to monitor your oral health with your systemic condition in mind and to advise you appropriately over time.

Maintaining Oral Health With Psoriatic Arthritis

Good oral hygiene is important for everyone, but for people living with psoriatic arthritis, maintaining consistent dental care routines is especially beneficial. Here are some practical, evidence-informed suggestions. You can also review practical oral health maintenance guidance as part of your long-term prevention plan:

Daily Oral Hygiene

Brush teeth at least twice daily using a fluoride toothpaste. An electric toothbrush may be helpful if PsA affects grip strength or hand mobility. Clean between teeth daily using interdental brushes or floss.

Managing Dry Mouth

If your medications cause dry mouth, speak with your dentist about appropriate management strategies. These may include fluoride-containing dry mouth products, staying well hydrated, and using sugar-free chewing gum to stimulate saliva flow.

Regular Dental Check-Ups

Attending regular dental check-ups and professional hygiene appointments allows your dental team to monitor gum health, identify early changes, and provide preventative care before issues develop.

Communicating With Your Healthcare Team

Keep your dentist informed of any changes to your medications or disease activity. Equally, if your rheumatologist makes significant changes to your treatment plan, this is worth discussing with your dentist in the context of any planned dental procedures.

Discussing Timing of Treatment

If you are planning dental implant treatment, it is worth exploring with both your rheumatologist and your dentist whether the timing of the procedure can be planned around periods of lower disease activity, where clinically appropriate.

Are There Alternatives to Dental Implants?

For some patients with psoriatic arthritis who may not be ideal implant candidates at a particular point in time, there are alternative tooth replacement options worth discussing with a dental professional. These include:

  • Dental bridges: Fixed restorations that span a gap, supported by adjacent teeth
  • Removable dentures: Partial or full dentures that can replace one or more teeth without the need for surgery

It is important to note that implants remain a commonly discussed and widely used option even for patients with systemic conditions, provided suitability is carefully assessed. Many people with well-managed psoriatic arthritis successfully undergo implant treatment following appropriate planning and clinical collaboration.

A detailed consultation with a dental implant specialist can help you understand all available options and which may be most appropriate for your individual circumstances.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants with psoriatic arthritis can be a suitable treatment option for many patients, but individual clinical assessment is essential before any decision is made.
  • Systemic inflammation, bone density, and immunosuppressive medications are all important factors that your dental team will wish to evaluate.
  • Collaboration between your dentist, rheumatologist, and GP helps ensure that treatment is planned safely and at an appropriate time.
  • Maintaining excellent gum health before and after implant treatment is especially important for patients with autoimmune conditions.
  • Dry mouth caused by PsA medications increases the risk of tooth decay and gum disease, making preventative oral care particularly important.
  • Regular dental check-ups allow your dental team to monitor your oral health in the context of your systemic condition and advise you accordingly.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have dental implants if I am taking methotrexate for psoriatic arthritis?

Many patients taking methotrexate have undergone dental implant treatment, but individual assessment is essential. Methotrexate can influence immune function and bone metabolism, so your dental clinician will typically liaise with your rheumatologist before proceeding. Factors such as your current dosage, disease activity, and overall health will all be considered. Treatment can often be timed and managed appropriately. A thorough clinical evaluation, including imaging and a review of your medical history, will help determine whether and when implant treatment may be appropriate for you.

Does psoriatic arthritis affect the jaw or teeth directly?

Psoriatic arthritis can sometimes involve the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), causing jaw pain or stiffness. The systemic inflammatory process associated with PsA may also contribute to a higher risk of gum disease in some individuals. Additionally, dry mouth caused by certain PsA medications can increase the risk of tooth decay. These factors do not necessarily prevent dental implant treatment, but they do reinforce the importance of regular dental monitoring and professional oral health care for people living with this condition.

Will biologic medications affect how my dental implant heals?

Biologic therapies used for psoriatic arthritis, such as TNF-alpha inhibitors, work by modulating parts of the immune system. This can theoretically influence post-surgical healing and infection risk following implant placement. However, many patients on biologics have undergone successful implant treatment. Your dental clinician should be made aware of all biologic medications you take, and collaboration with your prescribing specialist is advisable. Timing of surgery may be planned in relation to your medication schedule where this is clinically relevant.

How do I know if I have enough bone for a dental implant?

Bone volume and quality in the jaw is assessed through dental imaging, typically including an X-ray and, for implant planning, a cone beam CT (CBCT) scan. This gives your dental team a three-dimensional view of the bone structure at the implant site. If bone volume is found to be insufficient, options such as bone grafting may be considered to build up the site before implant placement. For people with psoriatic arthritis, bone density assessment may be particularly relevant given the potential effects of chronic inflammation and long-term medication use.

Should I tell my dentist I have psoriatic arthritis?

Yes — always inform your dentist about any systemic health conditions, including psoriatic arthritis, at every appointment. This allows your dental team to monitor your oral health with your condition in mind, consider any implications of your medications, and plan treatments safely. This is especially important if you are considering dental implants or any other surgical dental procedure. Providing a current and complete medical history enables your dental team to give you the most appropriate and safe care.

Is gum disease more common in people with psoriatic arthritis?

Some research suggests that people with psoriatic conditions may have a higher prevalence of periodontal (gum) disease, likely related to systemic inflammatory mechanisms shared between the conditions. Dry mouth caused by PsA medications can further increase the risk. Gum disease is also a significant factor in dental implant outcomes, as active periodontal disease can compromise implant success. For these reasons, achieving and maintaining good gum health is an important preparatory and ongoing step for people with PsA who are considering or have received dental implants.

Conclusion

Understanding whether dental implants with psoriatic arthritis are a safe and suitable option is an important question, and one that deserves a careful, individualised answer. The information in this article outlines the key factors that influence implant suitability for people living with this condition — including the role of systemic inflammation, bone health, immunosuppressive medications, and gum disease risk.

For many patients with well-managed psoriatic arthritis, dental implants can be a clinically appropriate tooth replacement option following thorough assessment and multidisciplinary planning. However, suitability is always determined on an individual basis, taking into account your current health status, disease activity, and medication profile.

If you are considering dental implants and live with psoriatic arthritis, the most valuable step you can take is to book a comprehensive consultation with a qualified dental implant clinician. Early assessment means early guidance — and the opportunity to address any factors that may affect your suitability or outcomes before treatment begins.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

Are Dental Implants Safe if You Have High Blood Pressure?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have been diagnosed with high blood pressure and are considering replacing missing teeth, it is entirely natural to wonder whether dental implants are a safe option for you. Many patients search online with exactly this concern — wanting to understand whether their cardiovascular health could affect their suitability for implant treatment.

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is one of the most common long-term health conditions in the United Kingdom, affecting around one in three adults. Because dental implant placement is a minor surgical procedure, patients with hypertension understandably want reassurance before moving forward.

This article explains what the relationship between dental implants and high blood pressure means in clinical practice, what factors your dental team will typically consider, and why a thorough personal assessment is always the appropriate starting point. It does not replace a professional consultation, but it does aim to give you a well-informed, balanced understanding of the key considerations involved.

Can You Have Dental Implants If You Have High Blood Pressure?

Dental implants may be suitable for patients with high blood pressure, provided blood pressure is well-managed and medically stable. Safety depends on individual health factors assessed during a clinical examination. Dentists will typically liaise with your GP and consider your medications, blood pressure readings, and overall cardiovascular health before recommending treatment.

Understanding High Blood Pressure and Why It Matters in Dental Treatment

High blood pressure (hypertension) is a condition in which the force of blood pushing against the artery walls is consistently higher than it should be. It is typically defined as a sustained reading at or above 140/90 mmHg, although this threshold may vary depending on clinical guidelines and individual circumstances.

Hypertension often has no obvious symptoms, which is why it is sometimes called the "silent condition." It is, however, associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events, including heart attack and stroke. For this reason, managing blood pressure effectively is a priority in general health care.

In the context of dental procedures, and particularly minor oral surgery such as implant placement, elevated blood pressure can raise certain procedural considerations. These include the potential for increased bleeding, interaction between local anaesthetics and blood pressure medications, and how the body responds to the mild physiological stress of a dental procedure.

This does not mean dental treatment cannot proceed — it means that careful clinical assessment is essential beforehand. Many patients with well-controlled hypertension undergo dental implant treatment safely and successfully each year in the UK. What matters is that treatment is appropriately planned with full knowledge of your medical history.

How Blood Pressure Levels Are Assessed Before Implant Treatment

Before any implant procedure is undertaken, a thorough medical history review is standard practice. For patients with hypertension, this assessment typically involves a number of specific considerations.

Pre-operative blood pressure measurement is commonly performed at the start of dental appointments. This gives the treating clinician a baseline reading and allows them to assess whether proceeding is appropriate on that particular day. Most dental clinicians follow guidance from bodies such as the British Society for Cardiovascular Prevention and Rehabilitation when interpreting blood pressure thresholds in the context of dental treatment.

Medication review is also an important part of pre-treatment planning. Many patients with hypertension take antihypertensive medications such as beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, or calcium channel blockers. Some of these medications can interact with local anaesthetics — particularly those containing vasoconstrictors such as adrenaline (epinephrine). Your dental team will consider this carefully and may use alternative anaesthetic formulations where clinically appropriate. If you are also taking immune-modifying medicines, this guide to dental implants with immunosuppressant medication is also relevant.

Liaison with your GP or cardiologist may be recommended, particularly if blood pressure is poorly controlled or if there are other cardiovascular concerns. Good communication between dental and medical professionals helps ensure that implant treatment is approached safely and with full consideration of your overall health profile.

Clinical Explanation: Why Implant Surgery Requires Cardiovascular Considerations

Dental implant placement is a minor surgical procedure performed under local anaesthesia. While it is generally well-tolerated and carries a good safety profile in suitable patients, it does involve some physiological demands on the body that are relevant when hypertension is present.

During any surgical procedure — even a minor one — the body may experience a degree of stress response. This can cause a temporary rise in blood pressure and heart rate. In patients whose blood pressure is already elevated or poorly controlled, this response may be more pronounced, which is why baseline cardiovascular stability is an important factor in pre-operative assessment.

Additionally, some local anaesthetic solutions used in dentistry contain adrenaline (a vasoconstrictor), which helps to prolong the numbing effect and reduce bleeding in the surgical area. Adrenaline can have cardiovascular effects, including a temporary increase in heart rate and blood pressure. In patients with certain heart conditions or those taking specific medications, lower concentrations or alternative formulations may be more appropriate.

The implant itself — a titanium post placed into the jawbone — is biocompatible and does not directly affect cardiovascular function. The primary clinical considerations relate to the procedural aspects of placement rather than the implant material itself. Understanding how dental implants work and what the placement process involves can help patients feel more confident when discussing their specific circumstances with their dental team.

When Implant Treatment May Need to Be Deferred or Modified

There are circumstances in which a dental clinician may recommend deferring implant treatment until certain conditions are better managed. This is not a blanket exclusion from treatment — it reflects responsible clinical planning aimed at protecting patient safety.

Poorly controlled or undiagnosed hypertension is one such circumstance. If a patient attends for a pre-operative assessment and records a blood pressure reading that falls above a clinically safe threshold (often cited as 180/110 mmHg or higher in dental guidance), a responsible clinician will typically recommend deferral until blood pressure is better managed, and may advise the patient to consult their GP promptly.

Recent cardiovascular events — such as a heart attack or stroke within the past six months — are generally considered a period during which elective dental procedures should be postponed. This allows time for cardiovascular stabilisation and appropriate medical review. For transplant recipients, this timing discussion is often even more important, as outlined in this article on dental implants after organ transplant.

Medication changes or recent adjustments to antihypertensive therapy may also influence timing. If a patient has recently started a new medication or had their dosage altered, the dental team may wish to confirm that the patient's blood pressure response has stabilised before proceeding.

These considerations exist not to discourage treatment, but to ensure it is undertaken at the safest and most appropriate time for each individual patient.

The Role of Dental Anxiety in Blood Pressure Management

It is worth noting that dental anxiety — which is extremely common — can temporarily raise blood pressure in the dental chair, even in patients without a diagnosed cardiovascular condition. For patients with hypertension, this effect may be more significant.

Managing dental anxiety is therefore an important component of care for this group of patients. Open communication with your dental team about any concerns you have is always encouraged. Many modern dental practices offer strategies to support anxious patients, including clear explanations of each step of the procedure, gentle pacing of treatment, and in some cases, sedation options where clinically appropriate.

If anxiety around dental procedures is something you experience regularly, discussing this openly during your consultation allows the dental team to tailor their approach accordingly. A calm, well-prepared patient is likely to have a more stable blood pressure response during treatment.

Medications for High Blood Pressure and Their Oral Health Implications

Patients with hypertension should also be aware that some antihypertensive medications can have oral health side effects that are relevant to implant treatment planning.

Dry mouth (xerostomia) is a known side effect of certain antihypertensive drugs, including some diuretics and calcium channel blockers. Saliva plays an important protective role in oral health — it helps to neutralise acids, wash away bacteria, and support the natural healing process. Reduced saliva flow can increase the risk of tooth decay, gum disease, and oral infections, all of which are relevant to the long-term success of dental implants.

Gum overgrowth (gingival hyperplasia) is associated with a class of calcium channel blockers, most notably nifedipine. This condition causes the gum tissue to become enlarged, which can complicate implant placement and affect the long-term health of the tissues surrounding the implant.

Bleeding tendencies may also be relevant in patients taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications — sometimes prescribed alongside antihypertensives — as these affect how blood clots during and after a surgical procedure. Your dental clinician will always review your full medication list as part of a pre-treatment assessment.

For patients managing gum health alongside implant treatment, understanding dental implant maintenance and gum health may provide useful context.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice for Patients with High Blood Pressure

Maintaining excellent oral health is important for everyone, but there are particular reasons why patients with hypertension may wish to pay close attention to their dental health.

Emerging research continues to explore associations between gum disease (periodontitis) and cardiovascular health. While the relationship is complex and causation has not been definitively established, there is sufficient evidence to suggest that chronic oral inflammation may have systemic implications. Keeping gums healthy through consistent oral hygiene practices is therefore sensible from both a dental and general health perspective.

Practical oral health advice for patients with hypertension includes:

  • Brush teeth twice daily using a fluoride toothpaste and a soft-to-medium bristle toothbrush
  • Clean between teeth daily using interdental brushes or floss to reduce plaque and gum inflammation
  • Attend regular dental check-up appointments so that any changes in oral health can be identified early
  • Stay well hydrated, particularly if dry mouth is a side effect of your medication
  • Inform your dental team of all medications you are taking, including over-the-counter remedies and supplements
  • Discuss with your GP if your blood pressure readings remain consistently elevated before scheduling elective dental procedures
  • Avoid smoking, which negatively affects both cardiovascular and oral health, and significantly reduces dental implant success rates

When to Seek Professional Dental Assessment

Whether you are at the early research stage of considering dental implants or you are actively preparing for a consultation, there are several situations where speaking to a qualified dental professional is the appropriate next step.

You may wish to arrange an assessment if:

  • You have been told by your GP that your blood pressure is elevated and you are wondering how this affects your dental treatment options
  • You are taking antihypertensive medication and want to understand how this may be managed around dental procedures
  • You have experienced dry mouth, gum changes, or oral discomfort that you suspect may be related to your medication
  • You have missing teeth and want to understand whether dental implants could be a suitable option given your medical history
  • You have had a recent cardiovascular event and want to know when it may be appropriate to resume dental treatment

A consultation with an experienced implant dentist allows for a full review of your medical history, a clinical examination of your oral health, and a conversation about the most appropriate treatment pathway for your individual circumstances. Treatment suitability is always determined on a case-by-case basis. You can find out more about what to expect during a dental implant consultation booking by visiting the clinic's dedicated information pages.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants may be suitable for patients with high blood pressure, but suitability depends on individual clinical assessment
  • Well-controlled, medically stable hypertension does not automatically exclude a patient from implant treatment
  • Pre-operative blood pressure measurement and full medication review are standard parts of implant treatment planning
  • Certain antihypertensive medications can affect oral health, including causing dry mouth or gum changes — inform your dental team of all medications
  • Poorly controlled blood pressure may mean deferral of treatment until readings are stabilised
  • Good oral hygiene and regular dental attendance are important for all patients, including those with hypertension
  • Anxiety management strategies can be discussed with your dental team to help keep blood pressure as stable as possible during appointments

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have dental implants if I have high blood pressure?

Many patients with high blood pressure do proceed with dental implant treatment successfully. The key factor is whether blood pressure is well-managed and medically stable. Your dental team will review your medical history, current medications, and blood pressure readings before recommending a treatment plan. If blood pressure is poorly controlled, your dentist may advise you to speak with your GP before proceeding. Suitability is always determined on an individual basis through clinical assessment.

Does local anaesthetic affect blood pressure?

Certain local anaesthetic solutions used in dentistry contain adrenaline (a vasoconstrictor), which can cause a temporary increase in heart rate and blood pressure in some patients. This is generally well-tolerated, but in patients with certain cardiovascular conditions or those taking specific medications, an alternative formulation may be more appropriate. Your dentist will select the most suitable anaesthetic option based on your full medical history and current medications.

Will my dentist check my blood pressure before implant treatment?

Yes, pre-operative blood pressure measurement is common practice before dental implant procedures, particularly for patients who have disclosed a history of hypertension. This gives your dental team a baseline reading on the day and helps them assess whether it is appropriate to proceed. If blood pressure is recorded above a safe threshold, the appointment may be rescheduled to allow time for medical review.

Can blood pressure medications affect my dental implants?

Certain antihypertensive medications can have oral health implications. Calcium channel blockers may cause gum overgrowth (gingival hyperplasia), which can affect the tissues surrounding an implant. Diuretics and other medications may cause dry mouth, which can affect oral healing and long-term implant health. Anticoagulant medications may influence bleeding during implant placement. Always provide your dental team with a full and up-to-date list of all medications you are taking.

Is dental implant surgery risky for someone with a heart condition?

Dental implant placement is a minor surgical procedure, and for many patients — including those with well-managed cardiovascular conditions — it can be performed safely. However, risk assessment must be individualised. Patients with recent cardiovascular events, poorly controlled blood pressure, or complex cardiac histories will require more detailed pre-operative assessment, and in some cases, liaison between the dental team and the patient's cardiologist or GP. This ensures treatment is timed and planned appropriately.

How can I prepare for a dental implant consultation if I have high blood pressure?

Bring a current, complete list of all medications — including doses — to your consultation. If your GP has provided recent blood pressure readings, these can be helpful for your dental team to review. Note down any symptoms you have experienced, including dry mouth, gum changes, or dental sensitivity. Being open and thorough about your medical history enables your dental team to plan your care safely and with your wider health in mind.

Conclusion

High blood pressure is a very common condition, and it is entirely understandable that patients living with hypertension want to be confident about the safety of dental implant treatment before proceeding. The good news is that well-controlled hypertension does not automatically prevent someone from benefiting from dental implants — but it does mean that careful, individualised clinical assessment is essential.

Dental implant safety in patients with high blood pressure depends on multiple factors: how well blood pressure is managed, what medications are being taken, whether there are any associated cardiovascular concerns, and the overall oral health of the patient. A thorough pre-treatment evaluation, honest communication between patient and dental team, and where appropriate, liaison with the patient's GP or cardiologist, allows treatment to be planned responsibly and safely.

Maintaining good oral health — through consistent oral hygiene, regular dental attendance, and awareness of medication-related oral effects — supports both the long-term success of dental implants and broader general health.

If you are considering dental implants and have concerns about high blood pressure, speaking with an experienced implant dentist is the most appropriate next step. An in-person consultation will allow for a personalised assessment of your circumstances and an honest, balanced discussion of your options.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

Are Dental Implants Suitable After an Eating Disorder?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

For many people who have experienced an eating disorder, the visible impact on their teeth can feel deeply personal and distressing. Conditions such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa are well-documented to cause significant dental damage — including severe enamel erosion, tooth sensitivity, and in some cases, tooth loss. It is entirely understandable that once recovery is underway, restoring a healthy, confident smile becomes an important priority.

Dental implants after an eating disorder is a topic many patients research privately before raising it with a dental professional. If you are in this situation, you are not alone, and asking these questions is an important first step.

This article explains what eating disorders can do to oral health, how they may affect dental implant suitability, what factors a dental professional will consider during assessment, and how to approach the conversation about restorative treatment during or after recovery.

Can You Have Dental Implants After an Eating Disorder?

Dental implants after an eating disorder may be suitable in many cases, but individual assessment is essential. A qualified dental professional will evaluate bone density, gum health, and overall oral condition before recommending treatment. Recovery status and general health are also important considerations. Suitability can only be determined through a thorough clinical examination.

How Eating Disorders Affect Oral Health

Eating disorders affect the body in wide-ranging ways, and the mouth is one of the most visibly impacted areas. Whether through nutritional deficiency, frequent vomiting, or restricted eating, the teeth and supporting structures can suffer considerable damage over time.

Bulimia nervosa is particularly associated with dental erosion caused by repeated exposure to stomach acid during purging episodes. This acid softens and gradually dissolves tooth enamel, leading to a characteristic appearance — teeth that appear thinner, more translucent, or shorter than normal. The back surfaces of the upper front teeth are often most affected.

Anorexia nervosa can lead to nutritional deficiencies that weaken teeth and compromise the density of the jawbone, which is the very structure that dental implants rely upon for stability.

Both conditions can also contribute to:

  • Increased tooth sensitivity
  • Higher risk of tooth decay
  • Dry mouth (xerostomia), which reduces the protective function of saliva
  • Gum inflammation or recession
  • In severe cases, complete tooth loss

Understanding the extent of this damage through a professional dental assessment is an important early step for anyone in recovery considering restorative treatment.

If nutritional risk is a concern in your case, this explainer on how vitamin B12 or iron deficiency can affect dental implant healing provides additional context.

The Clinical Science: Why Bone and Gum Health Matter for Implants

Dental implants work by replacing the root of a missing tooth with a small titanium post that is placed directly into the jawbone. Over a period of weeks to months, the bone grows around and integrates with this post — a process called osseointegration. A crown is then attached to restore the visible tooth.

For this process to be successful, the jawbone must have sufficient density and volume to support and retain the implant. This is where a history of an eating disorder becomes clinically relevant.

Prolonged nutritional deficiency — particularly low calcium and vitamin D intake — can reduce bone mineral density. In the context of dental implants, reduced bone density may mean:

  • A higher risk of implant failure due to inadequate integration
  • The potential need for bone grafting procedures before implant placement
  • A longer overall treatment timeline

Gum health is equally important. Chronic inflammation, gum recession, or active gum disease can all compromise the long-term success of implants. A dental professional will assess the health of the soft tissue surrounding potential implant sites before any treatment begins.

If you are interested in understanding more about dental implants and how they work, a detailed overview is available on the clinic website.

Recovery Status and Treatment Timing

One of the most important considerations for dental implants after an eating disorder is timing. Dental professionals will typically want to ensure that a patient is in a stable phase of recovery before proceeding with implant treatment.

This is not a judgement about a patient's journey — it is a clinically responsible approach for several important reasons:

Active purging behaviour continues to expose the mouth to stomach acid, which can damage natural teeth further and compromise the soft tissue environment around newly placed implants.

Nutritional intake must be adequate to support healing. Implant surgery, like any surgical procedure, requires the body to mount an effective healing response. This relies on sufficient protein, vitamins, and minerals.

Psychological readiness is also relevant. Major dental treatment is a significant commitment, and patients benefit from undertaking it when they feel emotionally supported and stable. Dental professionals understand this and are able to discuss timing sensitively and without judgement.

Many individuals who have recovered from an eating disorder may go on to have successful dental implant treatment. Timing and thorough assessment are important foundations of appropriate care.

What a Dental Assessment for Implants May Include

Before recommending dental implants after an eating disorder, a qualified implant dentist will carry out a thorough clinical assessment. This may include:

Dental X-rays or 3D CBCT scanning to evaluate the density and volume of the jawbone at potential implant sites. This imaging provides precise information that cannot be obtained through visual examination alone.

Gum health assessment to identify any signs of inflammation, recession, or periodontal (gum) disease that may need to be treated first.

Medical and dietary history to understand overall health, current nutritional status, and any medications that may affect healing or bone density.

If you have recent blood work or are unsure what to request, this guide on what blood test results matter before dental implant surgery can help you prepare for that discussion.

Review of existing teeth to assess the condition of remaining natural teeth and determine the most appropriate overall treatment plan.

Discussion of your recovery journey to understand where you are in your health and whether the timing feels right for you.

This assessment is entirely without judgement. Dental professionals are trained to take a whole-patient view, and many patients find these conversations easier than they had anticipated.

Oral Health Maintenance During and After Recovery

Regardless of whether dental implant treatment is immediately suitable, maintaining good oral health during recovery is genuinely important — both for the wellbeing of any remaining natural teeth and to create the best possible conditions for future restorative treatment.

Some practical steps that may help include:

After episodes of vomiting, avoid brushing teeth immediately, as the enamel is temporarily softened by acid. Rinsing with water or a fluoride mouthwash first can help neutralise acid before brushing after approximately 30 to 60 minutes.

Use a fluoride toothpaste appropriate for sensitive teeth if enamel erosion is a concern. A dental professional can recommend the most suitable product for your situation.

Stay well hydrated to help counteract dry mouth, which increases the risk of tooth decay.

Attend regular dental check-ups so that any new damage can be identified and managed early. Dental professionals can also apply fluoride treatments or protective varnishes to help preserve weakened enamel.

Discuss nutritional support with your GP or recovery team, as improving calcium and vitamin D intake may benefit both general and dental bone health.

If your routine includes nights or rotating schedules, this practical guide on whether shift work can affect dental implant healing can help with recovery planning.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

It is advisable to arrange a dental assessment if you notice any of the following, whether or not you are currently considering implant treatment:

  • Increased tooth sensitivity to temperature or sweet foods
  • Visible changes in the shape, colour, or surface texture of teeth
  • Loose teeth or changes in how your bite feels
  • Swollen, bleeding, or receding gums
  • Persistent dry mouth
  • Jaw discomfort or difficulty chewing
  • Areas of missing teeth affecting eating or confidence

A dental professional can assess these signs calmly and compassionately. Early assessment generally means more options are available and treatment tends to be more straightforward. There is no need to wait until symptoms become severe.

If you are already working with a healthcare team for your eating disorder recovery, it may be helpful to let your dental professional know, as this allows them to coordinate their care approach appropriately.

Can Bone Grafting Help if Bone Loss Has Occurred?

A question many patients ask is whether dental implants are still possible if bone loss has already occurred as a result of their eating disorder or tooth loss.

In many cases, bone grafting procedures can help rebuild lost bone volume and create a more suitable foundation for implants. Bone grafts may use synthetic materials or processed bone, and they work by encouraging the body to produce new bone tissue in the treated area.

The need for bone grafting will add time to the overall treatment journey, but it does not automatically rule out implant treatment. The feasibility of grafting, and whether it is appropriate in a given situation, is determined through the clinical assessment process.

Patients should be aware that outcomes will vary based on individual circumstances and that no dental professional can guarantee results without examination. Understanding what to expect from bone grafting and implant preparation is a useful step for those considering more complex restorative treatment.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants after an eating disorder may be suitable, but individual clinical assessment is always required before any treatment decisions are made.
  • Eating disorders — particularly bulimia and anorexia — can cause enamel erosion, bone density loss, gum problems, and tooth loss, all of which affect implant suitability.
  • Recovery stability, nutritional health, and oral tissue condition are all factors a dental professional will consider before recommending implants.
  • Bone grafting may be an option if bone volume has been reduced, but this needs to be evaluated individually.
  • Good oral hygiene habits and regular dental check-ups are beneficial at every stage of recovery, regardless of treatment plans.
  • Dental professionals approach these consultations with care and without judgement — there is no need to feel anxious about raising your history during an assessment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will a dentist judge me for having an eating disorder?

Dental professionals in the UK are trained to approach all patients with compassion, dignity, and respect. A history of an eating disorder is a medical matter that is relevant to planning safe treatment — it is not something that will be treated judgementally. Many patients find it helpful to share their background so that the dental team can offer the most appropriate and sensitive care. You are not obliged to disclose more than you feel comfortable sharing, but greater openness generally leads to better-tailored treatment planning.

How long after recovering from an eating disorder can I consider dental implants?

There is no single fixed timeframe that applies universally. The key consideration is that the individual is in a stable phase of recovery, with adequate nutritional intake and without active behaviours that could compromise healing. A dental professional and, where relevant, your wider healthcare team can help you determine when the timing may be appropriate. Some individuals pursue implant treatment within a year or two of recovery; for others, more time or preparatory dental work is needed first.

Can enamel erosion from an eating disorder be treated before implants?

Yes, in many cases damage caused by enamel erosion can be addressed using restorative dental treatments such as composite bonding, veneers, or crowns. These treatments may help protect remaining natural teeth and improve function and appearance before or alongside implant planning. The suitability of each approach depends on the extent of damage and individual oral health, both of which are assessed during a clinical examination.

Do dental implants require special care after placement?

Dental implants, once placed and healed, are maintained in a similar way to natural teeth — through twice-daily brushing with a soft-bristled brush, interdental cleaning, and regular professional check-ups. For individuals with a history of an eating disorder, the dental team may provide additional guidance to help protect the implants and surrounding tissue. Ongoing monitoring is an important part of long-term implant care for all patients.

Is it possible that I am not suitable for dental implants even after full recovery?

In some cases, the degree of bone loss or gum damage may mean that implants are not the most appropriate option at a given time, or that significant preparatory treatment is required first. Alternative tooth replacement options, such as bridges or dentures, may be discussed in these circumstances. A thorough clinical assessment is the only way to determine which options are realistically available, and a good dental professional will explain all suitable choices clearly and honestly.

Will NHS dentistry cover dental implants for people who have had an eating disorder?

Dental implants are not routinely available through NHS dental services in England and are generally provided privately. However, NHS treatment may be available for other aspects of restorative care. If cost is a concern, it is worth discussing payment plan options with the dental practice during your consultation, as many private clinics offer structured payment arrangements to make treatment more accessible.

Conclusion

Dental implants after an eating disorder is a topic that deserves careful, compassionate, and clinically informed discussion. For many people in recovery, restoring their smile is not merely cosmetic — it is part of rebuilding confidence and quality of life after a challenging health journey.

The important message is that implant treatment may well be possible, but its suitability depends on a range of individual factors including bone density, gum health, nutritional recovery, and overall stability. These factors can only be properly evaluated through a professional clinical assessment.

If you have a history of an eating disorder and are considering dental implants, the most helpful step you can take is to arrange a consultation with an experienced implant dentist who can review your oral health comprehensively and guide you through the options available to you.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

In the UK, patients may also wish to confirm that their treating clinician is listed on the General Dental Council (GDC) register and that the provider is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), where applicable.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

Are Dental Implants Worth It Compared to Doing Nothing?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Losing a tooth â€” or being told a tooth needs to be extracted â€” can leave you feeling uncertain about what to do next. Many patients find themselves weighing up whether dental implants are worth it or whether they can simply leave the gap and carry on as normal. It is one of the most common questions people search for online, and understandably so. The decision involves considering cost, time, comfort, and long-term oral health.

The reality is that both choosing treatment and choosing to do nothing carry consequences, and understanding those consequences is an important step in making an informed decision. Dental implants are one of several options available for replacing missing teeth, and they are widely regarded as a reliable, long-term solution â€” but they are not suitable for everyone, and suitability always depends on individual clinical assessment.

This article will explore what happens when a missing tooth is left untreated, explain how dental implants work, outline the potential benefits and considerations, and help you understand when seeking professional dental advice may be appropriate. The goal is to give you balanced, clinically responsible information so you can approach any conversation with your dentist feeling better informed.

Are dental implants worth it compared to doing nothing? For many patients, dental implants are considered a worthwhile long-term investment compared to leaving a gap untreated. A missing tooth left without replacement can lead to bone loss, shifting of neighbouring teeth, and changes in bite function over time. Dental implants help preserve jawbone structure, restore chewing ability, and maintain facial aesthetics. However, suitability varies, and a clinical assessment is always necessary before treatment.

What Happens When You Leave a Missing Tooth Untreated?

When a tooth is lost or extracted, it may seem harmless to leave the space empty â€” particularly if it is not visible when you smile. However, the consequences of doing nothing can develop gradually over months and years, often without obvious early symptoms.

The jawbone in the area of the missing tooth begins to resorb, meaning the bone tissue slowly reduces in volume because it is no longer stimulated by the tooth root. This process, known as alveolar bone resorption, can affect the shape of your jaw and face over time, potentially leading to a sunken or aged appearance around the mouth.

Neighbouring teeth may also start to drift or tilt into the empty space. This movement can alter your bite alignment, create uneven pressure when chewing, and make oral hygiene more difficult in areas where teeth have shifted. Opposing teeth â€” those on the opposite jaw â€” may begin to over-erupt into the gap, compounding alignment issues further.

In some cases, leaving a gap untreated can contribute to increased wear on remaining teeth, jaw discomfort, and difficulty eating certain foods. While these changes do not happen overnight, they can accumulate and become more complex to address the longer they are left.

Understanding these potential outcomes does not mean every missing tooth must be replaced urgently, but it highlights why a professional dental assessment is valuable in helping you understand the options available to you.

How Do Dental Implants Work?

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone to act as an artificial tooth root. Over a period of several weeks to months, the implant integrates with the surrounding bone through a biological process called osseointegration. Once this integration is complete, a custom-made crown, bridge, or denture is attached to the implant, restoring the appearance and function of the missing tooth.

Titanium is used because it is biocompatible, meaning the body generally accepts it without adverse reaction. The success of osseointegration is well documented in dental research, with implants demonstrating high long-term survival rates in published clinical studies.

The treatment process typically involves several stages. An initial implant consultation and clinical assessment â€” often including X-rays or a CBCT scan â€” determines whether there is sufficient bone volume and density to support an implant. If bone loss has occurred, additional procedures such as bone grafting may be discussed to create a suitable foundation.

Following implant placement, a healing period allows the implant to bond with the jawbone. Once healed, the final restoration is designed and fitted to match your natural teeth in shape, size, and colour. The entire process can take several months from start to finish, depending on individual circumstances and healing response.

The Underlying Dental Science: Why Bone Preservation Matters

To understand why dental implants are often considered beneficial compared to doing nothing, it helps to understand a little about how your jawbone functions.

Your teeth are anchored in a part of the jawbone called the alveolar ridge. Each tooth root transmits mechanical forces into this bone during everyday activities such as chewing. This stimulation is essential for maintaining bone density and volume â€” it signals to the body that the bone is still needed and should be preserved.

When a tooth is lost, that mechanical stimulation ceases in the affected area. Without it, the body begins to break down and reabsorb the bone tissue in a natural process of remodelling. Studies have shown that significant bone loss can occur within the first year following tooth extraction, with ongoing resorption continuing over subsequent years.

This bone loss is not merely a cosmetic concern. Reduced bone volume can affect the stability of adjacent teeth, alter the fit of existing dentures, and limit future treatment options. If a patient decides to pursue implant treatment after years of bone loss, more complex and costly preparatory procedures â€” such as bone grafting â€” may be required.

If you are comparing short-term delay with longer-term consequences, our guide on what happens if you delay dental implant treatment for years looks specifically at how timing can affect future options.

A dental implant, by functioning as an artificial root, restores mechanical loading to the jawbone. This stimulation helps maintain bone density in the area, which is one of the key clinical advantages implants offer compared to other tooth replacement options or leaving the gap untreated.

Potential Benefits of Dental Implants

Dental implants offer several potential advantages that may make them a worthwhile consideration for patients with missing teeth. It is important to note that individual outcomes vary, and the benefits listed here are based on general clinical evidence rather than guaranteed results.

Preservation of jawbone structure: As discussed, implants stimulate the jawbone and help reduce the rate of bone resorption that typically follows tooth loss.

Stability and function: Because implants are anchored directly in the bone, they provide a stable foundation for replacement teeth. Many patients report improved chewing ability and comfort compared to removable dentures.

Protection of neighbouring teeth: Unlike traditional dental bridges, implants do not require the preparation or reduction of adjacent healthy teeth to support a restoration.

Longevity: With appropriate care and regular dental maintenance, implants have the potential to last many years. Long-term clinical studies have reported high survival rates over periods of 10 to 20 years and beyond.

Aesthetic outcomes: Implant-supported crowns are individually crafted to blend with your natural teeth, offering a result that many patients find visually pleasing.

Improved confidence: Many patients describe feeling more comfortable eating, speaking, and smiling after implant treatment.

While these benefits are well supported by clinical evidence, it is essential to remember that outcomes depend on factors such as overall health, oral hygiene, and the specific clinical situation. A thorough assessment is always necessary before treatment begins.

Considerations and Limitations of Dental Implants

While dental implants are a well-established treatment, they are not without considerations that patients should be aware of before making a decision.

Surgical procedure: Implant placement involves oral surgery, which carries inherent risks including infection, swelling, discomfort, and â€” in rare cases â€” nerve injury. These risks are generally low when treatment is carried out by an experienced clinician, but they should be understood beforehand.

Time commitment: The treatment process spans several months, including healing time for osseointegration. Patients who require preparatory procedures such as bone grafting may find the timeline extended further.

Cost: Dental implants represent a financial investment, and they are not typically available on the NHS for cosmetic or routine tooth replacement. Many private clinics, however, offer payment plans to help make treatment more accessible.

Not suitable for everyone: Certain medical conditions, medications, or lifestyle factors (such as heavy smoking) may affect implant success. Adequate bone volume is also necessary, though preparatory treatments can sometimes address this.

Ongoing maintenance: Implants require the same standard of oral hygiene as natural teeth, including regular brushing, interdental cleaning, and routine dental check-ups. Peri-implantitis â€” inflammation around the implant â€” can develop if oral hygiene is neglected.

These considerations do not diminish the value of implant treatment, but they highlight the importance of having a thorough discussion with your dental team to understand whether implants are the most appropriate option for your circumstances.

Comparing Your Options: Implants, Bridges, Dentures, or No Treatment

When a tooth is missing, there are generally four paths a patient can take. Understanding each one can help frame the question of whether dental implants are worth it for your situation.

Dental implants provide a fixed, independent solution that preserves bone and does not rely on neighbouring teeth for support. They are often considered the closest replacement to a natural tooth in terms of function and appearance.

Dental bridges involve placing a prosthetic tooth anchored to the adjacent natural teeth, which must be prepared (reduced in size) to accommodate crowns. Bridges can be an effective solution but may place additional strain on supporting teeth over time.

Removable dentures are a non-surgical option that can replace one or several missing teeth. They are generally more affordable upfront but may feel less stable, can affect taste sensation, and do not prevent bone resorption.

Doing nothing avoids the cost, time, and procedures associated with treatment, but it carries the potential long-term consequences discussed earlier in this article, including bone loss, tooth movement, and changes to bite function.

Each option has its place, and the most suitable choice depends on individual factors including oral health, the location of the missing tooth, medical history, and personal preferences. A consultation with a qualified dental professional can help you explore your tooth replacement options in detail.

Some readers also find it useful to compare this with whether you can live normally without replacing missing teeth, especially if the gap is not currently causing obvious day-to-day problems.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

If you are living with a missing tooth or have recently been told that extraction may be necessary, seeking a professional dental assessment can help you understand the current state of your oral health and the options available to you.

There are certain situations where it may be particularly advisable to seek evaluation:

  • You have had a tooth missing for some time and are noticing changes in your bite, difficulty chewing, or shifting of other teeth.
  • You experience discomfort or sensitivity in the area surrounding a gap, which could suggest changes in the neighbouring teeth or gum tissue.
  • Your existing denture no longer fits comfortably, which may indicate bone changes in the jaw.
  • You are considering tooth replacement but are unsure which option may be most suitable for your clinical situation.
  • You have noticed changes in your facial appearance around the mouth or jaw area since losing a tooth.

These signs do not necessarily indicate an urgent problem, but they are worth discussing with a dental professional who can carry out a thorough examination. Early assessment can sometimes help preserve options that may become more limited over time.

It is important to remember that no dental treatment should be undertaken without a proper clinical examination, and any recommendations should be tailored to your individual needs.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice

While tooth loss can sometimes be unavoidable â€” due to trauma, genetic factors, or complex dental conditions â€” there are practical steps you can take to reduce the risk and maintain your oral health.

Maintain a thorough oral hygiene routine. Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between your teeth with interdental brushes or floss helps prevent the plaque accumulation that leads to gum disease and tooth decay â€” the two leading causes of tooth loss in adults.

Attend regular dental check-ups. Routine examinations allow your dentist to identify early signs of decay, gum disease, or other conditions before they progress to the point where tooth loss becomes a possibility.

Address dental problems promptly. If you experience toothache, bleeding gums, or sensitivity, seeking timely advice can often lead to simpler, less invasive treatment than waiting until the problem worsens.

Consider lifestyle factors. Smoking significantly increases the risk of gum disease and can impair healing following dental procedures, including implant placement. Reducing sugar intake also helps protect teeth from decay.

Protect your teeth during sport. Wearing a custom-fitted mouthguard during contact sports can help prevent traumatic tooth loss.

If you already have a missing tooth and have chosen to proceed with implant treatment, maintaining excellent oral hygiene around the implant is essential for its long-term success. Your dental team can advise you on the best cleaning techniques and tools for implant care.

Key Points to Remember

  • Leaving a missing tooth untreated can lead to bone loss, shifting of adjacent teeth, and changes in bite function over time.
  • Dental implants are a well-established, long-term option for replacing missing teeth that help preserve jawbone structure.
  • Implant treatment involves surgery, a healing period, and ongoing maintenance â€” it is not a quick fix, but rather a considered investment in oral health.
  • Not everyone is a suitable candidate for implants; a thorough clinical assessment is always required.
  • Alternative options including bridges and dentures are also available and may be more appropriate depending on individual circumstances.
  • Good oral hygiene and regular dental check-ups remain the foundation of preventing tooth loss and maintaining long-term oral health.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long do dental implants last?

With proper care and regular dental maintenance, dental implants have the potential to last many years â€” often decades. Long-term clinical studies have reported implant survival rates exceeding 90% over 10 to 15 years. However, longevity depends on several factors including oral hygiene, overall health, and lifestyle habits such as smoking. The implant crown may need replacement or adjustment over time due to normal wear. Regular check-ups allow your dentist to monitor the health of your implant and the surrounding tissues. It is important to understand that no dental restoration comes with a lifetime guarantee, and individual outcomes vary.

Is it painful to have a dental implant placed?

Implant placement is carried out under local anaesthetic, so you should not feel pain during the procedure. Sedation options may also be available for patients who feel anxious. After the procedure, some swelling, bruising, and discomfort are common, typically managed with over-the-counter pain relief and cold compresses. Most patients report that the discomfort is less than they anticipated. Your dental team will provide detailed aftercare instructions to support a comfortable recovery. If you have concerns about pain management, discuss these with your clinician during your consultation so they can tailor the approach to your needs.

Can I get a dental implant years after losing a tooth?

In many cases, yes â€” implant treatment can still be considered even if a tooth has been missing for several years. However, the longer a gap has been present, the more bone resorption may have occurred. If significant bone loss has taken place, a bone grafting procedure may be needed before an implant can be placed. This adds time and cost to the overall treatment. A clinical examination including imaging will determine the current condition of your jawbone and whether additional procedures are necessary. It is always worth having an assessment, as modern techniques can often address bone deficiency effectively.

Are dental implants available on the NHS?

Dental implants are generally not available through the NHS, as they are typically considered outside the scope of standard NHS dental provision. In very rare and specific circumstances â€” such as following oral cancer treatment or significant facial trauma â€” NHS funding may be considered. For most patients, dental implant treatment is provided privately. Many clinics offer flexible payment plans to help spread the cost. During your consultation, the clinic can discuss pricing and any available financial arrangements so you can make an informed decision that works within your budget.

What are the risks of dental implant treatment?

As with any surgical procedure, dental implant placement carries some risks. These can include infection at the implant site, damage to surrounding teeth or blood vessels, nerve injury resulting in numbness or tingling, and implant failure where osseointegration does not occur successfully. Sinus complications may arise with upper jaw implants. These risks are generally low and are further minimised when treatment is planned and carried out by an experienced implant clinician. A comprehensive assessment and careful treatment planning help identify and mitigate potential risks. Your dental team will discuss all relevant risks with you before treatment.

How do I care for a dental implant after treatment?

Caring for a dental implant is similar to caring for your natural teeth. Brush twice daily with a soft-bristled toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste, paying particular attention to the gum line around the implant. Interdental brushes are often recommended for cleaning around the implant post and beneath the crown. Avoid smoking, as it can impair healing and increase the risk of peri-implantitis â€” an inflammatory condition affecting the tissues around the implant. Attend regular dental check-ups and professional hygiene appointments so your dental team can monitor the implant and surrounding gum and bone health. Good daily care is essential for long-term implant success.

Conclusion

Deciding whether dental implants are worth it compared to doing nothing is a personal decision that depends on your individual oral health, lifestyle, and priorities. What is clear from the clinical evidence is that leaving a missing tooth untreated may lead to bone loss, shifting teeth, and changes in chewing function over time. For many patients, implant treatment can offer a stable and long-term way to restore function, but it is not the only option and it is not suitable for everyone.

If you are unsure whether implants are worth it in your circumstances, a clinical assessment can help you compare doing nothing with bridges, dentures, or implant treatment in a realistic, personalised way. Understanding the likely benefits, limitations, risks, timescales, and costs is the best basis for a well-informed decision.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
