title: What Dentists Don't Always Explain About Dental Implants
seoTitle: What Dentists Don't Explain About Dental Implants
description: Key facts about dental implants that patients often wish they knew sooner — healing timelines, bone requirements, risks, and lifelong aftercare explained clearly.

images.alt: What Dentists Don't Always Explain About Dental Implants

html:
Back to Blog
Patient Education 8 Apr 2026 15 min read

What Dentists Don't Always Explain About Dental Implants

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you are considering dental implants, you have probably already read about the benefits — improved chewing, natural appearance, and long-term durability. But many patients tell us that even after a consultation, they still have unanswered questions about what the process truly involves.

It is common for people to search online for a fuller picture of dental implant treatment because the information provided in a brief appointment does not always cover every detail. This is not necessarily a failing on the dentist's part — clinical appointments are time-limited, and the priority is often the immediate assessment. However, patients deserve a thorough understanding before committing to any treatment.

This article explores some of the aspects of dental implants that are not always fully explained — from the realities of healing and bone requirements to aftercare expectations and potential risks. The aim is to help you feel better informed and more confident when discussing treatment options with your dental professional. If you have specific concerns, a detailed clinical consultation is always the most reliable starting point.

What Do Dentists Not Always Explain About Dental Implants?

Dentists don't always fully explain that dental implant treatment involves a multi-stage process with variable healing times, specific bone density requirements, potential risks such as infection or implant failure, and a lifelong commitment to aftercare. Understanding these realities before treatment helps patients set realistic expectations and make informed decisions based on their individual clinical circumstances.

The Multi-Stage Nature of Implant Treatment

One of the most common areas of misunderstanding is the timeline. Dental implant treatment is rarely a single appointment — it is a carefully planned process that typically unfolds over several months.

The standard pathway involves an initial consultation and imaging, followed by surgical placement of the implant post into the jawbone. After placement, a healing period known as osseointegration is required, during which the titanium post fuses with the surrounding bone. This process generally takes between three and six months, depending on individual healing factors and the location of the implant.

Once osseointegration is confirmed, an abutment is fitted to the implant, and finally a custom-made crown is attached. In some cases, preparatory procedures such as bone grafting or a sinus lift may be needed before the implant can be placed, which adds additional time to the overall treatment plan.

Patients sometimes expect the process to be completed within a few weeks. Understanding from the outset that implant treatment is a phased journey — and that each stage serves an important clinical purpose — helps set realistic expectations. Your dentist should explain the anticipated timeline for your specific case during the initial consultation.

Bone Density and Why It Matters More Than You Might Think

Dental implants require a sufficient volume and density of jawbone to anchor securely. This is a critical factor that influences whether implant treatment is immediately feasible or whether preparatory work is needed first.

After tooth loss, the jawbone in the affected area begins to resorb — a natural biological process where the body gradually breaks down bone tissue that is no longer stimulated by a tooth root. The longer a gap has been present, the more bone may have been lost.

If bone levels are inadequate, procedures such as bone grafting or a sinus lift (for upper jaw implants) may be recommended to rebuild the area before implant placement. These are well-established procedures with a strong clinical track record, though like all surgical interventions they carry their own risks, which your dentist should discuss with you. They also add complexity, time, and cost to the overall treatment plan.

Not every patient is told about this possibility during an initial discussion, particularly if detailed imaging has not yet been carried out. A thorough assessment, ideally including a CBCT (cone beam computed tomography) scan, provides a clear picture of bone condition and allows your dentist to explain exactly what your treatment will involve. For patients concerned about bone grafting requirements, understanding the process can help alleviate anxiety considerably.

Osseointegration — The Healing Process Beneath the Surface

Osseointegration is the biological process that makes dental implants possible, yet it is one of the least discussed aspects with patients. After the implant post is surgically placed, the surrounding bone gradually grows around and bonds to the titanium surface. This fusion is what gives the implant its stability and long-term strength.

The process is not instantaneous. It typically takes three to six months, though this varies depending on factors including:

  • Location of the implant — the lower jaw tends to heal faster than the upper jaw due to differences in bone density
  • The patient's general health — conditions such as diabetes or osteoporosis may slow healing
  • Smoking status — tobacco use significantly impairs blood flow and can compromise osseointegration
  • Oral hygiene — infection around the implant site can interfere with healing

During this period, patients are usually fitted with a temporary restoration or advised to avoid placing pressure on the implant site. It is important to follow aftercare instructions carefully, as disturbing the implant during osseointegration can lead to failure.

Your dentist should explain what osseointegration involves, how long it is expected to take in your case, and what signs to watch for that might indicate a problem.

Potential Risks and Complications

Like any surgical procedure, dental implant placement carries risks. While implant treatment has a high success rate — with published clinical literature generally reporting figures between 95% and 98% for appropriately selected patients — complications can occur, and it is important that patients are aware of these before consenting to treatment.

Potential risks include:

  • Infection at the implant site — particularly in the early healing phase
  • Implant failure — where the implant does not integrate with the bone and becomes loose
  • Nerve damage — which may cause numbness, tingling, or altered sensation in the lip, chin, or tongue, particularly with lower jaw implants
  • Sinus complications — if an upper jaw implant protrudes into the sinus cavity
  • Peri-implantitis — a condition similar to gum disease that affects the tissues surrounding an established implant, potentially leading to bone loss and implant failure over time

These risks are relatively uncommon when treatment is carried out by an experienced, qualified implant dentist following a thorough assessment. However, patients should be informed about them as part of the consent process. If your dentist has not discussed potential complications, it is entirely appropriate to ask.

Aftercare Is a Lifelong Commitment

A common misconception is that once a dental implant is placed and the crown is fitted, the treatment is essentially "done." In reality, dental implants require ongoing care — just like natural teeth.

Although implants cannot develop cavities, the gum tissue and bone around them remain vulnerable to infection. Peri-implantitis — inflammation and infection of the tissues surrounding an implant — is one of the leading causes of late implant failure. It is often caused by inadequate oral hygiene, smoking, or a history of gum disease.

Effective implant maintenance includes:

  • Twice-daily brushing with a soft-bristled brush, paying careful attention to the gum line around the implant
  • Interdental cleaning using floss, interdental brushes, or a water flosser to clean areas that a toothbrush cannot reach
  • Regular dental check-ups and professional cleaning — typically every six months, though your dentist may recommend more frequent visits initially
  • Avoiding smoking, which significantly increases the risk of peri-implantitis
  • Wearing a nightguard if you grind your teeth, as excessive force can damage the implant crown or the underlying bone

Patients who maintain excellent oral hygiene and attend regular reviews can expect their implants to last many years. However, longevity is never guaranteed and depends on individual care and clinical factors.

The Real Cost Picture

Cost is one of the most frequently asked questions about dental implants, and it is also one of the areas where patients often feel they have not received complete information.

The headline price of an implant — the figure you may see advertised — typically covers the implant post, abutment, and crown. However, the total cost of treatment can vary considerably depending on:

  • Preparatory procedures — bone grafting, sinus lifts, or extractions may be required and are usually charged separately
  • Diagnostic imaging — CBCT scans and X-rays may carry additional fees
  • Temporary restorations — provisional teeth worn during the healing period
  • Sedation — if you opt for sedation during the surgical procedure
  • Follow-up appointments — reviews and adjustments during healing
  • Long-term maintenance — professional cleaning appointments and any future repairs or replacements to the crown

It is important to ask for a comprehensive, itemised treatment plan that includes all anticipated costs before proceeding. This allows you to make an informed financial decision and avoids unexpected charges later. Many practices offer finance options to help spread the cost, though these are subject to individual assessment and approval.

Not Everyone Is a Suitable Candidate

Dental implants are a well-established and effective treatment option, but they are not suitable for every patient. Several factors influence candidacy, and it is important that these are discussed honestly during the assessment process.

Factors that may affect suitability include:

  • Insufficient bone volume — though this can often be addressed with grafting procedures
  • Uncontrolled gum disease — active periodontal disease must be treated and stabilised before implant placement
  • Certain medical conditions — uncontrolled diabetes, autoimmune disorders, or conditions affecting bone metabolism may increase risk
  • Medications — some drugs, such as bisphosphonates used for osteoporosis, can affect bone healing
  • Smoking — significantly increases the risk of implant failure and peri-implantitis
  • Age considerations — implants are generally not placed until the jaw has finished developing, typically in the late teens

A thorough clinical assessment is the only reliable way to determine whether dental implants are appropriate for your individual situation. If implants are not suitable, your dentist should discuss alternative options such as bridges or dentures.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

If you are considering dental implants — or have already had implants placed — there are several situations where seeking a professional evaluation is advisable:

  • You have been living with a missing tooth and would like to understand your replacement options
  • You have noticed changes to your bite or shifting of surrounding teeth since losing a tooth
  • You experience discomfort, swelling, or bleeding around an existing implant
  • Your implant crown feels loose or does not feel right when biting
  • You have concerns about the healing process following recent implant surgery
  • You have a medical condition that may affect implant suitability and would like personalised advice

There is no obligation to proceed with treatment following a consultation. The purpose of an assessment is to provide you with clear, honest information about your options so that you can make a decision that feels right for you.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice

Whether or not you proceed with dental implant treatment, maintaining good oral health is essential for protecting your remaining teeth and supporting any existing dental work.

Practical steps include:

  • Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, spending at least two minutes each time
  • Clean between your teeth daily using interdental brushes or floss — this is where most plaque accumulates
  • Attend regular dental check-ups so that potential problems can be identified early
  • Limit sugary and acidic foods and drinks, which contribute to enamel erosion and decay
  • Do not smoke — smoking is one of the most significant risk factors for gum disease, tooth loss, and implant failure
  • Address dental problems promptly — a small issue left untreated can develop into something more complex and costly

If you already have dental implants, your aftercare routine is particularly important. Ask your dental team for specific guidance on the best tools and techniques for keeping your implants and surrounding tissues healthy.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implant treatment is a multi-stage process that typically takes several months from start to finish
  • Bone density plays a critical role in implant suitability — preparatory procedures may be needed
  • Osseointegration is the essential healing process that anchors the implant, and it cannot be rushed
  • Potential risks include infection, implant failure, nerve damage, and peri-implantitis — these should be discussed before treatment
  • Aftercare is lifelong — implants require diligent oral hygiene and regular professional reviews
  • A thorough clinical assessment is essential before any treatment decision, and patients should feel comfortable asking detailed questions

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does the entire dental implant process take from start to finish?

The total treatment time for dental implants varies considerably depending on individual circumstances. For a straightforward single implant with adequate bone, the process typically takes four to nine months — including the healing period for osseointegration. If preparatory procedures such as bone grafting or a sinus lift are required, the timeline may extend to twelve months or longer. Your dentist should provide a personalised estimate based on your clinical assessment, including diagnostic imaging, so that you have a clear understanding of the expected timeline before committing to treatment.

Can dental implants fail even after they have healed?

Yes, although it is uncommon. Late implant failure can occur months or even years after successful placement, most often due to peri-implantitis — a condition where infection and inflammation affect the tissues surrounding the implant, leading to bone loss. Other contributing factors include excessive mechanical force (such as teeth grinding), poor oral hygiene, smoking, and certain systemic health changes. Regular dental check-ups and a thorough home care routine are essential for monitoring implant health and catching any early signs of trouble before they progress.

Is dental implant surgery painful?

Dental implant placement is carried out under local anaesthesia, which means the area is fully numbed during the procedure. You should not feel pain during the surgery itself, though you may be aware of pressure and vibration. Some discomfort, swelling, and bruising may occur in the days following surgery, which is typically managed with over-the-counter pain relief and ice packs. Sedation options are available for patients who experience dental anxiety. Your dentist should discuss pain management options with you before the procedure so that you feel prepared and informed.

What happens if I do not have enough bone for an implant?

If imaging reveals that you do not have sufficient bone volume for implant placement, your dentist may recommend a bone grafting procedure. This involves placing bone material — which may be synthetic, sourced from a tissue bank, or taken from another area of your mouth — at the deficient site to encourage new bone growth. The graft typically needs several months to mature before implant placement can proceed. While this adds time and cost to treatment, it is a well-established procedure that can make implant treatment possible for many patients who would otherwise not be suitable candidates.

How long do dental implants last?

The longevity of dental implants depends on multiple factors, including the quality of the original placement, the patient's oral hygiene, overall health, and lifestyle habits such as smoking. With diligent care, the implant post itself can last many years — in some cases, several decades. The crown attached to the implant may need replacement or repair over time due to normal wear, typically after ten to twenty years. There is no guarantee of a specific lifespan, as individual outcomes vary. Regular professional reviews help ensure that any issues are identified and addressed early.

Are there alternatives to dental implants for replacing missing teeth?

Yes. Dental bridges and dentures are the most common alternatives. A bridge uses the teeth adjacent to the gap as supports for a fixed false tooth, while dentures are removable appliances that can replace one or more missing teeth. Each option has its own advantages and limitations. Bridges require preparation of neighbouring teeth, while dentures may feel less stable than fixed options. The most appropriate choice depends on your individual clinical situation, the number of teeth missing, bone condition, and personal preferences. A thorough assessment will help determine which option may be most suitable for you.

Conclusion

Dental implant treatment is a well-established and effective way to replace missing teeth, but it is not as simple as the summary descriptions often suggest. Understanding the full picture — from the multi-stage timeline and bone requirements to the potential risks and the lifelong commitment to aftercare — empowers you to make genuinely informed decisions about your dental health.

If you feel that aspects of dental implant treatment have not been fully explained to you, that is not unusual. The topics covered in this article represent some of the most common areas where patients tell us they would have liked more information earlier in the process.

The most important step you can take is to have a thorough conversation with a qualified dental professional who can assess your individual situation, explain your options clearly, and answer your questions without pressure. Good dental care is a partnership between patient and clinician, and being well-informed is an essential part of that relationship.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

title: What Does Insertion Torque Mean for Dental Implant Stability?
seoTitle: What Does Insertion Torque Mean for Implant Stability?
description: Learn what insertion torque means for dental implant stability, why it matters, and how clinicians use it to assess implant success in London.

images.alt: What Does Insertion Torque Mean for Dental Implant Stability?

html:
Back to Blog
Patient Education 13 Jul 2026 15 min read

What Does Insertion Torque Mean for Dental Implant Stability?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have been researching dental implants in London, you may have come across clinical terms that feel unfamiliar or confusing. One phrase that often appears in discussions around implant placement is insertion torque — yet very few patient-facing resources explain what it actually means or why it matters for the success of your treatment.

People increasingly search online for information about dental implant procedures before attending consultations. Understanding the clinical factors that influence implant stability can help you feel better informed and more confident when speaking with your dental team.

This article explains what insertion torque means in the context of dental implants, why clinicians pay close attention to it during the placement procedure, and how it relates to the broader goal of achieving a stable, long-lasting implant. It also outlines when professional dental assessment is important and what factors can influence implant outcomes.

As always, individual suitability for dental implant treatment depends on a thorough clinical assessment.

Featured Snippet Answer

What does insertion torque mean for dental implant stability?

Insertion torque refers to the rotational force required to place a dental implant into the jawbone during surgery. Measured in Newton centimetres (Ncm), it provides the clinician with an immediate indication of the primary stability of the implant — that is, how firmly the implant is anchored in the bone at the time of placement.

What Is Insertion Torque in Dental Implant Treatment?

Insertion torque is a measurement taken during the surgical placement of a dental implant. As the implant is threaded into a prepared site in the jawbone, the clinician uses a torque-controlled handpiece or wrench to monitor the level of resistance encountered. This resistance — expressed in Newton centimetres (Ncm) — reflects how tightly the implant engages with the surrounding bone tissue.

Think of it similarly to tightening a screw into wood. A screw driven into dense, firm wood requires more rotational force than one placed in softer material. In the same way, higher insertion torque values generally suggest that the bone surrounding the implant site is denser and that the implant is engaging securely.

Clinicians typically aim for an insertion torque value within a specific range. Values that are too low may suggest insufficient bone density or a poorly fitting implant site, raising questions about initial stability. Conversely, values that are excessively high can potentially create stress within the bone tissue.

It is important to note that insertion torque is just one of several clinical measurements used to assess implant stability, and its significance is always interpreted alongside other clinical findings.

Why Does Primary Stability Matter?

Primary stability refers to the mechanical anchorage of a dental implant immediately after it has been placed. It occurs through direct physical contact between the implant surface and the surrounding bone — before any biological integration has taken place.

Primary stability is widely considered an important factor in the early phase of implant treatment. A well-stabilised implant at the point of placement is less likely to experience unwanted movement during the critical early healing period. Excessive micromovement in the days and weeks following surgery can potentially interfere with the process through which the bone and implant bond together biologically.

This is why the insertion torque value recorded at the time of surgery is meaningful. It offers an immediate, in-the-moment reading of how securely the implant is seated. However, it is not the only factor that influences long-term outcomes. Bone quality, implant design, surgical technique, the patient's general health, and aftercare all play significant roles.

If you are considering dental implants and would like to understand more about how treatment suitability is assessed, exploring our single tooth implant treatment page may provide a helpful overview.

The Science Behind Osseointegration and Implant Stability

To understand why insertion torque matters, it helps to understand the biological process of osseointegration — the way in which a dental implant becomes permanently integrated with the jawbone over time.

When a titanium implant is placed into the jawbone, the body begins to recognise its surface as a scaffold for new bone growth. Over a period of weeks to months, bone cells gradually grow into the microscopic surface features of the implant, creating a strong biological bond. This process transforms the initial mechanical stability achieved at surgery into a durable, long-term anchorage.

The jawbone itself is living tissue with two main types relevant to implant placement: cortical bone (the dense outer layer) and trabecular or cancellous bone (the more spongy inner structure). Bone density varies considerably between individuals and between different sites within the jaw. The upper jaw (maxilla) typically has lower bone density than the lower jaw (mandible), which can influence both insertion torque values and the overall integration process.

Insertion torque, therefore, gives the clinician an immediate snapshot of the mechanical environment at the implant site. This helps inform decisions about loading protocols — for example, whether a temporary crown can be placed shortly after surgery, or whether a longer healing period is appropriate.

How Clinicians Use Insertion Torque to Guide Treatment Decisions

Insertion torque values do not exist in isolation. Experienced implant clinicians use them as one part of a broader clinical picture that guides decision-making throughout the treatment process. For a related explanation of healing dynamics, see primary vs secondary stability in the first 8 weeks.

Low insertion torque values may prompt the clinician to extend the healing period before placing the final restoration, allowing more time for osseointegration to occur before the implant is subjected to biting forces. In some cases, additional procedures such as bone grafting may be discussed.

Moderate to higher insertion torque values, within a clinically appropriate range, may indicate that conditions favour a more straightforward healing timeline. In certain circumstances, this can support decisions around immediate or early loading protocols — where a provisional restoration is placed within a short time of implant surgery.

Excessively high torque values can occasionally indicate that compression of the bone is occurring, which may not always be desirable. Surgical experience and technique play an important role in ensuring that implant placement is carried out in a controlled and measured manner.

All of these considerations are highly individual. What is clinically appropriate for one patient may differ significantly for another, depending on bone quality, implant type, jaw position, and overall health status.

Other Methods Used to Assess Implant Stability

Insertion torque is not the only tool available to clinicians when evaluating implant stability. Several complementary assessment methods are used in modern implant dentistry:

Resonance Frequency Analysis (RFA) is a non-invasive technique that uses a small magnetic peg attached to the implant to generate a vibration. The frequency of this vibration is translated into an Implant Stability Quotient (ISQ) score, providing a numerical indication of stability. RFA can be used both immediately after placement and at intervals during the healing period to monitor how integration is progressing.

Tactile assessment — the clinician's direct clinical experience of how the implant seats during placement — also provides valuable information alongside measured values.

Radiographic imaging, including dental X-rays and cone beam CT (CBCT) scans, provides detailed information about bone volume and quality before and after implant placement.

Together, these approaches allow a comprehensive picture of implant stability to be built up over the course of treatment, supporting clinical decisions at each stage.

Factors That Can Influence Insertion Torque and Implant Stability

A range of patient-specific and procedural factors can influence insertion torque values and, more broadly, the stability of a dental implant. You can also explore how bone quality and density influence implant stability:

Bone density and volume: Patients with good bone density in the jaw often achieve higher initial insertion torque values. Significant bone loss — which can occur following tooth extraction, gum disease, or prolonged tooth absence — may reduce available bone for implant engagement.

Implant design: The geometry, thread design, diameter, and surface characteristics of a dental implant all influence how it interacts with bone during placement.

Surgical technique: The precision of the implant site preparation, including the size of the pilot hole drilled and the protocol used for sequential drilling, directly affects the torque values achieved.

Patient health: Certain systemic health conditions and medications can affect bone metabolism and healing capacity. These are assessed during pre-treatment planning.

Jaw location: Bone characteristics differ between the upper and lower jaw, and even between different regions within the same jaw.

Understanding these variables helps explain why implant treatment planning is tailored to each individual and why a thorough pre-treatment assessment — including detailed imaging — forms an essential part of the process.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Appropriate

If you are considering dental implants or have recently undergone implant placement, there are several circumstances in which it would be appropriate to seek professional dental advice:

  • Persistent discomfort or pain in the area of an implant that does not settle as expected during the healing period
  • Swelling, redness, or warmth around the implant site that develops or worsens after the initial post-surgical period
  • A sensation that the implant feels loose or that something does not feel right with your restoration
  • Difficulty biting or chewing that persists beyond the expected healing phase
  • Any changes to the gum tissue around the implant, including recession, bleeding on brushing, or visible bone changes

None of these symptoms necessarily indicate a serious problem, and many can have straightforward explanations. However, early professional assessment is always preferable to delaying review, as prompt clinical evaluation allows any concerns to be addressed in a timely manner.

If you are in the early stages of considering implants, a consultation with a clinician experienced in dental implant assessment can help clarify whether treatment is suitable for your individual circumstances.

Oral Health and Prevention: Supporting Long-Term Implant Success

While insertion torque and clinical factors during surgery are important, long-term implant stability ultimately depends significantly on what happens after the implant is placed. Maintaining good oral health is one of the most important things a patient can do to support a successful outcome.

Oral hygiene: Dental implants require thorough daily cleaning. Plaque that accumulates around the implant can lead to a condition called peri-implantitis — an inflammatory condition affecting the tissue and bone around the implant — which can compromise long-term stability. Brushing twice daily with a soft-bristle brush, flossing or using interdental brushes, and following any specific aftercare guidance from your dental team all play an important role.

Smoking: Smoking has a well-documented effect on bone healing and gum health. Patients who smoke are generally considered at higher risk of implant complications, and this is discussed as part of pre-treatment assessment.

Diet: Eating a balanced diet that supports bone health — including adequate calcium and vitamin D — can be beneficial. Avoiding very hard or sticky foods in the early healing period is also typically advised.

Regular dental check-ups: Routine professional reviews allow your clinician to monitor the health of your implant, surrounding bone, and soft tissues over time. Early identification of any changes allows prompt management.

Managing systemic health: Conditions such as uncontrolled diabetes can affect healing and bone health. Working with your wider healthcare team to maintain general health supports implant success.

You may also find it helpful to read how to care for your dental implants daily for further practical guidance.

Key Points to Remember

  • Insertion torque is the rotational force measured when a dental implant is placed into the jawbone, expressed in Newton centimetres (Ncm).
  • It provides a direct indication of primary stability — how firmly the implant is seated in the bone at the time of surgery.
  • Insertion torque is one of several tools used to assess implant stability; clinicians also use resonance frequency analysis, imaging, and clinical experience.
  • Bone density, implant design, surgical technique, jaw location, and patient health all influence insertion torque values and overall implant stability.
  • Osseointegration — the biological bonding of bone to the implant surface — is the goal of the healing phase and determines long-term stability.
  • Good oral hygiene, regular dental check-ups, and maintaining general health are essential to supporting long-term implant success.
  • Suitability for dental implant treatment always requires individual clinical assessment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a higher insertion torque always better for dental implants?

Not necessarily. While moderate-to-higher insertion torque values within a clinically appropriate range can indicate good primary stability, excessively high values may create undue compression within the bone. The goal is to achieve a torque value that provides stable anchorage without placing excessive stress on surrounding tissue. The appropriate range can vary depending on implant design, bone type, and the specific clinical situation. Your clinician will interpret insertion torque alongside other clinical information rather than viewing a single number in isolation.

Can dental implants be placed if bone density is low?

In some cases, yes — though this depends on the degree of bone loss and its location. When insufficient bone volume or density is present, procedures such as bone grafting or sinus augmentation may be considered to build up the site before implant placement. These options are assessed on an individual basis during the treatment planning process. Pre-treatment imaging, including cone beam CT scanning, allows clinicians to evaluate bone quality and quantity in detail before making recommendations.

How long does it take for a dental implant to fully integrate with the bone?

Osseointegration typically takes between three and six months, though this varies between individuals and depends on factors including bone quality, the location of the implant within the jaw, the patient's general health, and the specific implant system used. The upper jaw generally requires a longer integration period than the lower jaw due to differences in bone density. Your clinician will advise on the expected healing timeline for your individual situation and will monitor progress before placing the final restoration.

What is resonance frequency analysis and how does it complement insertion torque measurement?

Resonance frequency analysis (RFA) is a non-invasive technique used to assess implant stability both at the time of placement and during the healing period. A small magnetic peg is attached to the implant and a device generates a vibration, measuring the resonant frequency to produce an Implant Stability Quotient (ISQ) score. Unlike insertion torque, which is measured only during placement, RFA can be repeated at follow-up appointments. The two measurements provide complementary information — insertion torque captures the initial mechanical engagement, while RFA tracks stability as healing progresses.

Can peri-implantitis affect implant stability after successful placement?

Yes. Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the gum tissue and bone around a dental implant, typically caused by bacterial plaque. If left unmanaged, it can lead to progressive bone loss around the implant, which may ultimately compromise stability even when initial placement was successful. This underlines the importance of ongoing oral hygiene and regular professional maintenance appointments. Early detection through routine monitoring allows timely intervention, which is more likely to be effective than treatment at an advanced stage.

Does insertion torque affect the decision about when to place a crown on the implant?

Insertion torque is one factor that clinicians may consider when deciding on the timing of placing the final or temporary crown (restoration). Higher insertion torque values, combined with good overall clinical findings, may in some circumstances support earlier restoration placement — sometimes called immediate or early loading. Lower values may indicate that a longer healing period is advisable before the implant is subjected to functional biting forces. However, this decision is always based on a combination of clinical findings and is discussed with each patient individually.

Conclusion

Insertion torque is a clinically meaningful measurement that helps dental professionals assess the initial stability of a dental implant at the time of placement. It reflects the degree to which an implant mechanically engages with the surrounding jawbone, and it forms part of a broader picture that guides treatment decisions — from healing timelines to restoration planning.

Understanding what insertion torque means can help patients feel more informed when discussing their dental implant treatment with their clinical team. However, it is important to recognise that implant stability is a dynamic process, beginning with mechanical anchorage at surgery and progressing through the biological bonding of osseointegration over the months that follow.

Long-term success is supported by careful pre-treatment planning, skilled surgical technique, appropriate healing protocols, and diligent ongoing oral hygiene. Individual outcomes vary, and suitability for treatment must always be determined through professional assessment.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

If you have questions about dental implants or would like to explore whether treatment may be appropriate for your situation, speaking with a qualified dental professional is the most reliable next step.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

What Factors Determine the Ideal Implant Diameter?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have been researching dental implants, you may have come across terms like "implant diameter" and wondered why it matters. It is a question many patients ask when trying to understand what makes a dental implant suitable for their individual situation. The size of an implant — particularly its diameter — is not a one-size-fits-all decision, and it plays a significant role in the long-term success of the treatment.

Dental implant diameter refers to the width of the titanium fixture that is placed into the jawbone. Choosing the correct diameter requires careful clinical evaluation and cannot be determined by an online article alone. Factors such as the amount of available bone, the location of the missing tooth, and a patient's overall oral health all influence the decision.

This article explains what dental implant diameter means, why it matters, and what variables a clinician will assess when determining the most appropriate size. Understanding these factors can help you feel more informed before attending a consultation.

What Is Dental Implant Diameter and Why Does It Matter?

Dental implant diameter refers to the width of the implant fixture — the screw-shaped component inserted into the jawbone to act as an artificial tooth root. Implant diameters typically range from around 3.0 mm for narrow or mini implants to 6.0 mm or more for wide-diameter implants, with standard diameters generally falling between 3.5 mm and 4.5 mm.

The diameter of an implant is clinically significant for several reasons. A wider implant generally provides greater surface contact with the surrounding bone, which can contribute to improved stability. However, selecting an implant that is too wide for the available bone can compromise bone integrity and neighbouring structures, such as adjacent tooth roots or nerves.

Conversely, an implant that is too narrow for the bite forces it will need to withstand may be at greater risk of mechanical failure over time. The implant diameter must therefore be balanced carefully against both the biological environment and the functional demands placed on it. This is why implant diameter selection is a clinical decision made on an individual basis — it is not determined by patient preference alone.

Understanding this concept can reassure patients that the process of implant planning is thorough and tailored, rather than arbitrary.

The Role of Bone Width and Bone Density

One of the most important clinical factors influencing implant diameter selection is the width of the alveolar bone — the ridge of bone that holds the teeth. When a tooth is lost, the surrounding bone can gradually resorb over time, reducing the available width and height. This means that the longer a tooth has been missing, the less bone may be available to accommodate an implant.

A clinician will typically use dental imaging — such as cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) or digital X-rays — to assess bone dimensions accurately before recommending an implant size. If bone width is limited, a narrower diameter implant may be selected, or bone augmentation procedures may be considered to build up the site before implant placement.

Bone density also plays a role. Denser bone, commonly found in the lower jaw (mandible), tends to provide better initial implant stability. Areas of lower bone density, such as parts of the upper jaw (maxilla), may influence the diameter and length of implant chosen to optimise the chances of successful osseointegration — the process by which the implant fuses with the surrounding bone.

If you are curious about whether your bone structure might support implants, a consultation with a qualified implant dentist is the appropriate starting point. You can learn more about the dental implant assessment process to understand what an initial evaluation typically involves.

Tooth Position and Functional Load

The location of the missing tooth within the dental arch is another key factor in determining the most appropriate implant diameter. Different teeth are subject to different levels of biting force, and this directly influences implant sizing considerations.

Front teeth (anterior region): Incisors and canines experience lighter lateral forces compared to back teeth. In the anterior region, aesthetics are also a significant consideration. The available bone in this area is often narrower, and implant placement must account for the visual outcome as well as function. Narrower diameter implants are frequently used in the front of the mouth.

Back teeth (posterior region): Premolars and molars are responsible for the majority of chewing function and are subject to considerable vertical and lateral forces. Wider diameter implants are often preferred in the posterior region to provide greater surface area and resist these higher functional loads.

The width of the tooth being replaced also provides a guide — the implant and its restoration should ideally reflect the natural proportions of the missing tooth without impinging on adjacent roots or compromising the interdental papillae (the gum tissue between teeth).

Adjacent Tooth Roots and Anatomical Structures

When selecting an implant diameter, the clinician must also carefully consider the proximity of neighbouring tooth roots and critical anatomical structures. Placing an implant too close to an adjacent root can cause damage to that tooth and compromise the health of surrounding bone.

In the upper jaw, structures such as the maxillary sinuses must be considered. In the lower jaw, the inferior alveolar nerve — which provides sensation to the lower lip and chin — runs within the mandible and must be avoided during implant placement.

The space available between adjacent teeth, often measured in millimetres, will naturally limit how wide an implant diameter can be. Generally, a minimum distance of around 1.5 mm between the implant surface and adjacent roots is considered clinically appropriate, though this can vary based on individual anatomy.

This is precisely why detailed three-dimensional imaging is so valuable during implant planning. It allows the clinician to map out the exact position of nerves, sinuses, and adjacent roots, ensuring the chosen implant diameter fits safely and comfortably within the available space. Treatment planning of this kind is a hallmark of responsible implant care.

Clinical Explanation: How Osseointegration Relates to Implant Diameter

Osseointegration is the biological process by which the titanium implant fixture becomes directly bonded to the surrounding jawbone. It is the foundation upon which the long-term success of a dental implant depends. Understanding this process helps explain why diameter selection matters so much.

Titanium is used for implants because it is biocompatible — the body does not reject it, and bone cells are able to grow directly onto and around the implant surface. Over a healing period of several weeks to months, the bone gradually integrates with the implant, providing a stable anchor for the final restoration.

The surface area of the implant in contact with bone is directly related to its diameter and length. A wider diameter implant offers greater surface area, which may support osseointegration in certain anatomical situations — particularly where bone density is lower. However, the benefit of increased diameter must always be weighed against the risk of encroaching on adjacent structures or compromising the surrounding bone walls.

Implant manufacturers design implants with varying surface textures and coatings to enhance osseointegration, but diameter remains one of the fundamental variables a clinician controls during the planning phase. This is why no two implant treatment plans are identical — each patient's bone biology and anatomy is unique.

Narrow Diameter Implants: When Are They Used?

Narrow diameter implants (NDIs), sometimes referred to as mini implants, typically range from approximately 2.9 mm to 3.3 mm in diameter. They are not simply a smaller version of standard implants — they have specific clinical indications and are not universally appropriate for all patients.

Narrow diameter implants may be considered in situations such as:

  • Limited bone width in the anterior region where bone augmentation is not suitable or desired
  • Small tooth spaces where standard implants would not fit without compromising adjacent roots
  • Replacement of smaller teeth, such as lower incisors or lateral incisors, where the anatomy is naturally narrower
  • Transitional use as a temporary support during healing phases

It is important to understand that narrow diameter implants carry different mechanical considerations compared to standard implants. They may be subject to a higher risk of fracture under heavy occlusal load if placed in inappropriate sites. This is why patient selection and clinical judgement are essential — narrow implants in the right situation can be highly effective, but they are not suitable for every case.

Discussing the full range of mini dental implant options available with a qualified clinician will help clarify which type of implant might be most appropriate for your individual needs.

Wide Diameter Implants and Their Applications

Wide diameter implants generally refer to fixtures of 5.0 mm or greater. They are typically used in the posterior regions of the mouth — particularly where molar teeth are being replaced — and in cases where the bone is wide enough to accommodate them safely.

The potential advantages of wide diameter implants in appropriate cases include:

  • Greater initial stability (primary stability) at the time of placement, which may support earlier loading protocols in suitable cases
  • Improved resistance to the high biting forces typically found in the molar region
  • Better support for wider restorations that more closely replicate the natural proportions of molar teeth

However, wide diameter implants are not without clinical considerations. Adequate bone width is essential — placing a wide implant in insufficient bone can result in thin bone walls around the fixture, which may compromise long-term bone health. Additionally, the risk of proximity to the mandibular nerve or maxillary sinus may be more pronounced with wider implants in certain anatomical areas.

As with all implant decisions, the appropriateness of a wide diameter implant depends entirely on individual clinical assessment. Imaging, bone quality evaluation, and occlusal analysis all form part of a thorough pre-treatment planning process.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

If you are considering dental implants, or have experienced tooth loss and are exploring your options, seeking professional dental evaluation is an important first step. A clinical assessment allows a qualified implant dentist to evaluate the factors discussed throughout this article in the context of your individual oral health.

You may wish to arrange a consultation if you:

  • Have experienced tooth loss or have been advised that tooth extraction may be necessary
  • Have been wearing a denture and wish to explore a more fixed tooth replacement
  • Are concerned about bone loss following tooth loss
  • Have previously been told you may not be suitable for implants due to bone volume — advances in planning and bone augmentation techniques mean that suitability should always be reassessed with up-to-date imaging
  • Experience discomfort or instability with an existing prosthesis

A dental consultation is not a commitment to treatment. It is an opportunity to receive an informed, personalised clinical opinion about your options and the suitability of different implant approaches for your situation.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

Prevention and Oral Health: Protecting Your Bone for Implant Success

Maintaining good oral health before, during, and after dental implant treatment is essential. Bone health in particular plays a central role in implant diameter selection and long-term implant success.

Preserve existing teeth where possible: Tooth loss leads to progressive bone resorption. The sooner a missing tooth is replaced — or the longer existing teeth are maintained — the more bone will be available for future implant placement.

Control gum disease: Periodontitis (advanced gum disease) is one of the leading causes of bone loss around teeth and implants. Regular dental examinations and professional cleaning help identify and manage gum disease early.

Avoid smoking: Smoking has a well-documented negative impact on healing and osseointegration. Patients who smoke are generally advised to reduce or stop before and after implant placement.

Maintain a nutritious diet: Adequate calcium and vitamin D support bone density, which may positively influence the bone environment around implants.

Attend regular dental check-ups: Even after successful implant placement, ongoing professional monitoring ensures early identification of any changes around the implant site.

If you are planning ahead for dental implant treatment, a dental implant maintenance appointment can help establish a healthy oral environment before the process begins.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implant diameter is a clinical decision based on multiple individual factors — it is not a standard size applied to every patient.
  • Available bone width and density are among the most important variables influencing implant diameter selection.
  • Tooth position matters: front teeth and back teeth require different implant size considerations due to aesthetic and functional differences.
  • Adjacent structures, including neighbouring roots, nerves, and sinuses, must be mapped carefully before implant diameter is finalised.
  • Narrow and wide diameter implants each have specific clinical indications — their suitability depends entirely on individual anatomy and case requirements.
  • Maintaining bone health through good oral hygiene, regular check-ups, and lifestyle choices supports the best possible environment for implant treatment.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a wider dental implant always perform better?

Not necessarily. A wider implant provides greater surface area in contact with bone, which can support stability in appropriate cases. However, if the available bone is insufficient in width, placing a wider implant can compromise the surrounding bone walls and neighbouring structures. The ideal implant diameter is the one that best fits the individual's bone anatomy, tooth position, and functional requirements — as determined through clinical assessment and imaging.

Can I have a dental implant if I have experienced bone loss?

Bone loss does not automatically rule out dental implants. Depending on the degree of bone loss, various approaches may be considered, including bone augmentation procedures that rebuild the available bone volume before implant placement. A thorough clinical assessment including three-dimensional imaging is required to evaluate the extent of bone loss and determine the most appropriate course of action for each patient.

How long does the implant planning process take before the diameter is decided?

The planning process varies depending on the complexity of the case. For straightforward implant placements, a single consultation including clinical examination and X-rays may be sufficient to inform planning decisions. For more complex cases involving bone assessment, multiple missing teeth, or anatomical considerations, further imaging such as CBCT scanning and a more detailed review period may be required. Your clinician will outline a clear timeline during the initial consultation.

Is implant diameter the same as implant length?

No. Implant diameter refers to the width of the fixture, while implant length refers to how deep the implant is placed into the bone. Both measurements are clinically significant and are selected based on available bone dimensions and the specific requirements of each treatment site. A clinician will assess both variables as part of the implant planning process.

Are narrow diameter implants as reliable as standard implants?

Narrow diameter implants can be highly effective when used in appropriate clinical situations — such as replacing smaller teeth in areas with limited bone width. However, they carry different mechanical properties compared to standard implants and may not be suitable for replacing teeth in areas subject to high biting forces, such as molars. Reliability depends on correct patient selection, careful planning, and appropriate aftercare.

Will the diameter of my implant affect how my final crown looks?

Yes, implant diameter can influence the design of the final crown and its emergence profile — the way the crown transitions from the implant at gum level. Appropriate diameter selection helps create a restoration that appears natural in proportion to adjacent teeth and supports healthy gum contours around the implant site. Your clinician and the dental laboratory will work together to achieve an aesthetic and functional outcome suited to your individual smile.

Conclusion

Understanding what factors determine the ideal dental implant diameter can help patients feel more informed and prepared when exploring implant treatment. The diameter of a dental implant is one of several carefully considered clinical variables — shaped by available bone width, tooth position, functional demands, and the proximity of important anatomical structures.

There is no single "correct" implant diameter that applies to every patient. The right choice depends on a thorough, individualised clinical assessment that takes the full picture of a patient's oral health into account. Whether narrow, standard, or wide diameter implants are being considered, the underlying principle remains the same: the chosen implant must fit safely within the available bone, support the restoration it will carry, and protect the surrounding biological environment.

Dental implant diameter selection is a clinical science, and advances in digital imaging and treatment planning continue to support more detailed and accurate implant planning. If you are considering dental implants or have questions about your suitability, consulting with a qualified implant dentist in London is the most appropriate and informative next step.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a GDC-registered dental professional.

What Happens at a Dental Implant Consultation? (Step by Step)

Written By

Dental Implants Team

If you are considering dental implants London, the consultation is your first and most important step. It is an assessment appointment — not a procedure — designed to evaluate your oral health, discuss your goals and determine whether implant treatment may be suitable for your situation.

Many patients feel uncertain about what to expect at an implant consultation, so this guide walks you through the typical process step by step. It is worth noting that every consultation is personalised. What is discussed and assessed will depend on your individual circumstances, medical history and clinical findings.

There is no obligation to proceed with treatment following a consultation. It is an opportunity to gather information, ask questions and make an informed decision in your own time.

Step 1: Discussing Your Dental and Medical History

Your consultation will typically begin with a detailed discussion about your health. This helps your dental team understand any factors that may influence treatment planning or healing.

What Will Be Discussed?

  • General health — including any long-term conditions such as diabetes, heart disease or osteoporosis
  • Medications — certain medications can affect healing, bone metabolism or bleeding, so your dental team needs a complete picture
  • Previous dental treatments — including past extractions, root canal treatments, dentures or previous implant work
  • Lifestyle factors — such as smoking, which can influence healing and long-term implant health
  • Allergies or sensitivities — to ensure materials and medications used are appropriate for you

This conversation is confidential and is conducted to ensure your safety and the quality of your care. Being open and thorough at this stage helps your dental team plan effectively.

Step 2: Clinical Examination of Your Teeth and Gums

A hands-on clinical examination allows your dentist to assess the current state of your oral health. This is a gentle, non-invasive process and an essential part of understanding your treatment needs.

What Does the Examination Include?

  • Gum health assessment — checking for signs of gum disease, inflammation or recession that may need to be addressed before implant treatment
  • Condition of remaining teeth — evaluating the health of your existing teeth and any restorations
  • Bite evaluation — assessing how your upper and lower teeth come together, which influences implant positioning and restoration design
  • Soft tissue assessment — examining the gum tissue in the area where implants may be placed

If any existing oral health issues are identified — such as gum disease or decay — these may need to be treated before implant placement can be considered. Your dentist will explain any preliminary steps and why they are important.

Step 3: Imaging and Diagnostic Scans

To plan implant treatment accurately, your dental team needs a detailed understanding of the bone and anatomy beneath the gum line. This is typically achieved through diagnostic imaging.

What Types of Imaging May Be Used?

  • Dental X-rays — standard radiographs that provide a two-dimensional view of your teeth, roots and bone levels
  • CBCT scans (3D imaging) — cone beam computed tomography provides a three-dimensional view of the jawbone, allowing precise assessment of bone volume, density and the position of nerves, sinuses and other anatomical structures
  • Intraoral photographs — clinical photographs may be taken to document your current oral condition and support treatment planning

Not all imaging is required at every consultation. Your dentist will determine which scans are appropriate based on your individual case. CBCT scans, where needed, provide a level of detail that supports more accurate implant positioning and reduces the risk of complications.

Step 4: Assessing Implant Suitability

Based on the information gathered from your medical history, clinical examination and imaging, your dentist will assess whether dental implants may be a suitable option for you.

Key Factors Considered

  • Bone support — whether there is sufficient bone volume and density to support an implant, or whether bone grafting may be needed
  • Space and alignment — whether there is adequate space for both the implant and the restoration, and how the implant will relate to neighbouring teeth
  • Medical considerations — whether any health conditions or medications may affect treatment planning, healing or long-term success
  • Oral health status — whether any existing conditions need to be addressed before implant treatment can proceed

It is important to understand that not every patient will be suitable for implant treatment, and suitability cannot be confirmed until a full assessment has been completed. If implants are not appropriate for your situation, your dentist will explain the reasons and discuss alternative options.

Step 5: Discussing Treatment Options

If the assessment suggests that implant treatment may be suitable, your dentist will discuss the options available to you. This is a collaborative conversation, not a one-way recommendation.

What Might Be Discussed?

  • Number of implants — whether a single implant, multiple implants or a full-arch solution is most appropriate for your needs
  • Treatment alternatives — other options such as bridges or dentures may be discussed where relevant, so you can compare and make an informed choice
  • Phased treatment planning — in some cases, treatment may be planned in stages, particularly if preparatory procedures such as bone grafting or gum treatment are needed first
  • Material options — the type of implant and restoration material may be discussed based on your clinical needs and preferences

Your dental team should welcome your questions at this stage. Understanding your options fully is an important part of making a decision that feels right for you.

Step 6: Explaining the Procedure and Healing Process

Your dentist will provide a clear explanation of what the implant procedure involves, so you know what to expect if you choose to proceed.

What Will Be Explained?

  • Implant placement — an overview of how the implant is surgically placed into the jawbone under local anaesthetic
  • Healing stages — the process of osseointegration (bone fusion), which typically takes several weeks to months depending on individual healing
  • Temporary restorations — whether a temporary tooth or denture will be provided during the healing period
  • Final restoration — how and when the permanent crown, bridge or denture will be fitted
  • Maintenance expectations — the ongoing care required to support the long-term health of your implant, including oral hygiene and regular dental reviews

Timelines for healing and treatment completion vary between patients and cannot be guaranteed in advance. Your dentist will provide an estimated timeline based on your individual case, but flexibility should be expected as healing is a biological process that differs from person to person.

Step 7: Transparent Cost Discussion

A clear understanding of costs is an essential part of treatment planning. During your consultation, the financial aspects of your proposed treatment should be discussed openly and transparently.

What to Expect

  • Written treatment plan — a detailed document outlining the proposed treatment stages, timeline and costs
  • What is included — clarity on which elements are covered in the quoted price, such as the implant, abutment, restoration and follow-up reviews
  • Additional costs — any preparatory procedures (such as bone grafting or extractions) that are not included in the main quotation
  • Finance options — if available, information about spreading the cost through monthly payments (subject to status and lender approval)

You should never feel pressured to commit to treatment at the consultation stage. A written quotation allows you to review the costs at home and make a decision in your own time. For more detail on pricing, visit our page on cost of dental implants London.

How Long Does a Dental Implant Consultation Take?

The length of a dental implant consultation can vary depending on the complexity of your case and the assessments required. As a general guide:

  • Typical duration — most implant consultations last between 30 and 60 minutes, though some may be longer if detailed imaging or complex discussion is needed
  • Follow-up appointments — in some cases, a second appointment may be needed to review scan results, finalise the treatment plan or carry out additional assessments

Your dental team will let you know at the time of booking approximately how long to allow for your appointment. It is always better to allow sufficient time so that the consultation is thorough and unhurried.

What Should You Bring to Your Consultation?

Being prepared for your consultation helps ensure that the appointment is as productive as possible. Here are some things you may wish to bring or have ready:

  • A list of your current medications — including dosages and how long you have been taking them
  • Details of any medical conditions — particularly those that may affect healing or bone health
  • Previous dental records or X-rays — if you have recent imaging from another practice, bringing it along may save time and avoid duplicate scans
  • A list of questions or concerns — writing down anything you want to ask ensures you do not forget during the appointment
  • Details of your GP or medical consultant — in case your dental team needs to liaise with your healthcare providers

If you do not have all of this information to hand, do not worry — your dental team can work with what is available and follow up on anything else that is needed.

Dental Implant Consultations in London

At our CQC-regulated practice in South Kensington, we approach every implant consultation with care, thoroughness and transparency. We understand that considering dental implants is a significant decision, and we believe you deserve all the information you need to make that decision confidently.

Our consultations are patient-led. We listen to your concerns, assess your situation carefully and explain your options clearly — without pressure or obligation. If implant treatment is suitable for you, we provide a detailed written treatment plan with transparent pricing. If it is not, we explain why and discuss alternatives that may help.

We welcome patients at all stages of their decision-making process — whether you are just beginning to explore the idea of implants or are ready to proceed with a plan. Our team is here to support you with honest, professional guidance every step of the way.

If you would like to find out more about what an implant consultation involves, or if you are ready to take the first step, please book a consultation in London. Our experienced team will be happy to welcome you and answer any questions you may have.

This article provides general information about what typically happens during a dental implant consultation. Individual consultations may vary depending on clinical findings, medical history and treatment complexity. Suitability for implant treatment cannot be confirmed until a full assessment has been completed. This content is not a substitute for personalised dental advice. Please consult your dentist for guidance specific to your situation.
