title: Why Does My Face Look Sunken After Tooth Loss?
seoTitle: Why Does My Face Look Sunken After Tooth Loss?
description: Discover why tooth loss can cause a sunken facial appearance, how bone resorption affects your jawline, and what treatment options may help restore structure.

images.alt: Why Does My Face Look Sunken After Tooth Loss?

html:
Back to Blog
Patient Education 25 Mar 2026 15 min read

Why Does My Face Look Sunken After Tooth Loss?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have lost one or more teeth, you may have noticed gradual changes to the shape of your face over time. Perhaps your cheeks appear hollower, your chin seems more prominent, or the lower third of your face looks shorter than it once did. These changes can feel unsettling, and it is entirely natural to want to understand why they are happening.

Many people search online to understand why their face looks sunken after tooth loss, often noticing these changes months or even years after the teeth were originally lost. The concern is common, and you are certainly not alone in experiencing it.

This article explains the biological processes behind facial changes following tooth loss, why the jawbone can gradually lose volume without the stimulation that natural teeth provide, and what treatment approaches may be available to help. Understanding the connection between missing teeth and facial structure is an important step, and where changes are a concern, seeking professional dental advice can help clarify what options may be suitable for your individual situation.

We will cover the causes, the science behind bone resorption, signs to look out for, and the preventative steps that may help preserve your oral health and facial structure.

Why Does Your Face Look Sunken After Tooth Loss?

Featured Snippet: A sunken face after tooth loss is typically caused by jawbone resorption. When teeth are missing, the underlying bone no longer receives the mechanical stimulation it needs to maintain its density and volume. Over time, the jawbone gradually shrinks, reducing the structural support for the overlying facial tissues and causing a collapsed or sunken appearance around the cheeks, lips, and chin.

How Tooth Loss Affects Your Facial Structure

Your teeth do far more than help you chew food and speak clearly. They play a crucial role in maintaining the structural framework of your face. Each natural tooth root sits within the jawbone, and every time you bite or chew, those roots transmit mechanical forces into the surrounding bone. This stimulation signals the body to continue renewing and maintaining bone tissue in that area.

When a tooth is lost â€” whether through decay, gum disease, trauma, or extraction â€” that stimulation ceases in the area where the root once sat. Without it, the body begins to reabsorb the bone in a natural process known as alveolar bone resorption. This process can begin within weeks of tooth loss and continues progressively over months and years.

The more teeth that are missing, and the longer they have been absent, the more significant the bone loss tends to be. This reduction in jawbone volume directly affects the contour of the face, as there is less underlying structure to support the cheeks, lips, and soft tissues. The result can be a noticeably sunken or aged appearance, even in relatively young patients.

The Science Behind Jawbone Resorption

To understand why the face changes shape, it helps to understand a little about how bone works. Bone is living tissue that is constantly being remodelled. Specialised cells called osteoblasts build new bone, whilst cells called osteoclasts break down and reabsorb old bone. In a healthy jaw with a full set of teeth, these two processes are broadly balanced.

The tooth roots act as anchors within the alveolar bone â€” the ridge of bone that houses the tooth sockets. Each time you bite down, the pressure travels through the tooth root into this bone, stimulating osteoblast activity and encouraging ongoing bone maintenance.

When a tooth is removed, the socket begins to heal, but without continued stimulation, osteoclast activity outpaces new bone formation. Studies suggest that the alveolar ridge can lose up to 25% of its width within the first year following extraction, and this resorption continues over subsequent years, albeit at a slower rate.

In cases where multiple teeth are missing, particularly across an entire arch, the cumulative bone loss can be substantial, fundamentally altering the proportions of the lower face. This is the primary mechanism behind the sunken facial appearance many patients notice.

Common Signs of Facial Changes After Tooth Loss

Facial changes caused by missing teeth and bone resorption tend to develop gradually, which means they can sometimes go unnoticed until they become quite pronounced. Some of the common signs include:

  • Hollow or sunken cheeks: The cheeks may lose their natural fullness as the underlying bone and tissue support diminishes.
  • Thinning lips: As bone volume decreases, the lips can lose their support and appear thinner or turned inward.
  • A shorter lower face: The distance between the nose and chin may appear reduced, sometimes described as facial collapse.
  • A more prominent chin: With reduced bone height in the upper or lower jaw, the chin can appear to protrude more than before.
  • Deepening of lines around the mouth: Wrinkles and folds around the mouth, sometimes called marionette lines, may become more pronounced.
  • Changes to how dentures fit: If you wear dentures, you may notice they become loose over time as the ridge they rest on continues to shrink.

These changes can affect confidence and self-esteem. If you have noticed any of these signs, a dental professional can assess the extent of any bone loss and discuss what options may be appropriate.

Who Is Most at Risk of Facial Changes?

Whilst anyone who has lost teeth can experience some degree of bone resorption, certain factors may increase the extent or speed of these changes:

  • Multiple missing teeth: The more teeth that are absent, the greater the area of unstimulated bone, and the more significant the potential for facial change.
  • Long-standing tooth loss: Bone resorption is a progressive process, so individuals who have been missing teeth for many years may experience more noticeable changes.
  • Long-term denture wear without implant support: Traditional dentures sit on the gum surface and do not stimulate the underlying bone in the same way that tooth roots do. Over time, the ridge beneath the denture can continue to resorb.
  • Gum disease history: Periodontal disease can cause bone loss around teeth even before they are lost, meaning the starting point for resorption may already be reduced.
  • General health factors: Conditions such as osteoporosis, nutritional deficiencies, and certain medications may influence bone density and remodelling.

Understanding your individual risk factors is something a dental professional can help with during a thorough clinical assessment.

How Dental Implants May Help Preserve Facial Structure

One of the most widely discussed treatment options for addressing bone loss after tooth loss is dental implant treatment. Dental implants are small titanium posts that are surgically placed into the jawbone, where they integrate with the surrounding bone tissue through a process called osseointegration.

Once integrated, implants function similarly to natural tooth roots. They transmit biting and chewing forces into the jawbone, providing the mechanical stimulation needed to help maintain bone density in the area. This is one of the key distinctions between implants and other tooth replacement options such as traditional bridges or dentures, which rest on the gum surface or are supported by adjacent teeth.

Research suggests that dental implants may help slow or reduce further bone resorption in the areas where they are placed. For patients who have already experienced some degree of facial change, replacing missing teeth with implants may help preserve remaining bone and support the facial soft tissues.

However, it is important to note that not every patient is a suitable candidate for implant treatment. Factors such as the amount of remaining bone, general health, oral hygiene, and lifestyle habits all play a role in determining suitability. A detailed clinical examination and imaging, such as a CBCT scan, are typically required before any treatment recommendations can be made.

Other Treatment Options to Consider

Dental implants are not the only option for replacing missing teeth, and the most appropriate treatment will depend on your individual circumstances. Other approaches include:

Dentures: Modern dentures can be well-crafted to restore appearance and function. However, as they sit on the gum surface, they do not directly stimulate the underlying bone. Over time, ongoing bone resorption may affect their fit, requiring periodic adjustments or relining.

Implant-retained dentures: For patients who wear dentures but are experiencing ongoing bone loss, implant-retained dentures may offer an alternative. These combine the convenience of a denture with the stability and bone-stimulating benefits of implants. Typically, a small number of implants are placed to anchor the denture securely.

Dental bridges: Bridges replace missing teeth by anchoring to adjacent natural teeth. They can restore appearance effectively, though they do not directly address bone resorption in the area of the missing tooth root.

Each option has its own advantages and considerations. A dental professional can discuss these with you in detail, taking into account your oral health, preferences, and clinical needs.

Can Bone Loss Be Reversed?

Once jawbone resorption has occurred, the lost bone does not regenerate on its own. However, there are clinical procedures that may help rebuild bone volume in certain cases.

Bone grafting is a surgical procedure in which bone material â€” sourced from the patient's own body, a donor, or a synthetic substitute â€” is placed in the area of deficiency. Over time, this graft material can integrate with the existing bone, increasing its volume and density. Bone grafting is sometimes carried out as a preparatory step before dental implant placement, particularly when the remaining bone is insufficient to support an implant.

Sinus lift procedures may be recommended when bone loss has occurred in the upper jaw near the sinus cavities. This procedure raises the sinus membrane and places bone graft material beneath it to increase the height of bone available for implant placement.

These procedures are not suitable for everyone, and outcomes depend on a range of individual factors. If you are concerned about bone loss, a consultation with a dental implant specialist can help determine whether bone augmentation procedures might be appropriate in your case.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice

Whilst it is not always possible to prevent tooth loss entirely, there are practical steps that may help reduce the risk and, in turn, help preserve facial structure:

  • Maintain good oral hygiene: Brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between teeth with interdental brushes or floss helps protect against decay and gum disease â€” the two leading causes of tooth loss.
  • Attend regular dental check-ups: Routine examinations allow your dentist to identify potential problems early, before they progress to the point where tooth loss becomes a possibility.
  • Address gum disease promptly: If you notice bleeding gums, persistent bad breath, or gum recession, seek dental advice. Early treatment of gum disease can help prevent the bone loss that accompanies its progression.
  • Consider tooth replacement sooner rather than later: If you have already lost a tooth, discussing replacement options with your dentist promptly may help limit the extent of bone resorption that occurs in the intervening period.
  • Eat a balanced diet: Adequate calcium, vitamin D, and other nutrients support overall bone health, including the jawbone.
  • Avoid smoking: Smoking is a significant risk factor for gum disease, implant failure, and impaired bone healing.

Taking a proactive approach to oral health is one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of tooth loss and its associated facial changes.

Key Points to Remember

  • Tooth loss removes the mechanical stimulation that keeps the jawbone healthy, leading to gradual bone resorption.
  • Bone resorption is the primary cause of the sunken facial appearance many people notice after losing teeth.
  • Changes to facial shape can develop gradually over months and years following tooth loss.
  • Dental implants may help preserve jawbone density by mimicking the function of natural tooth roots, though suitability varies.
  • Bone grafting procedures may be an option for patients who have already experienced significant bone loss.
  • Maintaining good oral hygiene and attending regular dental check-ups are amongst the most effective preventative measures.

Frequently Asked Questions

How quickly does the jawbone change after losing a tooth?

Bone resorption can begin within the first few weeks following tooth loss. Research indicates that the most significant changes in bone width tend to occur during the first 12 months, with studies reporting up to 25% reduction in ridge width within this initial period. The rate of resorption then typically slows but continues progressively over subsequent years. The speed and extent of change can vary considerably between individuals, depending on factors such as overall health, the number of teeth lost, and whether replacement teeth have been placed.

Can dentures prevent facial collapse?

Traditional removable dentures replace the visible portion of missing teeth and can restore appearance and chewing function. However, because they rest on the gum surface rather than being anchored within the bone, they do not provide the same level of stimulation to the jawbone that natural tooth roots or dental implants do. As a result, bone resorption may continue beneath the denture over time, which can lead to gradual changes in facial shape and an increasingly poor denture fit. Implant-retained dentures may offer improved bone preservation compared with conventional dentures.

Is facial collapse from tooth loss reversible?

Once bone resorption has occurred, the lost bone does not naturally regenerate. However, certain clinical procedures such as bone grafting may help rebuild bone volume in some cases. Replacing missing teeth with dental implants may also help slow or limit further bone loss in the treated area. The degree to which facial appearance can be improved depends on individual factors, including the extent of existing bone loss and overall health. A thorough clinical assessment is essential to determine what treatment options may be appropriate for each patient.

At what age is tooth loss most likely to cause facial changes?

Tooth loss can affect facial structure at any age, though the changes may be more noticeable in older adults, partly because age-related changes to skin elasticity and soft tissue volume can compound the effects of bone resorption. However, younger patients who lose teeth and do not have them replaced may also experience significant jawbone changes over time. The key factor is not age itself but the duration and extent of tooth loss, combined with individual biological factors that influence bone remodelling.

Does losing back teeth affect facial appearance?

Yes, losing posterior (back) teeth can affect facial appearance, even though these teeth are not visible when you smile. Back teeth play an important role in maintaining the vertical height of the bite and supporting the cheeks. When multiple back teeth are lost, the bite can collapse vertically, causing the lower face to appear shorter and the cheeks to look hollow. This is sometimes particularly noticeable when dentures are removed. Replacing missing back teeth can help restore proper bite height and facial support.

How can I find out if I have experienced bone loss?

Bone loss in the jaw is typically assessed through clinical examination and dental imaging. Your dentist may use standard dental X-rays to evaluate bone levels around existing teeth, or a more detailed three-dimensional scan such as a cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) scan to assess bone volume and density more precisely. If you are concerned about changes to your facial shape following tooth loss, booking a dental consultation is a sensible first step. Your dentist can assess your individual situation and discuss any findings with you.

Conclusion

A sunken facial appearance after tooth loss is a common concern, and understanding the underlying cause â€” jawbone resorption â€” can help make sense of the changes you may be noticing. When teeth are lost, the bone that once supported them gradually diminishes without the stimulation it needs to maintain itself. Over time, this can alter the proportions and contours of the face.

The good news is that there are treatment options available that may help address missing teeth and, in some cases, preserve or rebuild bone volume. From dental implants to bone grafting and implant-retained dentures, modern dentistry offers a range of approaches that can be tailored to individual needs.

However, the most important step is seeking professional guidance. Every patient's situation is different, and what is appropriate for one person may not be suitable for another.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

If you have concerns about facial changes related to tooth loss, or if you would like to understand your options, speaking with a qualified dental professional is the best place to start. Early assessment can help ensure you receive the most appropriate advice for your circumstances.

This article is intended for educational purposes only and does not constitute clinical advice or diagnosis. Treatment suitability depends on individual clinical assessment by a qualified dental professional.

Why Does My Implant Collect More Plaque Than My Natural Teeth?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many people who have had a dental implant placed notice something slightly unexpected during their daily oral hygiene routine — the area around the implant seems to gather plaque more readily than their natural teeth. If you have found yourself wondering about this, you are certainly not alone. It is one of the most common questions patients ask following implant treatment, and it is a very valid concern.

Understanding why dental implant plaque accumulation occurs is important not just for curiosity, but for protecting your long-term oral health. Plaque build-up around an implant can, over time, contribute to a condition known as peri-implantitis — a form of gum disease that affects the tissues surrounding the implant. Some patients first notice this through subtle gum changes around an implant.

In this article, we explain the biological and structural reasons why implants can be more susceptible to plaque, what that means for your daily oral care routine, and when it may be appropriate to seek a professional assessment. The information here is intended to be educational and reassuring, helping you feel more confident in caring for your implant.

Why Does My Dental Implant Collect More Plaque Than My Natural Teeth?

Dental implant plaque accumulation occurs because implants lack the natural biological structures of real teeth, such as the periodontal ligament and cementum, which help resist bacterial adhesion. The titanium surface and crown junction can also create micro-gaps and surface textures that encourage plaque to gather, requiring more thorough and specific cleaning techniques.

The Key Difference Between Implants and Natural Teeth

To understand why implants may collect more plaque, it helps to first appreciate how natural teeth and implants differ structurally.

Natural teeth are anchored into the jawbone via the periodontal ligament — a network of fibres that attaches the root to the surrounding bone. This ligament forms part of a sophisticated biological barrier that helps resist bacterial invasion. Additionally, the gum tissue around natural teeth forms a tight seal called the junctional epithelium, which offers a degree of protection against bacterial penetration.

Dental implants, by contrast, are titanium posts that integrate directly into the jawbone through a process called osseointegration. While this creates an incredibly stable and durable foundation, the implant does not benefit from the same biological attachment mechanism as a natural tooth root. The gum tissue attaches to the implant surface in a slightly different way — the connection is functional, but it is generally considered less resistant to bacterial challenge than the seal around a natural tooth.

This fundamental structural difference means that bacteria can find it somewhat easier to establish themselves in the region where the implant meets the gum — the peri-implant sulcus — compared with the equivalent area around a natural tooth.

Why the Surface of an Implant Encourages Plaque Build-Up

Beyond the biological differences, the physical characteristics of the implant and its crown can also play a role in plaque accumulation.

Titanium implant fixtures — the part embedded in the jawbone — are often deliberately given a roughened surface at the microscopic level. This micro-rough texture is intentional and beneficial during the healing phase because it encourages bone cells to bond with the implant surface more effectively, supporting osseointegration.

However, this same surface texture, if exposed to the oral environment above the gumline due to gum recession, can also provide an ideal landscape for bacteria to adhere to and colonise.

Additionally, the implant-abutment junction — the join between the titanium post and the abutment component that connects to your crown — can create a very small gap or micro-gap. Bacteria are opportunistic and can accumulate in this region, which is difficult to access with standard brushing alone.

The material of the crown itself may also differ slightly from natural enamel in terms of surface energy and how readily bacteria adhere to it, depending on the material used. Regular professional monitoring can help identify and manage any concerns about plaque in these areas. You can learn more about overall dental implant treatment options and what is involved in long-term implant care.

The Clinical Science: How Plaque Affects Implants Differently

The way plaque interacts with an implant is not identical to how it interacts with a natural tooth, and this distinction matters clinically.

With a natural tooth, the periodontal fibres provide a physical and immunological barrier. The blood supply to the periodontal ligament brings immune cells that can mount a localised defence against bacterial invasion to some degree.

Around an implant, the connective tissue attaches in parallel fibres running along the implant surface, rather than in the perpendicular, anchored arrangement seen around natural teeth. This means there is less of a structural barrier to bacterial migration moving deeper toward the bone.

When plaque is allowed to accumulate undisturbed around an implant, the initial inflammatory response in the surrounding gum tissue is called peri-implant mucositis — a reversible condition similar to gingivitis around natural teeth. If plaque control is not improved at this stage, the inflammation can progress to peri-implantitis, which involves bone loss around the implant and is considerably more complex to treat. The resilience of this tissue response is also influenced by blood supply during implant healing.

Research suggests that implants may progress from mucositis to peri-implantitis more rapidly than natural teeth progress from gingivitis to periodontitis under similar plaque conditions, reinforcing why specific cleaning habits around implants are so important.

Signs That Plaque May Be Causing a Problem Around Your Implant

Most people with healthy implants and good oral hygiene will not experience significant issues. However, it is worthwhile knowing which signs may indicate that plaque is beginning to have an effect on the tissues surrounding your implant.

Signs that may warrant a professional assessment include:

  • Bleeding or tenderness around the implant when brushing or using interdental brushes
  • Redness or swelling of the gum tissue immediately surrounding the implant crown
  • An unpleasant taste or odour that does not resolve with brushing
  • Visible changes in the appearance of the gum around the implant, including the gum appearing to recede or pull away
  • Discomfort or sensitivity in the implant area, particularly when chewing

It is important to note that implants themselves do not have nerves in the way natural teeth do, so significant discomfort around an implant is a signal to seek professional advice promptly. These symptoms do not necessarily mean something serious has developed, but early review allows your dental team to assess the situation and recommend appropriate care.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

If you notice any of the signs described above, or if you simply feel uncertain about how well you are managing plaque around your implant, it is sensible to arrange a professional assessment sooner rather than later.

Your dentist or dental hygienist will be able to:

  • Assess the health of the gum and bone tissue surrounding the implant
  • Identify any early signs of peri-implant mucositis or peri-implantitis
  • Provide professional cleaning around the implant using appropriate instruments that do not damage the implant surface
  • Advise you on refined cleaning techniques tailored to your specific implant placement and crown design

Routine implant maintenance appointments are widely recommended as part of responsible aftercare. The frequency of these appointments will depend on your individual clinical circumstances, which your dental team can advise you on. Early professional intervention when any concerns arise may support better outcomes, though results will depend on individual clinical circumstances.

If you are concerned about the health of your implant or are due a review, you may wish to explore our implant aftercare and maintenance guidance for further information.

How to Clean Around a Dental Implant Effectively

Good daily oral hygiene around a dental implant requires a slightly adapted approach compared to cleaning natural teeth. The following evidence-informed practices are generally recommended — however, your dental team may advise specific techniques based on your implant type and position.

Brushing

Use a soft-bristled toothbrush and brush twice daily, taking care to angle the brush gently toward the gum margin around the implant crown. Electric toothbrushes can be effective and are generally considered safe for use around implants — your dentist can confirm the most appropriate choice for you.

Interdental Cleaning

This is arguably the most important aspect of implant hygiene. Interdental brushes in the appropriate size for your implant spaces help remove plaque from the areas a standard toothbrush cannot reach. Water flossers (oral irrigators) are also widely recommended for cleaning around implants as they can flush debris from beneath the gum margin.

Flossing

Implant-specific floss or PTFE floss can be used around implants. Some patients find a floss threader helpful for accessing beneath the crown. Wrapping floss around the implant base in a C-shape and moving it gently below the gum margin can help dislodge plaque.

Mouthwash

An antimicrobial mouthwash may be recommended in certain circumstances, though this should be guided by your dental professional rather than used routinely without advice.

Prevention and Long-Term Implant Health

Preventing plaque build-up around a dental implant is fundamentally about consistency and technique. The most effective protective measures centre on:

  • Daily interdental cleaning — every day, without exception
  • Regular professional maintenance — attending hygiene appointments as recommended by your dental team
  • Routine implant monitoring — periodic X-rays and clinical checks allow your dentist to assess bone levels and catch any early changes
  • Smoking cessation — smoking is strongly associated with increased peri-implant complications and impaired healing; support to stop smoking is available through your GP and NHS resources
  • Managing medical conditions — conditions such as uncontrolled diabetes are associated with greater susceptibility to peri-implant disease; working with your GP to manage systemic health supports implant longevity
  • Maintaining a balanced diet — reducing fermentable carbohydrates limits the fuel available to plaque bacteria

Implants can achieve good long-term outcomes when properly maintained, though individual results will vary depending on clinical circumstances. Understanding the specific hygiene requirements of your implant is one of the most valuable things you can do to protect your investment in your oral health. If you are considering implant treatment or have recently had an implant placed, you can contact our London team for personalised aftercare guidance.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implant plaque accumulation is common and occurs due to structural differences between implants and natural teeth — it does not indicate that something has gone wrong
  • Implants lack the periodontal ligament found around natural teeth, making the surrounding gum tissue slightly more vulnerable to bacterial challenge
  • The micro-rough surface of titanium implants and the implant-abutment junction can provide areas where plaque more readily adheres
  • Unchecked plaque around an implant can progress from reversible mucositis to peri-implantitis, which affects the surrounding bone
  • Daily interdental cleaning and regular professional maintenance appointments are essential for long-term implant health
  • Any signs of bleeding, swelling, discomfort, or gum changes around an implant warrant a professional assessment

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a dental implant to attract more plaque than a real tooth?

Yes, it is relatively common for patients to notice more plaque around their implant. This is primarily because implants lack the natural periodontal attachment of real teeth, and the implant surface and crown junction can create areas where bacteria gather more easily. It does not mean your implant is failing, but it does highlight the importance of thorough, consistent oral hygiene and regular professional cleaning. Your dental hygienist can assess your plaque control and advise on the most effective cleaning routine for your specific implant.

What is peri-implantitis and how does it differ from gum disease?

Peri-implantitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the gum and bone tissue surrounding a dental implant, caused primarily by bacterial plaque. It is similar in some respects to periodontitis (gum disease) around natural teeth, but the progression can differ due to the structural differences between implants and natural teeth. Early-stage peri-implant inflammation (peri-implant mucositis) is reversible with improved plaque control. More advanced peri-implantitis involving bone loss requires professional treatment and is more complex to manage. Early detection is therefore very important.

Can I use an electric toothbrush on my dental implant?

In most cases, electric toothbrushes are considered safe and effective for cleaning around dental implants. Sonic and oscillating-rotating electric brushes can help remove plaque more thoroughly than manual brushing alone. However, you should always follow the guidance of your own dental team, as they can advise on the most appropriate type of brush and technique based on your implant design and position. Avoid using very stiff bristles, which could potentially irritate the surrounding gum tissue.

How often should I have my dental implant professionally cleaned?

The frequency of professional implant maintenance will depend on your individual clinical circumstances, including your overall gum health, plaque control, and whether you have any risk factors such as smoking or diabetes. Many patients attend every three to six months for professional cleaning and monitoring. Your dental team will advise on the most appropriate recall interval for you. Consistent professional maintenance is considered an important factor in supporting long-term implant health, alongside individual clinical circumstances.

Why do implants not feel sensitivity the way natural teeth do?

Dental implants integrate directly with the jawbone and do not contain a pulp (nerve and blood vessel tissue) as natural teeth do. This means implants themselves will not produce the same type of sensitivity to temperature or pressure that natural teeth can. However, the bone and gum tissue surrounding the implant do have a nerve supply, so discomfort in the area around an implant — particularly if persistent — should always be assessed by a dental professional. The absence of sensitivity in the implant crown does not mean problems cannot develop in the surrounding tissues.

Can plaque around an implant cause bad breath?

Yes, plaque accumulation around a dental implant can contribute to bad breath (halitosis). Bacteria in plaque produce volatile sulphur compounds, which are a common cause of unpleasant oral odour. If you notice a persistent bad taste or odour associated with your implant area despite thorough brushing, this may indicate plaque build-up or early peri-implant tissue changes. A professional assessment can identify the cause and guide appropriate treatment. Improving interdental cleaning around the implant and attending regular hygiene appointments can help address this.

Conclusion

Understanding why dental implants can collect more plaque than natural teeth helps you take a more informed and proactive approach to your daily oral hygiene. The structural differences between an implant and a natural tooth — including the absence of the periodontal ligament and the characteristics of the implant surface — mean that targeted, consistent cleaning is essential, not optional.

The good news is that with the right oral hygiene habits and regular professional maintenance, the vast majority of implants remain healthy and functional for many years. Dental implant plaque accumulation is a manageable concern, not an inevitable problem.

If you have any concerns about your implant — whether related to plaque, gum changes, discomfort, or simply wanting reassurance — seeking professional advice is always the appropriate step. Early assessment supports the best possible outcomes.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

title: Why Does My Implant Crown Feel Loose and What to Do

description: Wondering why your implant crown feels loose? Learn the common causes, warning signs, and what steps to take. Professional dental advice for London patients.

images.alt: Why Does My Implant Crown Feel Loose and What to Do

html:

Patient Education 7 Mar 2026 14 min read

Why Does My Implant Crown Feel Loose and What to Do

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Noticing that your implant crown feels loose can be an unsettling experience. After investing time and care into restoring your smile with a dental implant, any unexpected movement or wobble understandably causes concern. It is one of the most common reasons patients search online for reassurance and guidance â€” and rightly so, because understanding what may be happening is an important first step.

A loose implant crown does not always indicate a serious problem, but it is something that warrants attention. There are several possible reasons why an implant crown may begin to feel less secure, ranging from a simple loosening of the connecting component to more complex underlying issues. Each situation is different, and the appropriate course of action depends on the specific cause.

This article explains the most common reasons an implant crown may feel loose, what signs to be aware of, how the issue is typically addressed in a clinical setting, and when it may be appropriate to seek professional dental advice. Understanding the possible causes can help you feel more informed and confident about taking the right next step for your oral health.

A loose implant crown typically occurs when the abutment screw connecting the crown to the implant fixture becomes loosened, or when the cement holding the crown in place begins to deteriorate. Less commonly, it may indicate an issue with the implant itself. A professional clinical assessment is needed to identify the exact cause and determine the most appropriate course of action.

How a Dental Implant Crown Is Structured

To understand why an implant crown might feel loose, it helps to know how the restoration is constructed. A dental implant system typically consists of three main components:

  • The implant fixture â€” a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone, where it integrates with the bone over time through a process called osseointegration.
  • The abutment â€” a connector piece that sits on top of the implant fixture and provides a stable platform for the crown.
  • The crown â€” the visible tooth-shaped restoration that is either cemented or screw-retained onto the abutment.

Each of these components plays a critical role in the stability of the final restoration. When patients describe their implant crown feeling loose, the sensation may originate from any one of these connection points. In many cases, the implant fixture itself remains firmly integrated within the bone, and the looseness is related to the abutment or crown connection â€” which is often a more straightforward matter to address.

Understanding this layered structure helps explain why a dental professional needs to examine the implant carefully to determine exactly where the issue lies before recommending any treatment.

Common Causes of a Loose Implant Crown

Several factors can contribute to an implant crown feeling loose. The most frequently encountered causes include:

Abutment Screw Loosening

The small screw that secures the abutment to the implant fixture can gradually loosen over time due to normal chewing forces, minor micro-movements, or inadequate initial torque during placement. This is one of the most common and typically most straightforward causes to address.

Cement Washout

For cement-retained crowns, the dental cement bonding the crown to the abutment may degrade over months or years. Saliva exposure, temperature changes from hot and cold foods, and general wear can all contribute to cement breakdown, resulting in a crown that feels mobile.

Prosthetic Component Wear

Over time, the mechanical components of the implant system may experience wear, particularly in patients who clench or grind their teeth (bruxism). This can affect the fit between the crown and the abutment.

Issues With Osseointegration

In rarer cases, the implant fixture itself may not have fully integrated with the jawbone, or it may have lost integration due to infection or excessive loading. This requires careful clinical and radiographic assessment.

Each cause requires a different clinical approach, which is why professional evaluation is essential.

Signs and Symptoms to Be Aware Of

Recognising the signs early can help ensure timely professional assessment. Patients who have a loose implant crown may notice one or more of the following:

  • A clicking or rocking sensation when biting, chewing, or pressing on the crown with the tongue
  • Visible movement of the crown when touched
  • A change in the way the teeth bite together, which may feel as though the crown has shifted slightly
  • Discomfort or mild tenderness around the implant site, particularly during eating
  • An unusual taste in the mouth, which could suggest cement breakdown or the beginning of bacterial accumulation around the loose component
  • Gum inflammation or redness around the base of the crown

It is worth noting that some of these symptoms may be subtle initially. A crown may feel slightly different without being visibly loose. If you notice any change in how your implant crown feels or functions, it is sensible to arrange a dental assessment rather than waiting for the problem to progress.

Remaining calm and observant is helpful â€” most causes of a loose implant crown are manageable when identified early.

The Clinical Science Behind Implant Crown Stability

The long-term success of a dental implant depends heavily on a biological process called osseointegration. After the titanium implant fixture is placed in the jawbone, the surrounding bone cells gradually grow and bond directly to the surface of the implant over a period of several weeks to months. This creates a remarkably strong and stable foundation â€” similar in many ways to a natural tooth root anchored in bone.

Once osseointegration is complete, the implant is capable of withstanding normal biting and chewing forces. However, the mechanical components above the bone level â€” the abutment and crown â€” are subject to ongoing stress. Every time you bite down, lateral and vertical forces are transmitted through the crown, into the abutment, through the screw connection, and into the implant fixture.

Over thousands of chewing cycles, even precisely engineered components can experience micro-movement. This is why periodic dental reviews are valuable â€” they allow your dentist to check the integrity of all components, assess the health of the surrounding bone and gum tissue, and identify any early signs of loosening before symptoms become noticeable.

Maintaining healthy bone and gum tissue around the implant is equally important, as infection (peri-implantitis) can compromise the bone support and, in turn, the stability of the entire implant system.

What to Do If Your Implant Crown Feels Loose

If you suspect your implant crown is loose, there are some practical steps you can take whilst arranging a professional assessment:

Avoid Wiggling the Crown

It may be tempting to test the movement with your fingers or tongue, but repeatedly manipulating a loose crown can worsen the problem, damage the abutment screw, or introduce bacteria beneath the restoration.

Be Cautious With Eating

Try to avoid chewing hard or sticky foods on the affected side. Reducing the mechanical load on the implant crown can help prevent further loosening or component damage.

Maintain Oral Hygiene

Continue brushing and cleaning around the implant site gently. Good oral hygiene helps reduce the risk of bacterial build-up, which is particularly important if there is a gap forming between the crown and the abutment.

Contact Your Dental Practice

Arrange an appointment with your dental professional as soon as is practical. A loose implant crown is not typically a dental emergency, but it does benefit from timely assessment. Your dentist can perform a clinical examination and take radiographs to determine the cause and recommend an appropriate solution.

Do Not Attempt to Re-cement the Crown Yourself

Over-the-counter dental adhesives are not suitable for implant restorations and could interfere with the proper clinical repair.

How a Dentist May Address a Loose Implant Crown

The treatment for a loose implant crown depends entirely on the underlying cause, which your dentist will determine through careful examination. Common approaches include:

Retightening the Abutment Screw

If the abutment screw has loosened, the dentist can remove the crown, clean the components, and retighten the screw to the manufacturer's recommended torque setting using a calibrated torque wrench. This is often a relatively quick and straightforward procedure.

Re-cementing the Crown

For cement-retained crowns where the cement has failed, the crown can be cleaned and re-cemented with fresh dental cement. The dentist will also assess whether the abutment and crown fit remain satisfactory.

Component Replacement

If any prosthetic component shows signs of wear, fracture, or damage, it may need to be replaced. Modern implant systems are designed with interchangeable parts, making this process manageable.

Assessing Implant Integration

If there is any concern about the implant fixture itself, radiographic imaging and clinical tests can assess whether osseointegration has been maintained. Further treatment planning would be discussed on an individual basis if needed.

Treatment suitability always depends on a thorough clinical examination and individual assessment.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

While a slightly loose-feeling crown may not always represent an urgent situation, there are circumstances where seeking prompt dental advice is particularly important:

  • The crown has come off completely â€” keep it safe and clean, and contact your dental practice promptly
  • You experience persistent or worsening pain around the implant site
  • There is noticeable swelling, redness, or pus around the gum tissue near the implant
  • You notice bleeding from the gum tissue surrounding the implant when brushing
  • The implant itself feels mobile, rather than just the crown
  • You have difficulty eating or biting due to changes in the position of the crown

These symptoms may indicate infection, mechanical failure, or other conditions that benefit from early professional attention. It is always better to have a concern assessed and find it to be minor than to delay and risk a more complex issue developing.

Your dental team is there to help, and most implant-related concerns can be resolved effectively when addressed in a timely manner.

How to Help Maintain Your Implant Crown Long-Term

Taking good care of your dental implant can help reduce the likelihood of complications, including crown loosening. Here are some practical steps:

  • Brush twice daily with a soft-bristled toothbrush, paying careful attention to the gum line around the implant
  • Use interdental brushes or floss designed for use around implants to clean areas that a regular toothbrush may miss
  • Attend regular dental reviews â€” your dentist can monitor the implant, check component tightness, and assess the health of the surrounding tissues
  • Discuss bruxism with your dentist if you clench or grind your teeth, as a protective night guard may be recommended to reduce excessive force on the implant crown
  • Avoid using your teeth as tools â€” opening packaging or biting hard objects can place unusual stress on the restoration
  • Maintain overall gum health â€” healthy gum and bone tissue provide the foundation for long-term implant stability, so managing conditions such as gum disease is important

Prevention is always preferable to treatment, and consistent oral care is one of the most effective ways to support the longevity of your implant restoration.

Key Points to Remember

  • A loose implant crown is a relatively common issue that can often be resolved with professional treatment
  • The most frequent cause is loosening of the abutment screw or failure of the cement holding the crown
  • Avoid manipulating the loose crown with your fingers or tongue, and reduce chewing on that side
  • Arrange a dental appointment promptly to have the cause assessed
  • Regular dental reviews and good oral hygiene help maintain long-term implant stability
  • Treatment suitability depends on individual clinical assessment â€” your dentist will recommend the most appropriate approach for your situation

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a loose implant crown a dental emergency?

A loose implant crown is not usually classified as a dental emergency, but it does warrant prompt professional attention. If the crown has come off entirely or you are experiencing significant pain, swelling, or signs of infection, contact your dental practice as soon as possible. In most cases, arranging an appointment within a few days is appropriate. Avoiding hard foods on the affected side and maintaining gentle oral hygiene around the area can help in the interim. Your dentist will assess the situation and determine the best course of action based on the specific cause.

Can a loose implant crown be fixed without replacing the implant?

In the majority of cases, yes. A loose implant crown is most commonly caused by a loosened abutment screw or cement failure â€” both of which can typically be addressed without any intervention to the implant fixture itself. The dentist can retighten the screw, re-cement the crown, or replace a worn component as needed. It is relatively uncommon for the implant fixture to be the source of the problem, but this can be confirmed through clinical examination and imaging. Each case is assessed individually to determine the most appropriate solution.

How long should an implant crown last before it loosens?

A well-maintained implant crown can function effectively for many years. However, there is no universal guarantee of a specific lifespan, as longevity depends on factors including oral hygiene, bite forces, the quality of the original restoration, and individual patient factors such as bruxism. Some patients may never experience loosening, while others may require minor component maintenance over time. Regular dental reviews allow your dentist to monitor the implant system and address any early signs of wear or loosening before they become problematic.

What happens if I ignore a loose implant crown?

Leaving a loose implant crown unaddressed may allow bacteria to accumulate beneath the restoration, potentially leading to infection of the surrounding gum and bone tissue â€” a condition known as peri-implantitis. Additionally, a loose crown can cause uneven bite forces, which may damage the abutment screw or other components further. In some cases, the crown could detach entirely, creating a risk of swallowing or inhaling the restoration. Seeking timely dental assessment helps prevent minor issues from developing into more complex and costly problems.

Will my dental insurance cover the repair of a loose implant crown?

Coverage varies significantly between insurance policies. Some dental insurance plans may cover the cost of re-cementing or retightening an implant crown, while others may classify it as a prosthetic repair with different levels of coverage. It is advisable to check your individual policy details or contact your insurance provider directly. Your dental practice may also be able to provide a treatment estimate to help you understand the costs involved before proceeding with any recommended work.

Can I prevent my implant crown from becoming loose?

While it is not possible to guarantee that an implant crown will never loosen, you can significantly reduce the risk through consistent oral hygiene, regular dental check-ups, and managing habits such as teeth grinding. If your dentist identifies that you clench or grind your teeth, wearing a custom night guard can help protect the implant and its components from excessive force. Avoiding very hard foods and not using your teeth to open or tear objects also reduces unnecessary stress on the restoration.

Conclusion

A loose implant crown is understandably concerning, but in most cases, it is a manageable issue with well-established clinical solutions. Whether the cause is a loosened abutment screw, cement deterioration, or component wear, your dental professional can assess the situation and recommend the most appropriate course of action for your individual circumstances.

The key is not to ignore the symptoms. Early assessment typically leads to simpler, more straightforward treatment. Maintaining good oral hygiene, attending regular dental reviews, and being mindful of habits that place excessive force on your teeth all contribute to the long-term success of your implant restoration.

If your implant crown feels loose or you have noticed any changes in how it feels or functions, arranging a professional assessment is a sensible next step.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

Why Does My Implant Crown Feel Slightly Different After Several Years?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

It is not uncommon for patients to notice that their implant crown feels slightly different after several years — perhaps a subtle change in the way it bites, a minor shift in sensation, or simply a feeling that is hard to put into words. Many people turn to the internet for reassurance, unsure whether this is a normal sign of aging in the restoration or something that warrants a closer look.

Dental implant crowns are designed to be long-lasting and highly functional, but like all dental restorations, they exist within a dynamic oral environment that changes over time. The surrounding gum tissue, adjacent natural teeth, and even the position of your jaw can evolve across the years.

This article aims to explain the most common reasons why an implant crown may feel different after several years, what changes are considered normal, and which situations may benefit from a professional dental assessment. Understanding these factors can help you feel more informed and confident about your dental health.

An implant crown feeling slightly different after several years is relatively common and may result from changes in bite alignment, natural wear of the crown material, minor shifts in surrounding gum tissue, or slight loosening of the abutment screw. While some changes are normal, a dental examination can help determine whether any adjustment or intervention is appropriate.

What Is an Implant Crown and How Does It Work?

A dental implant crown is the visible, tooth-like restoration that sits on top of the titanium implant fixture embedded in the jawbone. It is typically connected via a small component called an abutment, which acts as a connector between the implant body and the crown itself.

Unlike natural teeth, implant crowns do not have a periodontal ligament — the network of fibres that connects natural tooth roots to the surrounding bone and provides sensory feedback. This means the way you perceive biting force and sensation through an implant crown is inherently different from a natural tooth, and this difference may become more noticeable over time, particularly as the surrounding natural teeth experience their own age-related changes.

The crown material — whether porcelain, zirconia, or a composite — is highly durable, but it is not impervious to gradual wear or minor changes over years of normal function. Understanding the nature of these restorations helps contextualise why subtle changes in feel can occur and why monitoring them professionally is a sensible approach.

Common Reasons an Implant Crown May Feel Different Over Time

There are several well-recognised reasons why an implant crown might feel subtly different after several years of use. These range from entirely normal wear-related changes to situations that may warrant clinical review.

Natural wear of crown material: Over time, the biting surface of an implant crown can undergo gradual wear, especially in patients who grind or clench their teeth. This may alter the feel of the bite slightly.

Changes in adjacent natural teeth: Natural teeth can shift, wear down, or be restored, all of which may subtly change the relationship between the implant crown and surrounding teeth.

Gum tissue changes: The soft tissue around the implant may remodel gently over years, affecting the way the crown sits at the gum margin and how it feels when touched.

Bite changes: Your overall bite pattern — known as occlusion — can change due to factors such as tooth movement, restoration of other teeth, or changes in the jaw joint.

Abutment screw dynamics: In some cases, the small internal screw holding the crown to the implant can loosen marginally over time, creating a subtle change in the feel of the crown during biting. This is often discussed clinically as a loose implant screw.

If you have noticed any of these changes, scheduling a review with your dental professional is a reasonable and sensible step.

The Clinical Science Behind How Implant Crowns Interact With the Jaw

To understand why implant crowns can feel different over time, it helps to consider some of the underlying dental science — explained in straightforward terms.

Natural teeth are suspended in the jaw by the periodontal ligament, a dense network of fibres that acts almost like a subtle shock absorber. This ligament also provides proprioception — essentially, the sensory awareness of how hard you are biting and where your teeth are meeting. When a tooth is replaced with a dental implant, this ligament is absent. The implant integrates directly with the bone in a process called osseointegration, which is what makes implants stable and long-lasting.

However, because there is no periodontal ligament, the brain receives different sensory feedback from an implant crown compared to a natural tooth. Over time, your natural teeth may migrate or wear slightly, while the implant crown remains fixed. This mismatch between the static implant crown and the evolving natural dentition can contribute to subtle changes in how the crown feels during biting, chewing, or even at rest.

Additionally, the surrounding bone itself can undergo minor remodelling over many years, which may subtly influence the gum profile around the implant. This is a natural biological process, not necessarily a sign that anything is wrong — though it is worth monitoring.

To learn more about how dental implants integrate with the jaw and what to expect long-term, explore our single tooth implant treatment information.

Signs That Might Benefit From a Professional Dental Review

While many subtle changes in how an implant crown feels are benign, there are certain symptoms that make a professional dental assessment a sensible course of action. It is important to approach these calmly — experiencing any of the following does not automatically indicate a serious problem, but a clinical examination can provide clarity.

You may wish to arrange a dental review if you notice:

  • A change in how the crown meets the opposing teeth during biting or chewing
  • Any sensation of movement or looseness in the crown
  • Tenderness or mild discomfort in the gum tissue around the implant
  • Visible changes in the gum margin, such as recession revealing the edge of the crown
  • Difficulty chewing on the side where the implant is located
  • A feeling that the crown is sitting higher or lower than before
  • Any persistent sensitivity in the surrounding area

None of these symptoms should be a cause for alarm, but they do benefit from professional assessment. Early review often means straightforward management — for example, a simple bite adjustment or retightening of an abutment screw — rather than more complex intervention later.

If you have concerns about your implant, arranging a dental implant review with a qualified dental professional is a sensible first step.

How Bite Changes Can Affect the Feel of an Implant Crown

The way your upper and lower teeth meet — your occlusion — is not static. Over the course of several years, a range of factors can cause the bite to shift, and these changes may be particularly noticeable in relation to an implant crown.

Natural teeth have a small degree of movement within the periodontal ligament, allowing them to adapt gradually to bite forces and minor positional changes. An implant crown, firmly anchored in bone, cannot move in the same way. As a result, if the surrounding natural teeth shift — even by a fraction of a millimetre — the implant crown may begin to feel like it is in a slightly different position relative to the bite. If this topic sounds familiar, you may also find this article on teeth shifting around an existing implant helpful.

Similarly, if other teeth have been restored, crowned, or extracted since the implant was placed, these changes alter the overall bite pattern. Jaw joint changes, which can occur with age or as a result of habits such as teeth grinding, may also influence the feel of the bite.

In many cases, a straightforward bite adjustment — a procedure known as occlusal equilibration — carried out during a routine dental review can resolve the sensation effectively. This involves the dentist carefully assessing where the teeth meet and making minor, precise adjustments to the crown surface. It is a conservative and common procedure.

The Role of Teeth Grinding and Clenching (Bruxism)

Bruxism — the habit of grinding or clenching the teeth, often during sleep — is a significant factor in how dental restorations perform and feel over time. Many people are unaware they grind their teeth until a dentist identifies signs of wear.

For patients with implant crowns, bruxism can accelerate wear of the crown surface, potentially alter the bite, and place additional stress on the implant and abutment. Over several years, this may contribute to the sensation that the crown feels different or that the bite has changed.

If bruxism is identified, a custom-made occlusal splint (sometimes called a night guard) is often recommended. This is a removable appliance worn during sleep that helps to protect both natural teeth and implant restorations from the effects of grinding forces. It does not cure bruxism, but it serves as an effective protective measure.

Discussing your habits with your dentist — including any jaw soreness in the morning, headaches, or tooth sensitivity — can help identify whether bruxism may be contributing to any changes you are experiencing with your implant crown.

Maintenance and Prevention: Caring for Your Implant Crown Long-Term

Good maintenance is fundamental to the long-term performance and comfort of a dental implant crown. While implant crowns cannot develop decay in the way natural teeth can, the surrounding tissues and the implant components require consistent care.

Practical steps to support long-term implant health:

  • Brush twice daily using a soft-bristled toothbrush, ensuring you clean gently around the base of the implant crown where it meets the gum.
  • Use interdental cleaning aids such as floss, interdental brushes, or a water flosser to clean between the implant crown and adjacent teeth.
  • Attend routine dental and hygiene appointments so that any changes in the crown, bite, or surrounding tissues can be identified and addressed promptly.
  • Inform your dentist of any changes in how the crown feels, even if subtle. Changes noted early are generally easier to manage.
  • Wear a night guard if recommended, particularly if you are aware of or have been advised about teeth grinding or clenching.
  • Avoid very hard foods that place excessive force on any dental restoration, including implant crowns.
  • Do not use your teeth as tools — opening packaging or biting fingernails can place unexpected stress on restorations.

For comprehensive guidance on looking after your implant long-term, your dental hygienist is an excellent resource and can tailor advice to your individual situation. Learn more about professional implant maintenance support and how regular visits can contribute to implant longevity.

Key Points to Remember

  • It is relatively common for an implant crown to feel subtly different after several years of use.
  • Changes may be due to natural wear of the crown material, bite changes, gum tissue remodelling, or minor loosening of the abutment screw.
  • Because implant crowns do not have a periodontal ligament, they interact with the bite differently to natural teeth, and this difference may become more noticeable over time.
  • Many changes are manageable with straightforward dental review and conservative adjustments.
  • Symptoms such as looseness, persistent discomfort, or visible gum changes around the implant are worth having assessed professionally.
  • Consistent home care and regular dental appointments are the foundation of long-term implant crown health.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a dental implant crown to feel different after a few years?

Yes, it is not unusual for patients to notice subtle changes in how an implant crown feels after several years. Factors such as natural wear of the crown surface, changes in surrounding teeth, bite evolution, and gum tissue remodelling can all contribute. Because implant crowns are fixed in bone without a periodontal ligament, they do not adapt to bite changes in the way natural teeth do. If the change is notable or accompanied by other symptoms, a dental review is advisable.

Could my implant crown be loose?

It is possible for the abutment screw — which connects the crown to the implant body — to loosen over time. This may produce a sensation of slight movement or instability in the crown. This is generally a straightforward matter for a dental professional to address. It is important not to ignore this sensation, as a loose crown left unmanaged may put uneven stress on the implant. A routine appointment to assess and, if needed, retighten the screw is the appropriate course of action.

Can the gum around an implant crown change over time?

Yes, the gum tissue surrounding a dental implant can undergo gradual changes over the years. Minor recession or remodelling of the soft tissue is a recognised occurrence and may cause the crown to appear to sit slightly differently. In some cases, the edge of the crown or the abutment beneath may become marginally visible. Regular professional monitoring allows any changes to be tracked and assessed within the context of your overall implant health.

Does teeth grinding affect an implant crown differently to a natural tooth?

Yes, bruxism (teeth grinding and clenching) can affect implant crowns differently to natural teeth. Natural teeth have some degree of flexibility due to the periodontal ligament, whereas implant crowns are rigidly anchored. This means grinding forces are transmitted differently, and there is a potential for accelerated wear on the crown surface. If you grind your teeth, your dentist may recommend a protective night guard to preserve both your implant restoration and natural teeth.

How often should I have my dental implant reviewed?

Most dental professionals recommend a clinical review of your dental implant at least once a year, typically as part of your routine dental examination. Some patients may benefit from more frequent monitoring, particularly if there are concerns about gum health, bite changes, or implant stability. Your dentist and hygienist are best placed to recommend a review schedule suited to your individual circumstances and oral health needs.

When should I contact my dentist about a change in my implant crown?

You should contact your dentist if you notice any of the following: a sensation of movement or looseness in the crown, persistent discomfort or tenderness around the implant, a notable change in how the crown feels during biting or chewing, visible changes in the surrounding gum tissue, or any swelling or unusual appearance in the area. These symptoms do not necessarily indicate a serious problem, but they benefit from timely professional assessment to determine the appropriate course of action.

Conclusion

If your implant crown feels slightly different after several years, you are not alone in noticing this. The oral environment changes naturally over time, and a fixed implant crown exists within a dynamic system of natural teeth, gum tissue, and bone that continues to evolve. In many cases, the changes you perceive are the result of normal processes such as crown wear, bite evolution, or minor gum tissue remodelling — all of which can be assessed and managed effectively with professional guidance.

What matters most is that you do not dismiss subtle changes or feel uncertain about whether to seek advice. Early professional review is generally straightforward and can provide reassurance or identify a minor adjustment that restores your comfort and confidence in your restoration.

Regular dental examinations and professional hygiene visits remain among the most effective ways to monitor the long-term health and performance of your dental implant, alongside a consistent home care routine.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

This article is intended for general educational purposes only and does not constitute personalised dental advice. Individual diagnosis and treatment recommendations require a clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.
