Implant Health

Dental Implant Infection: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why infections may develop around dental implants, the signs to be aware of, and how professional assessment can help protect implant health.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Clinical Implant Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Dental implants are designed to integrate with the jawbone and function like natural tooth roots, providing stable support for replacement teeth. With appropriate care, implants can serve patients well for many years.

However, in some cases, infection may develop in the tissues surrounding an implant. Patients may notice swelling, discomfort, or bleeding around the implant area — symptoms that should not be ignored, but equally should not cause undue alarm.

Early assessment is important to determine the cause of any symptoms and to identify appropriate management options. Professional evaluation can help protect both implant stability and the health of surrounding oral tissues, giving patients the best opportunity to maintain their implant long term.

What Is a Dental Implant Infection?

A dental implant infection refers to an infection that affects the gum tissue or bone surrounding a dental implant. It is most commonly associated with bacterial build-up around the implant site, which can trigger an inflammatory response in the surrounding tissues.

In its early stages, implant infection typically involves inflammation of the gum tissue immediately around the implant — a condition known as peri-implant mucositis. At this stage, the supporting bone is usually unaffected, and the condition may be reversible with appropriate professional care.

If the infection progresses, it may begin to affect the bone that supports the implant — a more advanced condition known as peri-implantitis. This can compromise the foundation of the implant and, without treatment, may affect long-term implant stability.

It is important to note that not all symptoms around an implant indicate infection or implant failure. Discomfort or minor gum changes can have a range of causes, which is why clinical assessment is important for an accurate diagnosis.

Common Causes of Implant Infection

Implant infections can arise from a combination of factors. Understanding the potential causes can help patients take proactive steps to protect their implant health.

Bacterial Plaque Accumulation

Just as natural teeth are susceptible to plaque build-up, so too are dental implants. Bacteria that accumulate around the implant margin can cause inflammation of the surrounding gum tissue. Without regular professional cleaning and diligent home care, this bacterial presence may progress to infection.

Inadequate Oral Hygiene

Implants require consistent and thorough oral hygiene, including brushing, interdental cleaning, and the use of appropriate cleaning aids. Insufficient cleaning around implant sites can allow bacteria to flourish and increase the risk of peri-implant infection.

Gum Disease & Systemic Factors

Patients with a history of gum disease may be at higher risk of developing peri-implant infections. Additionally, systemic health factors such as diabetes, smoking, or conditions that affect the immune system may influence the body's ability to manage bacteria around implant sites.

Restoration Issues & Bite Forces

Poorly fitting restorations, excess cement left beneath the gum line, or excessive bite forces on the implant may contribute to tissue irritation and create conditions that favour bacterial growth. Trauma to the implant area can also be a contributing factor.

Signs and Symptoms of Implant Infection

The signs of a dental implant infection can vary depending on the severity of the condition. Some patients may experience only mild symptoms, while others may notice more pronounced changes. Being aware of possible indicators can help patients seek timely professional advice.

Redness or Swelling

Inflammation of the gum tissue around the implant, presenting as redness, puffiness, or localised swelling, may indicate the early stages of peri-implant infection.

Bleeding on Brushing

Bleeding when brushing or gently touching the gums around an implant is not normal and may suggest underlying inflammation that warrants professional evaluation.

Bad Taste or Discharge

A persistent unpleasant taste in the mouth or discharge (including pus) around the implant site may indicate active infection and should be assessed promptly.

Tenderness or Mobility

Gum tenderness or discomfort around the implant, or any noticeable movement of the implant itself, may indicate advanced infection affecting the supporting structures.

Potential Risks of Untreated Implant Infection

When a peri-implant infection is identified early, it can often be managed effectively through professional intervention. However, if infection is left unaddressed, there are potential consequences that patients should be aware of.

Continued inflammation of the surrounding tissues can cause progressive damage to the gum and the bone that supports the implant. Over time, this may lead to a loss of supporting bone around the implant, weakening the foundation upon which the implant relies for stability.

As bone loss progresses, implant stability may be reduced, and in more advanced cases, there is an increased likelihood of implant failure. At this stage, the implant may need to be removed, and further treatment — potentially including bone grafting — may be required before a replacement implant can be considered.

It is worth noting that the progression from early gum inflammation to advanced bone loss is not inevitable. With appropriate professional care and monitoring, many peri-implant infections can be managed before they reach an advanced stage.

Treatment Approaches for Implant Infection

Treatment for a dental implant infection depends on clinical findings, including the severity of the infection and the extent of any bone involvement. A range of approaches may be considered.

Professional Cleaning Around the Implant

Thorough debridement of the implant surface and surrounding tissues may help manage infection by removing bacterial deposits. Specialised instruments are used to clean without damaging the implant surface. Regular implant maintenance appointments are an important part of ongoing care.

Management of Gum Inflammation

Where infection is limited to the soft tissues, targeted anti-inflammatory or antimicrobial therapies may be used alongside professional cleaning to help manage the condition. Improved oral hygiene techniques may also be recommended to reduce the risk of recurrence.

Restoration Adjustment

If a poorly fitting restoration or excess cement is contributing to the infection, adjusting or replacing the implant crown or bridge may form part of the treatment plan. Ensuring the restoration fits precisely can help reduce bacterial trapping and tissue irritation.

Monitoring & Ongoing Assessment

In some cases, particularly where infection is at an early stage, careful monitoring alongside improved hygiene may be appropriate. Regular review appointments allow clinicians to track the health of the implant and surrounding tissues over time.

Implant Removal & Replacement

In severe cases where infection has caused significant bone loss and the implant can no longer be maintained, implant removal may be necessary. Following healing and, where required, bone grafting, a replacement implant may be considered.

Treatment options vary depending on the extent of infection. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

Importance of Early Professional Assessment

Early diagnosis of a peri-implant infection may help protect implant stability and reduce the need for more extensive treatment. When infection is identified at the mucositis stage — before the supporting bone is affected — it is generally more straightforward to manage.

Assessment typically involves a clinical examination of the gum tissues around the implant, probing to check for deepened pockets, and dental imaging such as digital X-rays to evaluate the condition of the surrounding bone. These findings help the clinician determine the most appropriate course of care.

Treatment planning varies depending on bone health, gum condition, and the patient's overall medical history. What may be appropriate for one patient may not be suitable for another, which is why individualised assessment is essential.

Professional monitoring through regular maintenance appointments helps maintain long-term implant health and allows any changes to be identified early. Assessment and treatment planning for dental implant concerns are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine the most appropriate course of care.

Dental Implant Pain: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why discomfort may develop around a dental implant, the signs to be aware of, and how professional assessment can help identify the most appropriate care.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Clinical Implant Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Dental implants are designed to function like natural tooth roots, integrating with the jawbone to provide stable, long-lasting support for replacement teeth. For most patients, implants function comfortably and without issue once the healing period is complete.

However, in some cases, patients may experience discomfort or pain around an implant. This discomfort may occur shortly after placement as part of the normal healing process, or it may develop weeks, months, or even years later. The underlying cause can vary — it may involve the surrounding tissues, bite pressure, infection, or a problem with the implant components themselves.

Whatever the timing or nature of the discomfort, professional dental assessment can help determine the underlying cause and identify appropriate treatment options. In many cases, implant pain can be managed effectively once the source has been identified.

Is Dental Implant Pain Normal?

It is quite common for patients to experience mild discomfort during the early healing phase following implant placement. Some tenderness, swelling, or sensitivity around the surgical site is a normal part of the body's healing response and typically subsides within a few days to a couple of weeks.

However, if pain persists beyond the expected healing period, intensifies rather than improves, or develops after a period of comfortable function, this may indicate an underlying issue that warrants investigation. Delayed or persistent pain should always be evaluated by a dental professional, as early assessment can help identify the cause before it progresses.

It is worth noting that the nature, intensity, and timing of implant discomfort can vary considerably between individuals. What one patient experiences may differ from another, which is why clinical evaluation is important for an accurate diagnosis.

Common Causes of Implant Pain

Dental implant pain can arise from a number of different causes. Identifying the specific factor — or combination of factors — is essential for determining the most appropriate treatment approach.

Infection Around the Implant

Bacterial infection of the gum tissue or bone surrounding the implant — known as peri-implant mucositis or peri-implantitis — is one of the most common causes of implant discomfort. Infection may cause swelling, tenderness, and bleeding, and can compromise the supporting structures if left unaddressed.

Bite Pressure or Misalignment

If the implant restoration does not align correctly with the opposing teeth, excessive or uneven bite forces may be transmitted through the implant. This can lead to discomfort during biting or chewing and, over time, may place additional stress on the implant and surrounding bone.

Gum Tissue Inflammation

Inflammation of the soft tissues around the implant can occur independently of infection. Irritation from rough restoration margins, food impaction, or inadequate oral hygiene may contribute to gum tenderness and discomfort in the implant area.

Component Problems & Healing Complications

In some cases, discomfort may arise from a loose or damaged implant component, such as the abutment or crown. Additionally, complications during the bone healing phase — including incomplete osseointegration — may result in ongoing sensitivity or discomfort around the implant site.

Signs and Symptoms of Implant Discomfort

The symptoms associated with dental implant pain can vary between individuals and depend on the underlying cause. Being aware of the signs that may warrant professional evaluation can help patients seek timely advice.

Pain When Biting or Chewing

Discomfort that occurs when pressure is applied through the implant — particularly during eating — may suggest bite misalignment, a loose component, or stress on the surrounding bone.

Swelling or Tenderness

Localised swelling, puffiness, or tenderness of the gum tissue around the implant may indicate inflammation or infection that requires clinical evaluation.

Gum Sensitivity

Heightened sensitivity in the gums surrounding the implant, including discomfort when brushing or touching the area, may be a sign of tissue irritation or early infection.

Persistent Discomfort

Ongoing or recurring discomfort around the implant site — particularly pain that does not resolve with time or that returns after a period of comfort — should be assessed to rule out underlying complications.

Potential Effects on Oral Function

When dental implant pain is left unaddressed, it may begin to affect everyday oral function. Understanding these potential effects can help patients appreciate the value of seeking timely professional assessment.

Chewing ability is often the first function to be affected. Patients may begin to avoid chewing on the side of the painful implant, which can alter eating habits and place additional strain on other teeth. Over time, this compensatory behaviour may contribute to uneven wear or discomfort elsewhere in the mouth.

Bite balance can also be disrupted. If an implant is causing pain due to misalignment or a component issue, the way the upper and lower teeth come together may be affected, potentially contributing to further discomfort or strain on the jaw joints.

In cases where an underlying infection or bone healing complication is responsible for the pain, implant stability itself may be at risk. Early intervention can help address these issues before they progress to a point where more extensive treatment is required.

Perhaps most importantly, persistent implant discomfort can affect overall oral comfort and confidence in the implant. Professional assessment can help restore both function and peace of mind.

Treatment Options for Implant Pain

The most appropriate treatment for dental implant pain depends on the underlying cause, which can only be determined through thorough clinical assessment. A range of approaches may be considered.

Professional Implant Cleaning & Maintenance

If bacterial build-up or early gum inflammation is contributing to discomfort, professional cleaning around the implant may help reduce symptoms. Regular implant maintenance appointments are an important part of ongoing implant care and can help identify issues before they progress.

Adjustment of Bite Alignment

Where bite misalignment is contributing to implant pain, careful adjustment of the implant restoration or opposing teeth may help redistribute bite forces more evenly. This can often be achieved through minor modifications to the implant crown without the need for more extensive treatment.

Treatment of Inflammation or Infection

If gum inflammation or peri-implant infection is identified, targeted treatment may help manage the condition and reduce discomfort. This may involve antimicrobial therapies, improved hygiene protocols, or surgical intervention in more advanced cases.

Repair or Replacement of Implant Components

If a loose, damaged, or worn implant component is responsible for the discomfort, repair or replacement of the affected part may help resolve the issue. In cases where the implant itself has failed, implant replacement or removal may need to be considered following a full assessment.

Treatment options vary depending on the underlying cause. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

Importance of Professional Implant Assessment

Implant discomfort should always be evaluated by a dental professional, regardless of when it develops or how mild it may seem. Pain is the body's way of signalling that something may require attention, and in the context of dental implants, early assessment can make a significant difference to the outcome.

A thorough examination may involve clinical assessment of the gum tissues, probing around the implant to check for pocket depth, and dental imaging to evaluate the condition of the surrounding bone. Implant stability testing may also be carried out to assess whether the implant remains securely integrated with the jawbone.

Early diagnosis of the underlying cause can help prevent more complex complications from developing. What may begin as minor gum inflammation could, if left unaddressed, progress to bone loss or implant instability. Timely professional evaluation helps ensure the most conservative and effective treatment approach is identified.

Denture Stability

Dentures Moving While Eating: Causes and Treatment Options

Understanding why dentures may slip or shift during meals, the factors that affect denture stability, and how professional assessment can help identify suitable solutions.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Denture & Implant Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Dentures are designed to restore the ability to chew and speak comfortably after tooth loss. For many patients, they provide a practical and effective means of replacing missing teeth and maintaining everyday oral function.

However, some denture wearers experience movement or slipping while eating — particularly when biting into firmer foods or chewing for extended periods. This instability can make mealtimes uncomfortable and may affect confidence when eating in social settings.

Denture movement during eating is a common concern, and it can develop gradually over time as the shape of the jawbone and gum tissues changes. Professional dental assessment can help determine why the dentures are moving and identify appropriate treatment options to improve stability and comfort.

Why Dentures May Move While Eating

Conventional dentures rely on the shape and contour of the gum tissue and underlying jawbone for support and retention. When the denture fits well and the supporting structures are intact, the denture is held in position by suction, muscle control, and the close adaptation of the denture base to the gum surface.

Over time, however, the jawbone naturally remodels following tooth loss — a process known as bone resorption. As the bone recedes, the ridge that supports the denture becomes flatter and narrower, reducing the surface area available for denture retention. This is particularly common in the lower jaw, where denture stability is often more difficult to achieve.

As these changes occur, the fit of the denture may become less precise, allowing movement during chewing or biting. The forces generated during eating can dislodge a denture that no longer fits securely, leading to slipping, rocking, or lifting away from the gum.

The degree of denture movement varies between individuals and depends on factors such as the extent of bone resorption, the type of denture, and the foods being eaten.

Common Causes of Denture Instability

Denture instability while eating is rarely caused by a single factor. In most cases, a combination of contributing elements affects how securely the denture sits during function.

Jawbone Shrinkage After Tooth Loss

Following tooth extraction, the jawbone gradually resorbs over time. This reduces the height and width of the ridge that supports the denture, compromising fit and retention — particularly in the lower jaw where bone loss tends to be more pronounced.

Changes in Gum Shape

The soft tissues that line the denture-bearing area can change in shape and volume over time. Weight changes, medication, and the natural ageing process may all contribute to alterations in gum contour, affecting the fit of the denture.

Ill-Fitting Dentures

Dentures that were not accurately fitted at the outset, or that have not been adjusted as the mouth has changed, may lack the close adaptation needed for stable retention. An imprecise fit allows movement under the forces of chewing.

Material Wear & Lower Jaw Challenges

Over years of use, denture materials can wear, warp, or develop surface irregularities that affect fit. The lower jaw presents particular challenges for denture stability due to the presence of the tongue and the typically flatter ridge, which offers less natural retention.

Signs Dentures Are Not Stable While Eating

Denture instability while eating may develop gradually, and patients sometimes adapt their eating habits without fully recognising the extent of the problem. The following signs may indicate that denture stability has been affected.

Slipping During Chewing

Dentures that shift, rock, or lift away from the gums while chewing may no longer fit securely enough to withstand normal bite forces.

Difficulty Biting Into Foods

Struggling to bite into firmer foods such as apples, crusty bread, or raw vegetables may indicate that the denture lacks adequate stability for incising.

Clicking or Shifting Sounds

Audible clicking or shifting of the denture during meals can be an indication of poor retention and may cause self-consciousness when eating in company.

Avoiding Certain Foods

Many patients with unstable dentures gradually restrict their diet, avoiding foods that are difficult to chew. Over time, this can affect nutritional intake and reduce enjoyment of meals.

Potential Effects on Oral Function

When dentures move during eating, the effects extend beyond simple inconvenience. Understanding the wider impact can help patients appreciate the value of seeking professional advice.

Chewing efficiency is often significantly affected. Unstable dentures cannot generate the same bite force as well-fitting ones, which means food may not be broken down as thoroughly. This can affect digestion and may lead patients to favour softer, less nutritious foods.

Food choices and diet tend to become more restricted over time. Patients may avoid fibrous vegetables, fresh fruit, nuts, and lean meats — foods that are important for maintaining a balanced diet and overall health.

Confidence when eating in social settings can also be affected. The worry that dentures may slip or make noise during a meal can cause anxiety and lead some patients to avoid eating in public altogether.

Additionally, dentures that move excessively can place uneven pressure on the gum tissues, potentially causing sore spots, irritation, and discomfort that further compounds the problem.

Treatment Options to Improve Denture Stability

Treatment for denture instability depends on clinical findings, including the condition of the denture, the health of the gum tissues, and the amount of jawbone support available.

Denture Adjustment or Replacement

If the existing denture has become ill-fitting due to changes in the mouth, adjustment or the fabrication of a new, better-fitting denture may help improve stability. Modern denture materials and techniques can achieve a more precise fit than older dentures.

Denture Relining

Relining involves adding new material to the fitting surface of the denture to improve its adaptation to the current shape of the gum ridge. This can be a practical option when the denture teeth are still in good condition but the fit has deteriorated.

Implant-Retained Dentures

For patients who continue to experience instability despite denture adjustments, implant-retained dentures may offer a more reliable solution. Dental implants placed in the jawbone provide secure attachment points for the denture, significantly reducing movement during eating and speaking.

Full Arch Implant Solutions

In cases of extensive tooth loss, All-on-4 dental implants or a full arch implant bridge may provide a fixed alternative to removable dentures. These solutions are supported entirely by dental implants and do not rely on gum suction for retention.

Options vary depending on bone support and denture condition. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

When Implant-Supported Dentures May Be Considered

Dental implants can provide a stable foundation for dentures by creating fixed attachment points within the jawbone. Unlike conventional dentures, which rest on the gum surface, implant-retained dentures clip or lock onto implants, providing considerably improved stability during chewing and speaking.

This approach may be particularly beneficial for lower denture wearers, where bone resorption often makes conventional denture retention especially challenging. Even a small number of implants can make a meaningful difference to denture stability and patient comfort.

Whether implant-supported dentures are suitable depends on a number of factors, including the health and volume of the available jawbone, overall medical health, and the patient's expectations and preferences. A comprehensive clinical evaluation, including dental imaging, is necessary to determine whether this treatment pathway is appropriate.

For patients seeking a fully fixed solution, full mouth reconstruction using implant-supported bridges may also be an option worth discussing during the assessment process.

Importance of Professional Assessment

Denture stability problems should be evaluated by a dental professional who can assess both the condition of the denture and the health of the underlying oral structures. A clinical examination can help identify the specific cause of the movement and determine the most appropriate course of action.

Assessment may involve checking the fit and adaptation of the denture, evaluating the shape and height of the ridge, and assessing the health of the gum tissues. Where implant-supported solutions are being considered, imaging such as cone beam CT scans may be required to evaluate bone volume and plan implant placement.

Treatment planning varies depending on individual needs. What works well for one patient may not be suitable for another, which is why personalised assessment is an essential first step.

Assessment and treatment planning for denture stability concerns are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options.

Restoring Oral Function

Difficulty Chewing Due To Missing Teeth: Causes and Treatment Options

Understanding how tooth loss can affect chewing ability, the signs to be aware of, and the treatment pathways that may help restore comfortable oral function.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation — £80Call 020 71833573

✓ Comprehensive Assessment · ✓ Tailored Treatment Plans · ✓ Experienced Implant Team

Teeth play an essential role in breaking down food during chewing. Each tooth contributes to the overall efficiency of the bite, and when the dental arch is complete, the forces of chewing are distributed evenly across the teeth and supporting structures.

When one or more teeth are missing, this balance is disrupted. Chewing efficiency may be reduced, and some individuals find it increasingly difficult to bite into or chew certain foods comfortably. Over time, changes in chewing patterns can place additional stress on the remaining teeth and may affect overall oral health.

Difficulty chewing is a common concern among patients who have experienced tooth loss, and it is one that can have a meaningful impact on diet, nutrition, and quality of life. Professional dental assessment can help determine the cause of chewing difficulties and identify appropriate treatment options to support better oral function.

How Missing Teeth Affect Chewing Function

The teeth are designed to work together as a coordinated system. The front teeth (incisors and canines) are shaped to cut and tear food, while the back teeth (premolars and molars) are built to grind and crush it into smaller particles that can be swallowed and digested efficiently.

When one or more teeth are missing, this system is compromised. The remaining teeth must compensate for the gaps, often taking on forces they were not designed to bear. Chewing balance is disrupted, and the efficiency with which food is broken down may be noticeably reduced.

Over time, the remaining teeth may be subjected to additional pressure during chewing, which can accelerate wear, increase the risk of fractures, and contribute to further dental complications. Neighbouring teeth may also begin to drift or tilt into the empty space, further altering the bite and affecting oral function and comfort.

Common Causes of Chewing Difficulty

Chewing difficulty following tooth loss can result from a combination of factors. The severity of the problem often depends on the number and position of the missing teeth.

Loss of One or More Teeth

Even the loss of a single tooth can affect chewing efficiency, particularly if it is a molar or premolar that plays a key role in grinding food. The loss of multiple teeth has a more significant impact on the ability to break down food effectively.

Bite Imbalance

When teeth are missing, the forces of chewing are no longer evenly distributed. This imbalance can cause some teeth to bear excessive loads while others are underused, leading to discomfort and inefficient food breakdown.

Movement of Neighbouring Teeth

Teeth adjacent to a gap may gradually drift or tilt into the empty space. This movement can alter the alignment of the bite and further reduce chewing efficiency, making it harder for the teeth to meet in their correct positions.

Reduced Bite Strength & Jaw Changes

With fewer teeth to distribute chewing forces, overall bite strength may be reduced. Additionally, prolonged tooth loss can lead to changes in jaw alignment as the muscles and joints adapt to the altered bite pattern.

Signs That Missing Teeth Are Affecting Chewing

Chewing difficulties related to tooth loss often develop gradually. Patients may initially adapt their eating habits without fully recognising the extent of the problem. The following signs may indicate that missing teeth are affecting chewing function.

Difficulty With Harder Foods

Struggling to chew firmer or tougher foods — such as raw vegetables, nuts, or lean meats — may suggest that the remaining teeth cannot generate sufficient force or contact to break these foods down effectively.

Avoiding Certain Foods

Gradually limiting the range of foods eaten — particularly avoiding foods that require thorough chewing — can be a sign of reduced chewing efficiency and may affect nutritional intake over time.

Uneven Chewing Patterns

Favouring one side of the mouth while eating is a common adaptation when teeth are missing on the opposite side. This can place additional strain on the teeth and jaw on the working side.

Jaw Fatigue & Bite Changes

Feeling tiredness or discomfort in the jaw during or after meals, or noticing that the teeth no longer seem to meet together properly, may indicate changes in bite alignment related to tooth loss.

Potential Effects on Oral Health

When tooth loss is left unaddressed, the effects on oral health can extend beyond chewing difficulty. Understanding these potential consequences can help patients make informed decisions about treatment.

Reduced chewing efficiency is often the most immediately noticeable effect. As fewer teeth are available to break down food, patients may swallow larger food particles, which can affect digestion and may contribute to dietary limitations.

The remaining teeth are subjected to increased wear as they compensate for the missing ones. Teeth that bear excessive forces may develop cracks, chips, or accelerated surface wear, potentially leading to further dental problems.

Bite imbalance can develop as the teeth shift and the jaw adapts to the altered dental arch. This may affect comfort, contribute to jaw joint strain, and create areas where food traps more easily, increasing the risk of decay and gum disease.

Over the longer term, changes in jawbone structure may occur. Without the stimulation that tooth roots provide, the jawbone in the area of the missing teeth gradually resorbs, which can affect facial appearance and reduce the options available for future tooth replacement.

Treatment Options to Restore Chewing Function

Treatment for chewing difficulties caused by tooth loss depends on clinical findings, including the number and position of missing teeth, the condition of the remaining teeth, and the health of the jawbone.

Single Dental Implants

For patients missing an individual tooth, a single tooth implant may help restore chewing function in that area. The implant integrates with the jawbone and supports a replacement crown that functions like a natural tooth, helping to re-establish bite balance.

Multiple Dental Implants

When several teeth are missing, multiple dental implants may be placed to replace the lost teeth and restore a more complete chewing surface. The number and placement of implants depends on the clinical assessment and the specific pattern of tooth loss.

Implant-Supported Bridges

An implant-supported bridge uses two or more implants to support a row of replacement teeth. This approach may be suitable for patients missing consecutive teeth and can help restore chewing efficiency across a section of the dental arch.

Implant-Retained Dentures & Full Arch Solutions

For patients with more extensive tooth loss, implant-retained dentures or a full arch implant bridge may provide improved stability and chewing ability compared to conventional dentures. These solutions use dental implants to secure the prosthesis, reducing movement during eating.

Options vary depending on the number and position of missing teeth. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any treatment plan can be recommended.

Importance of Professional Assessment

Tooth loss and the chewing difficulties it causes should be evaluated by a dental professional who can assess the full picture — including the number of missing teeth, the condition of the remaining teeth, the health of the gums, and the volume and quality of the jawbone.

A comprehensive examination may involve bite analysis to understand how the remaining teeth come together, and dental imaging such as digital X-rays or cone beam CT scans to evaluate bone health and plan potential implant placement.

Treatment planning depends on bone health, oral function, and the patient's individual needs and goals. What may be appropriate for one patient may not be suitable for another, which is why personalised assessment is an essential first step.

Early assessment may also help prevent further complications. When missing teeth are replaced promptly, the risk of neighbouring teeth drifting, bone loss progressing, and additional teeth being compromised may be reduced.

Assessment and treatment planning for tooth loss and chewing difficulties are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options.

Failed Bone Graft: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why a bone graft may not heal as expected and what professional treatment options may be available following graft complications.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation020 71833573

Bone grafting is sometimes performed to restore bone volume before dental implant placement. The procedure aims to strengthen the jawbone in areas where bone support has been reduced, helping to create a stable foundation for future treatment.

In most cases, bone grafts heal successfully; however, in some situations the graft may not integrate as expected. Patients may experience symptoms such as delayed healing, discomfort or changes around the grafted area. When this occurs, professional dental assessment can help determine the underlying cause and whether additional treatment may be required.

Understanding the signs of a bone graft that has not healed properly can help patients seek timely professional advice, supporting better outcomes for any future implant treatment.

What Is a Failed Bone Graft?

A failed bone graft refers to a graft that does not integrate successfully with the surrounding jawbone. Rather than forming stable, healthy bone tissue, the grafted material may not bond properly with existing bone or may fail to stimulate sufficient new bone growth.

Healing may be incomplete or disrupted by a number of factors, and the graft site may show signs of infection, inflammation or poor tissue response. In such cases, clinical examination — often supported by dental imaging — is required to determine the cause of the complication and to plan appropriate next steps.

It is important to note that graft complications are not uncommon, and many patients who experience initial difficulties may still be suitable for further treatment following professional evaluation.

Why Bone Grafting Is Sometimes Needed

Bone grafting helps rebuild areas of jawbone that have been lost due to tooth extraction, gum disease, injury or prolonged denture wear. Over time, the jawbone naturally resorbs when teeth are missing, and this can leave insufficient bone to support dental implant treatment.

A bone graft may be recommended before placing dental implants to help restore adequate bone volume and density. Sufficient bone is important for implant stability, as implants need to integrate firmly with the surrounding jaw tissue to function effectively.

Some patients require grafting procedures such as ridge augmentation or a sinus lift to support long-term implant treatment. The type and extent of grafting required depends on the individual patient's bone structure and treatment plan.

Possible Causes of Bone Graft Failure

Several factors may contribute to a bone graft not healing as expected. In many cases, more than one factor may be involved, and a thorough clinical assessment is needed to identify the underlying cause.

Infection at the Graft Site

Bacterial infection around the surgical area can interfere with graft healing and may prevent successful integration with the surrounding bone.

Insufficient Blood Supply

Adequate blood flow is essential for graft healing. If the grafted area does not receive sufficient vascular supply, new bone formation may be compromised.

Graft Movement During Healing

If the graft material shifts or is disturbed during the healing period, it may not bond properly with the existing jawbone tissue.

Smoking and Lifestyle Factors

Smoking can significantly reduce blood flow and impair healing. Other systemic health conditions may also affect the body's ability to regenerate bone.

Reduced Bone Healing Capacity

Certain medical conditions, medications or age-related changes may reduce the body's natural ability to form new bone tissue at the graft site.

Poor Surgical Technique

The skill and precision of the grafting procedure can influence the outcome. Inadequate site preparation or graft placement may contribute to complications.

Signs and Symptoms of a Failed Bone Graft

The signs and symptoms of a bone graft that has not healed properly may vary depending on the cause and location of the graft. Patients who notice any of the following should seek professional dental advice.

Persistent swelling around the graft site
Ongoing discomfort or pain beyond the expected healing period
Signs of infection such as discharge or unpleasant taste
Delayed healing compared to the expected timeline
Gum changes or soft tissue recession near the surgical area
Lack of expected bone development on follow-up imaging
Loosening or exposure of graft material
Numbness or altered sensation in the surrounding area

Symptoms may vary depending on the type of graft, location, and individual healing response. Professional assessment is recommended if any concerns arise following a bone graft procedure.

Treatment Options After Bone Graft Complications

Treatment following a bone graft complication depends on clinical findings and the specific cause of the issue. A thorough examination — including dental imaging — may help determine the most appropriate course of action. Options may include:

Monitoring the Healing Process

In some cases, continued monitoring with follow-up imaging may be recommended to assess whether healing progresses over time. Not all graft concerns require immediate intervention.

Treating Infection or Inflammation

If infection is identified as a contributing factor, targeted treatment such as antibiotics or surgical debridement may help restore tissue health around the graft site.

Removing Compromised Graft Material

Where graft material has not integrated successfully, it may need to be carefully removed to allow healthy tissue to recover before any further treatment is considered.

Performing a New Bone Graft Procedure

In some cases, a new bone graft procedure may be recommended once the site has healed sufficiently. Treatment depends on clinical evaluation and the patient's overall oral health.

When Dental Implants May Still Be Possible

Experiencing a bone graft complication does not necessarily mean that dental implant treatment is no longer an option. In many cases, implant treatment may still be possible once adequate bone regeneration has been achieved through further grafting or alternative approaches.

Additional bone grafting procedures — such as a sinus lift or guided bone regeneration — may be recommended depending on the location and extent of bone loss. These procedures aim to rebuild sufficient bone volume to support stable implant placement.

Treatment planning depends on bone quality, overall oral health, and the patient's medical history. A comprehensive clinical assessment — including imaging — can help determine whether implant treatment may be appropriate and what preparatory steps may be required.

Importance of Professional Assessment

Bone graft complications require professional evaluation to accurately diagnose the cause and determine the most appropriate treatment pathway. Self-assessment is not sufficient, as many graft-related issues can only be identified through clinical examination and dental imaging.

Imaging such as CBCT scans may be needed to assess the extent of bone healing and to evaluate the condition of surrounding structures. This information is essential for developing a realistic treatment plan tailored to the patient's individual circumstances.

Assessment and treatment planning for bone graft complications and implant preparation are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate treatment options. Careful monitoring and timely intervention may support better outcomes for future implant treatment.

If healing following a bone graft procedure does not progress as expected, professional assessment can help determine whether further treatment or implant planning may be appropriate.

Patients may notice discomfort, movement or inflammation around the implant site. sections.title: What Is a Failed Dental Implant?

sections.title: Possible Causes of Implant Failure
sections.text: Possible Causes of Implant FailureDental implant failure may result from a combination of factors. Understanding the potential causes can help patients recognise when professional assessment may be beneficial.Infection Around the ImplantPeri-implantitis — a condition involving infection and inflammation of the tissue surrounding the implant — is one of the most common causes of late implant failure.Insufficient Bone SupportInadequate bone volume or density at the implant site may prevent the implant from achieving stable osseointegration, particularly if bone loss has occurred prior to placement.Implant OverloadExcessive bite pressure on the implant — whether from bruxism, premature loading, or an uneven bite — may place stress on the implant before or after integration.Poor OsseointegrationIn some cases, the implant may simply not integrate properly with the jawbone during the healing phase, preventing stable anchorage from being achieved.Systemic Health FactorsConditions such as uncontrolled diabetes, autoimmune disorders, or medications that affect healing may influence the body's ability to support successful implant integration.Smoking and Lifestyle FactorsSmoking can significantly impair blood flow and healing around the implant site, increasing the risk of both early and late implant failure.Multiple factors may contribute to implant complications. A thorough clinical assessment is required to determine the specific cause in each case.

sections.title: Potential Effects on Oral Health
sections.text: Potential Effects on Oral HealthWhen a dental implant fails and is not addressed in a timely manner, it may have a broader impact on surrounding oral structures. Understanding these potential effects can help patients appreciate the importance of seeking professional evaluation.A failing implant may compromise chewing ability, making it difficult to eat comfortably and potentially affecting diet and nutrition. If infection is present, it may lead to progressive bone loss around the implant site, reducing the bone volume available for any future restorative treatment.The stability of neighbouring teeth may also be affected if bone loss extends beyond the immediate implant site. In some cases, untreated implant complications can contribute to changes in bite alignment, placing additional stress on other teeth and dental restorations.Timely professional assessment may help limit the extent of these effects and support better outcomes for future treatment. Regular implant maintenance can also play an important role in identifying potential problems early.

sections.title: Treatment Options for a Failed Implant
sections.text: Treatment Options for a Failed ImplantTreatment for a failed dental implant depends on clinical findings, the cause of the failure, and the condition of the surrounding bone and tissue. A thorough assessment is essential before determining the most appropriate course of action. Options may include:Monitoring the ImplantIn some cases, particularly where symptoms are mild and the implant is still partially stable, careful monitoring with regular follow-up appointments may be recommended before considering intervention.Treatment of Infection or InflammationWhere peri-implantitis or infection is identified, targeted treatment — which may include professional cleaning, antimicrobial therapy, or surgical debridement — may help stabilise the implant and surrounding tissue.Removal of the Failed ImplantIf the implant cannot be salvaged, professional dental implant removal may be necessary. This procedure is carried out carefully to preserve as much surrounding bone as possible, supporting future treatment options.Replacement with a New Dental ImplantWhen appropriate, replacing a failed dental implant with a new one may help restore oral function. Treatment depends on clinical assessment, bone quality, and individual patient factors.

sections.title: When Implant Replacement May Be Considered
sections.text: When Implant Replacement May Be ConsideredFollowing the removal of a failed implant, a new implant may sometimes be placed once the site has healed sufficiently. The feasibility of replacement depends on the amount and quality of remaining bone, the health of the surrounding tissue, and the overall condition of the patient's oral health.In cases where bone volume has been reduced, bone grafting procedures may be recommended prior to placing a new implant. This can help rebuild the jawbone to provide a stable foundation for the replacement implant.Treatment planning for implant replacement is tailored to each patient and depends on individual clinical factors. A comprehensive assessment — including dental imaging — can help determine the most appropriate treatment pathway and timeline.

Attempting to manage symptoms without professional guidance may allow underlying issues to progress, potentially affecting surrounding bone and tissue.A thorough examination may involve clinical assessment, dental imaging such as CBCT scanning, and implant stability testing. These investigations help build an accurate picture of the implant's condition and the health of the surrounding structures.Assessment and treatment planning for dental implant complications are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options. Implant failure may occur in the early stages — during the initial healing period when the implant is expected to fuse with the bone (osseointegration) — or it may develop years after placement due to progressive bone loss, infection, or mechanical complications.

Clinical evaluation, often including dental imaging and implant stability testing, is required to determine whether an implant has failed and to identify the underlying cause. Understanding the type and timing of failure helps guide appropriate treatment planning.

Possible Causes of Implant Failure

Dental implant failure may result from a combination of factors. Understanding the potential causes can help patients recognise when professional assessment may be beneficial.

Infection Around the Implant

Peri-implantitis — a condition involving infection and inflammation of the tissue surrounding the implant — is one of the most common causes of late implant failure.

Insufficient Bone Support

Inadequate bone volume or density at the implant site may prevent the implant from achieving stable osseointegration, particularly if bone loss has occurred prior to placement.

Implant Overload

Excessive bite pressure on the implant — whether from bruxism, premature loading, or an uneven bite — may place stress on the implant before or after integration.

Poor Osseointegration

In some cases, the implant may simply not integrate properly with the jawbone during the healing phase, preventing stable anchorage from being achieved.

Systemic Health Factors

Conditions such as uncontrolled diabetes, autoimmune disorders, or medications that affect healing may influence the body's ability to support successful implant integration.

Smoking and Lifestyle Factors

Smoking can significantly impair blood flow and healing around the implant site, increasing the risk of both early and late implant failure.

Multiple factors may contribute to implant complications. A thorough clinical assessment is required to determine the specific cause in each case.

Signs and Symptoms of a Failed Implant

The signs of a failing or failed dental implant may vary depending on the cause and whether the failure is early or late-stage. Patients who notice any of the following should seek professional dental advice promptly.

Implant mobility or looseness
Pain or discomfort around the implant site
Swelling or inflammation of the surrounding gum tissue
Difficulty chewing or biting on the implant
Persistent infection or discharge near the implant
Receding gum tissue around the implant
A sensation that the implant has shifted position
Bone loss visible on dental imaging

Symptoms may vary depending on the type of failure and individual circumstances. Professional assessment is recommended if any concerns arise following implant treatment.

Potential Effects on Oral Health

When a dental implant fails and is not addressed in a timely manner, it may have a broader impact on surrounding oral structures. Understanding these potential effects can help patients appreciate the importance of seeking professional evaluation.

A failing implant may compromise chewing ability, making it difficult to eat comfortably and potentially affecting diet and nutrition. If infection is present, it may lead to progressive bone loss around the implant site, reducing the bone volume available for any future restorative treatment.

The stability of neighbouring teeth may also be affected if bone loss extends beyond the immediate implant site. In some cases, untreated implant complications can contribute to changes in bite alignment, placing additional stress on other teeth and dental restorations.

Timely professional assessment may help limit the extent of these effects and support better outcomes for future treatment. Regular implant maintenance can also play an important role in identifying potential problems early.

Treatment Options for a Failed Implant

Treatment for a failed dental implant depends on clinical findings, the cause of the failure, and the condition of the surrounding bone and tissue. A thorough assessment is essential before determining the most appropriate course of action. Options may include:

Monitoring the Implant

In some cases, particularly where symptoms are mild and the implant is still partially stable, careful monitoring with regular follow-up appointments may be recommended before considering intervention.

Treatment of Infection or Inflammation

Where peri-implantitis or infection is identified, targeted treatment — which may include professional cleaning, antimicrobial therapy, or surgical debridement — may help stabilise the implant and surrounding tissue.

Removal of the Failed Implant

If the implant cannot be salvaged, professional dental implant removal may be necessary. This procedure is carried out carefully to preserve as much surrounding bone as possible, supporting future treatment options.

Replacement with a New Dental Implant

When appropriate, replacing a failed dental implant with a new one may help restore oral function. Treatment depends on clinical assessment, bone quality, and individual patient factors.

When Implant Replacement May Be Considered

Following the removal of a failed implant, a new implant may sometimes be placed once the site has healed sufficiently. The feasibility of replacement depends on the amount and quality of remaining bone, the health of the surrounding tissue, and the overall condition of the patient's oral health.

In cases where bone volume has been reduced, bone grafting procedures may be recommended prior to placing a new implant. This can help rebuild the jawbone to provide a stable foundation for the replacement implant.

Treatment planning for implant replacement is tailored to each patient and depends on individual clinical factors. A comprehensive assessment — including dental imaging — can help determine the most appropriate treatment pathway and timeline.

Importance of Professional Implant Assessment

Implant complications should always be evaluated by a qualified dental professional. Attempting to manage symptoms without professional guidance may allow underlying issues to progress, potentially affecting surrounding bone and tissue.

A thorough examination may involve clinical assessment, dental imaging such as CBCT scanning, and implant stability testing. These investigations help build an accurate picture of the implant's condition and the health of the surrounding structures.

Assessment and treatment planning for dental implant complications are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options. Early assessment may help prevent further complications and support a wider range of treatment possibilities.

Failing Dental Bridge: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options

Understanding why a dental bridge may become unstable, how to recognise the signs, and what treatment options may be available.

Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation020 71833573

Dental bridges are commonly used to replace one or more missing teeth by anchoring an artificial tooth to the neighbouring natural teeth. They can provide a stable and functional restoration that supports chewing, speech and appearance for many years.

Over time, however, a bridge may become loose, unstable or less functional. Changes in the supporting teeth, gum health or underlying bone structure can all affect the long-term stability of a dental bridge. Patients may notice discomfort, movement or difficulty chewing — signs that the bridge may benefit from professional evaluation.

Professional dental assessment can help determine whether a bridge requires repair, replacement or whether alternative treatment — such as dental implant-supported restorations — may be appropriate.

What Is a Failing Dental Bridge?

A failing dental bridge is one that no longer functions as intended. This may involve loosening of the bridge itself, deterioration of the teeth that support it, or changes in the surrounding gum tissue that compromise its fit and stability.

Changes in bite alignment or the gradual progression of gum disease may also affect how well a bridge fits and functions. In some cases, the cement holding the bridge in place may weaken over time, allowing the restoration to shift or become detached.

It is important to note that not all bridge issues require immediate replacement. In many cases, clinical evaluation can determine whether adjustment, repair or monitoring is sufficient, or whether a more comprehensive treatment approach may be beneficial.

Common Causes of Bridge Failure

Several factors may contribute to a dental bridge becoming unstable or failing over time. In many cases, more than one factor may be involved.

Decay in Supporting Teeth

The teeth that anchor a bridge (abutment teeth) may develop decay beneath or around the bridge margins, weakening the foundation and compromising the fit of the restoration.

Weakening of Bridge Anchors

Over time, the structural integrity of abutment teeth may diminish due to previous restorations, fractures or progressive wear, reducing their ability to support the bridge.

Gum Disease

Periodontal disease affecting the gums and bone around the supporting teeth can lead to bone loss and reduced support for the bridge structure.

Long-Term Wear

Material fatigue and normal wear over many years of use may gradually reduce the integrity of the bridge, leading to chipping, cracking or loosening of the restoration.

Bite Pressure or Grinding

Bruxism or an uneven bite may place excessive force on the bridge, accelerating wear and increasing the risk of fracture or displacement.

Cement Failure

The dental cement securing the bridge to the abutment teeth may weaken or wash out over time, allowing the bridge to become loose or shift during function.

Signs That a Dental Bridge May Be Failing

The signs of a failing dental bridge may develop gradually. Patients who notice any of the following symptoms should consider seeking professional dental assessment.

Movement or looseness of the bridge
Discomfort or sensitivity while chewing
Food trapping around or beneath the bridge
Gum irritation, swelling or bleeding near the bridge
Changes in bite alignment or how teeth come together
A visible gap developing between the bridge and gum tissue
Unpleasant taste or odour around the bridge area
A cracked, chipped or worn bridge surface

Symptoms may vary depending on the condition of the bridge and the supporting teeth. Professional evaluation is recommended to determine the cause and appropriate treatment.

Treatment Options for a Failing Dental Bridge

Treatment for a failing dental bridge depends on the clinical findings, the condition of the supporting teeth, and the overall oral health of the patient. A thorough assessment is essential before determining the most appropriate course of action. Options may include:

Repairing or Adjusting the Existing Bridge

In some cases, a bridge that has become slightly loose may be re-cemented or adjusted. Minor repairs may help restore function without the need for a full replacement, depending on the condition of the supporting teeth.

Replacing the Bridge

Where the existing bridge or its supporting teeth have deteriorated beyond repair, a new bridge may be recommended. The design and material of the replacement bridge will depend on the clinical assessment and the condition of the remaining teeth.

Implant-Supported Restorations

Where traditional bridges are no longer viable, an implant-supported bridge or single tooth implant may help restore function without relying on adjacent teeth for support. Treatment depends on clinical assessment and bone health.

Treating Underlying Conditions

If gum disease, decay or other underlying conditions have contributed to bridge failure, these issues may need to be addressed before any replacement restoration is considered, to support a more predictable outcome.

When Dental Implants May Be Considered

Dental implants can replace missing teeth without relying on adjacent teeth for support, making them a potential alternative when a traditional bridge is no longer viable. Unlike conventional bridges, implants are placed directly into the jawbone and integrate with the surrounding bone to provide stable anchorage for crowns or bridge restorations.

For patients who have lost multiple teeth, an implant-supported bridge may provide stability without placing additional stress on remaining natural teeth. In cases of extensive tooth loss, a full arch implant bridge may be considered as part of a comprehensive treatment plan.

Suitability for dental implant treatment depends on individual clinical factors including bone health, gum condition and overall medical history. A comprehensive assessment — including dental imaging — can help determine whether implant treatment may be appropriate.

Importance of Professional Assessment

A failing dental bridge should be evaluated by a qualified dental professional to determine the cause and to plan appropriate treatment. Leaving a compromised bridge in place without assessment may allow underlying conditions — such as decay or gum disease — to progress, potentially affecting other teeth and structures.

A thorough examination may involve assessing the condition of the supporting teeth and gums, evaluating the fit and integrity of the bridge, and reviewing dental imaging to assess bone health beneath and around the bridge area.

Assessment and treatment planning for failing dental bridges and missing teeth solutions are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative options. Early assessment may support a wider range of treatment possibilities and help preserve surrounding dental structures.

Potential Effects on Oral Health

When complications from a failing root canal tooth are not addressed in a timely manner, they may have a wider impact on oral health. Understanding these potential effects can help patients appreciate the importance of seeking professional evaluation.

Persistent infection around the root of the tooth may gradually damage the surrounding jawbone, reducing bone volume in the area. This bone loss can affect the stability of neighbouring teeth and may also reduce the options available for future restorative treatment if the tooth is eventually lost.

In some cases, a failing root canal tooth may fracture — either partially or completely — particularly if it has not been protected by a crown. A fractured tooth may not be salvageable and could require extraction, leading to a gap that affects chewing function, appearance and the alignment of surrounding teeth.

Timely professional assessment may help identify problems before they progress, supporting a wider range of treatment options and potentially better outcomes.

Treatment Options for a Failing Root Canal Tooth

Treatment for a failing root canal tooth depends on the clinical findings, the condition of the tooth, and the extent of any infection or structural damage. A thorough assessment is essential to determine the most appropriate pathway. Options may include:

Further Endodontic Treatment

In some cases, retreatment of the root canal may be possible. This involves reopening the tooth, removing the existing filling material, cleaning the canals more thoroughly, and resealing them to address persistent or recurrent infection.

Restorative Treatment

If the tooth structure is weakened but the root canal itself remains intact, placing a crown or other protective restoration may help preserve the tooth and restore its function. An implant crown replacement may be considered if the tooth cannot support a traditional restoration.

Tooth Extraction

When the tooth cannot be preserved — due to extensive infection, fracture or insufficient remaining structure — extraction may be necessary. This is typically considered when other treatment options are unlikely to achieve a successful outcome.

Dental Implant Placement

Following extraction, a single tooth implant may help restore function and appearance without relying on neighbouring teeth for support. Treatment depends on clinical assessment, bone health and individual patient factors.

When Dental Implants May Be Considered

When a root canal treated tooth cannot be preserved, dental implants offer a potential solution for replacing the missing tooth. Unlike traditional bridges, implants are placed directly into the jawbone and do not require the preparation or modification of neighbouring teeth for support.

A dental implant integrates with the surrounding bone, providing a stable foundation for a crown that functions and looks similar to a natural tooth. For patients who have lost multiple teeth, implant-supported restorations may also be considered as part of a comprehensive treatment plan.

Suitability for implant treatment depends on several individual clinical factors, including the volume and quality of available bone, the health of surrounding gum tissue, and the patient's overall medical history. A comprehensive assessment — including dental imaging — can help determine whether implant treatment may be appropriate following extraction of a failing root canal tooth.

Importance of Professional Assessment

Accurate diagnosis of a failing root canal tooth requires professional evaluation. The signs and symptoms of root canal failure can sometimes resemble other dental conditions, and clinical examination — often supported by advanced imaging such as CBCT scanning — is essential for identifying the precise cause and extent of the problem.

Treatment planning varies depending on the severity of the problem, the condition of the tooth, and the health of surrounding structures. Early intervention may help prevent further complications and may preserve a wider range of treatment options.

Assessment and treatment planning for complex dental problems and tooth replacement options are available at our London clinic, where professional evaluation can help determine appropriate restorative solutions.

Assessment for a Failing Root Canal Tooth

If a previously treated tooth becomes painful or shows signs of infection, professional dental assessment can help determine whether the tooth can be preserved or whether replacement options such as dental implants may be appropriate.

Root canal treatment is often a fantastic way to save a tooth. However, a tooth that has had a root canal is "non-vital," meaning it no longer has a blood supply. Over time, these teeth can become brittle, much like a dry branch compared to a green one.

Because of this brittleness, root-filled teeth are prone to cracking or fracturing, sometimes vertically through the root. Once a vertical root fracture occurs, the tooth usually cannot be saved and requires extraction to prevent infection from destroying the surrounding bone.

At Dental Implants London, we focus on identifying these failing teeth early and replacing them with Dental Implants. These will not decay, will not need a root canal, and offers the strength of a healthy natural tooth.

Why Do They Fail?

Understanding why your treated tooth is giving you trouble is the first step to a lasting solution.

Vertical Root Fracture

A crack that starts from the root and extends upwards. These are often painful when biting and cause localized pockets of gum infection.

Re-Infection

Bacteria can leak back into the sealed canals over years. Re-treatment of a root canal may have a reduced likelihood of success compared with the initial procedure.

Structural Failure

The tooth structure may simply be too weak to hold a crown any longer, snapping off at the gum line.

Silent Bone Loss

Chronic low-grade infection at the tip of the root (apical periodontitis) can slowly eat away jawbone without causing acute pain.

Gum disease, or periodontitis, is a silent but destructive condition. It often starts without pain but progressively destroys the soft tissue and bone that support your teeth.

At Dental Implants London, we understand the distress this causes. Our approach is two-fold: halt the disease to protect remaining teeth, and rebuild the lost foundation to support long-lasting dental implants.

  • • Gums may be recessed, affecting aesthetics.

Putting a tooth on the implant too soon before the bone has healed, or excessive grinding (bruxism) without protection.

An abscessed tooth is a pocket of pus caused by a bacterial infection. It can occur at different regions of the tooth, but commonly affects the tip of the root (periapical abscess).

Unlike other parts of the body, teeth cannot "heal" themselves once the internal nerve tissue is dead and infected. Antibiotics can temporarily suppress the symptoms, but they cannot cure the infection. As long as the infected tooth remains, the bacteria will continue to destroy the surrounding jawbone and enter your bloodstream.

At Dental Implants London, we prioritize your systemic health. Our protocol involves the safe extraction of the infected tooth, thorough debridement (cleaning) of the infection site, and planning for a dental implant solution.

The Hidden Risks

Ignoring an infected tooth can lead to severe complications beyond just tooth loss.

Bone Destruction

The acidic byproduct of the infection dissolves jawbone, creating a cyst or large defect that makes future implant placement more difficult.

Systemic Health

Oral bacteria from abscesses have been linked to heart disease, diabetes complications, and other systemic inflammatory conditions.

Acute Flare-Ups

A chronic, painless infection can suddenly become acute, causing massive swelling, fever, and severe pain requiring emergency care.

Damage to Neighbors

The infection spreads laterally, often killing the nerves of healthy adjacent teeth and destabilizing them.

title: Loose Dental Bridge: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment Options
seoTitle: Loose Dental Bridge Causes & Treatment | London
description: Learn why a dental bridge may become loose, common symptoms, and treatment options including implant-supported bridges.

sections.text: Loose Dental Bridge: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment OptionsUnderstanding why a dental bridge may become loose, how to recognise the signs, and what professional treatment options may be available.Book Assessment1-Hour Consultation020 71833573

Dental bridges are commonly used to replace one or more missing teeth, restoring both function and appearance by anchoring an artificial tooth to the neighbouring natural teeth. When fitted correctly, a bridge can provide reliable service for many years.Over time, however, a dental bridge may become loose or unstable. Changes in the supporting teeth, the dental cement, or the underlying gum and bone structures can all affect bridge retention. Patients may notice movement during chewing, discomfort when biting, or difficulty with food becoming trapped around the bridge.Professional dental assessment can help determine the cause of bridge instability and identify appropriate treatment options — whether that involves repairing the existing bridge or considering alternative restorative solutions.

sections.title: What Is a Loose Dental Bridge?
sections.text: What Is a Loose Dental Bridge?A loose dental bridge is one that no longer fits securely on the supporting teeth (known as abutment teeth). Rather than remaining firmly in place, the bridge may shift, rock or lift slightly when pressure is applied during eating or biting.Movement may be caused by changes in the supporting teeth themselves — such as decay or structural weakening — or by deterioration of the cement that bonds the bridge to the teeth. In some cases, changes in gum health or bone structure beneath the bridge may also contribute to instability.Clinical evaluation is required to determine the underlying cause and to assess whether the bridge can be re-secured, repaired or whether alternative treatment may be more appropriate.

sections.title: Common Causes of a Loose Dental Bridge
sections.text: Common Causes of a Loose Dental BridgeSeveral factors may contribute to a dental bridge becoming loose. In many cases, more than one factor may be involved, and a thorough clinical assessment is needed to identify the specific cause.Wear of Dental CementThe cement used to bond a bridge to the supporting teeth may gradually weaken or wash out over time, reducing the strength of the bond and allowing the bridge to move.Decay in Supporting TeethTooth decay beneath or around the bridge margins can compromise the fit of the restoration, weakening the foundation and allowing bacteria to penetrate beneath the bridge.Gum DiseasePeriodontal disease affecting the gums and bone around the supporting teeth can lead to tissue recession and bone loss, reducing the support available for the bridge.Bite Pressure or GrindingBruxism or an uneven bite distribution may place excessive force on the bridge, accelerating cement failure and increasing the risk of the bridge becoming dislodged.Structural Changes in Supporting TeethThe abutment teeth may weaken over time due to previous restorations, fractures or progressive wear, reducing their ability to retain the bridge securely.Bridge Age and WearLike all dental restorations, bridges have a finite lifespan. Material fatigue and gradual wear over many years of use may eventually affect the fit and integrity of the restoration.

sections.title: Signs That a Dental Bridge May Be Loose
sections.text: Signs That a Dental Bridge May Be LooseThe signs of a loose dental bridge may develop gradually and can sometimes be subtle in the early stages. Patients who notice any of the following should consider seeking professional dental assessment.Movement or rocking of the bridge during chewingDiscomfort or sensitivity when biting downFood trapping around or beneath the bridgeChanges in how the teeth come together when bitingGum irritation, redness or swelling around the supporting teethAn unpleasant taste or odour around the bridge areaA feeling that the bridge is lifting or shiftingVisible gap developing between the bridge and gum tissueSymptoms may vary depending on the condition of the bridge and the supporting teeth. Professional evaluation is recommended to determine the cause and appropriate treatment.

sections.title: Potential Effects on Oral Function
sections.text: Potential Effects on Oral FunctionA loose dental bridge can affect several aspects of daily oral function. Understanding these potential effects may help patients appreciate the importance of timely professional assessment.Chewing efficiency may be reduced when a bridge is unstable, as patients may instinctively avoid using the affected area. This can lead to uneven bite distribution, placing additional stress on other teeth and potentially contributing to further dental complications over time.Oral comfort may also be affected, with patients experiencing intermittent discomfort or irritation around the bridge site. If food becomes trapped beneath a loose bridge, this can increase the risk of decay in the supporting teeth and may contribute to gum inflammation.In the longer term, a loose bridge that is not addressed may compromise the health of the supporting teeth — potentially leading to further tooth loss and reducing the options available for future restorative treatment.

sections.title: Treatment Options for a Loose Dental Bridge
sections.text: Treatment Options for a Loose Dental BridgeTreatment for a loose dental bridge depends on the clinical findings, the condition of the supporting teeth, and the overall oral health of the patient. A thorough assessment is essential before determining the most appropriate course of action. Options may include:Re-Cementing the Existing BridgeIn some cases — particularly where the bridge and supporting teeth are in good condition — the bridge may be cleaned and re-cemented to restore a secure fit. This is often the most straightforward option when cement failure is the primary issue.Repairing or Replacing the BridgeWhere the bridge itself has deteriorated or no longer fits properly, a new bridge may be recommended. The design and material of the replacement will depend on clinical assessment and the condition of the remaining teeth.Treating Underlying ConditionsIf decay, gum disease or other underlying problems have contributed to bridge instability, these conditions may need to be addressed before any replacement restoration is considered, to support a more predictable outcome.Implant-Supported RestorationsWhere traditional bridges are no longer viable, an implant-supported bridge may help restore stability without relying on adjacent natural teeth. Treatment depends on clinical assessment and bone health.

sections.title: When Dental Implants May Be Considered
sections.text: When Dental Implants May Be ConsideredDental implants can replace missing teeth without relying on adjacent natural teeth for support. This may be particularly relevant for patients whose supporting teeth are no longer strong enough to anchor a traditional bridge, or for those who have experienced repeated bridge failures.For patients missing a single tooth, a single tooth implant can provide an independent replacement that does not affect neighbouring teeth. Where multiple teeth are missing, an implant-supported bridge or full arch implant bridge may provide improved long-term stability compared to a traditional tooth-supported bridge.Suitability for dental implant treatment depends on individual clinical factors including bone health, gum condition and overall medical history.
